title: ARIA: Accountable Real-time Intelligence Arbiter

detail.title: ARIA: Accountable Real-time Intelligence Arbiter

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This research was conducted independently with no financial or personal relationships that could influence the work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No ethics approval was required. All experiments use algorithmically generated synthetic data only. No human subjects or personal data were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted as an independent research project.

detail.abstract: Motivation. Public administrations across Europe deploy algorithmic decision-making systems for social welfare, housing, and care. These systems present an accountability challenge that existing approaches cannot address: a system may satisfy every individual fairness constraint while systematically producing unjust outcomes at the population level over time. Problem. Existing fairness definitions-individual fairness, equal opportunity, counterfactual fairness-define fairness as a static property measurable at a single snapshot. None models the feedback loop between human judgment and model retraining-the central vector of temporal injustice. Method. We present ARIA and the Temporally Fair Arbitration System (TFAS) definition comprising five independently falsifiable conditions. The four-subsystem architecture is specified via SysML and BPMN 2.0 [18]. Analysis follows the SSM/CATWOE methodology with explicit adversarial stakeholder modelling. Results. We prove the Temporal Injustice Theorem: if the feedback coefficient δ ≥ 1, decision distributions across demographic groups diverge monotonically regardless of local correctness. We verify analytically (induction) and empirically (n=100,000 applications, B=200 bootstrap replications, multi-group extension to |G|=4). A 15×10 sensitivity analysis characterises violation rates across the (δ, β) space; δ≤0.6 produces the lowest violation fractions. Contribution. TFAS is the first fairness definition incorporating bounded human-reviewer feedback as a formal system parameter. Executable Python implementations of SS1 (SPC monitor), SS2 (escalation FSM), and SS4 (Merkle audit log)-the three formally verified subsystems-provide 30/30 passing unit tests; SS3 is specified in SysML/BPMN and awaits a future HMI prototype. The CI/CD deployment gate provides 1:1 TFAS condition coverage and implements EU AI Act Article 14.

title: Resilience as Strategy: Building a Digitally Enabled Supply Network for Sustainable Competitive Advantage

detail.title: Resilience as Strategy: Building a Digitally Enabled Supply Network for Sustainable Competitive Advantage

detail.abstract: Stryker Corporation operates as a high-performing global medical technology leader with consistent double-digit organic growth. However, its current operating model faces increasing pressure from supply chain fragility, integration strain from frequent acquisitions, a high-performance culture that risks short-term focus, and growing geopolitical and regulatory complexity. This paper presents a validated, execution-ready strategy — the Resilient Digital Supply Network (RDSN) — designed to transform Stryker's supply chain from a cost center into a resilient, intelligent competitive advantage. The RDSN strategy is built on four pillars: AI-enabled digital twin visibility, supplier diversification through near-shore and multi-source partnerships, accelerated modular digital health innovation, and workforce upskilling in data and supply chain analytics. The strategy was validated through five complementary frameworks including SWOT, PEST, Five Forces, Balanced Scorecard, and Key Success Factor analysis. Expected outcomes include 10% or greater annual organic growth, 95% or greater on-time delivery performance, full tier-1 and tier-2 supplier visibility, and 40% reduction in disruption response time. This playbook argues that supply chain resilience is no longer an operational concern — it is a strategic imperative.

title: Inference Cost Curves and Business Model Viability: When Does AI-as-a-Service Break Even?

detail.title: Inference Cost Curves and Business Model Viability: When Does AI-as-a-Service Break Even?
detail.abstract: The viability of AI-powered products and services depends fundamentally on inference economics-the per-query cost of running trained models in production. Yet most strategic analyses of AI business models treat inference cost as a static input rather than a dynamic variable that is declining along predictable experience curves. This paper applies experience curve theory and unit economics analysis to AI inference costs, modeling the tipping points at which AI-powered features become margin-positive across different industry verticals and use cases. The paper introduces the AI Inference Economics Model (AIEM), which demonstrates that inference cost dynamics follow a modified learning curve: costs decline predictably with cumulative scale and hardware improvements, but the rate of decline varies dramatically by model size, modality (text, image, audio, multimodal), and deployment architecture (cloud API, managed cloud, self-hosted, edge). Using publicly reported pricing data from major cloud AI providers and open-source deployment benchmarks, the paper maps breakeven thresholds for AI features across three business model archetypes: AI-enhanced SaaS products, AI-native consumer applications, and AI-powered enterprise workflows. The central finding is that many AI-powered business models that appear uneconomic at current inference costs are 12-18 months from margin viability-creating a strategic window for early movers willing to subsidize usage during the pre-breakeven period. The paper proposes the Pre-Breakeven Subsidy Strategy as a structured approach to exploiting this window, and concludes with implications for product leaders setting AI feature pricing, CFOs evaluating AI business model economics, venture capitalists assessing AI startup viability, and SaaS pricing strategists integrating AI features into existing products.

title: Do users forgive fallible artificial intelligence? The role of confidence, perceived accuracy, and trust in repeated advice utilisation

detail.title: Do users forgive fallible artificial intelligence? The role of confidence, perceived accuracy, and trust in repeated advice utilisation
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports organisational decision-making. Users often remain responsible for evaluating and integrating recommendations from opaque and fallible systems. This creates a repeated interaction setting where performance depends on how advice is utilised over time rather than initial adoption. We study advice utilisation in a controlled laboratory experiment where participants repeatedly interact with imperfect system advice. We examine how confidence, perceived accuracy, and trust shape utilisation and evolve following algorithm errors. Results show three patterns. First, users adapt after errors: utilisation decreases during error rounds but recovers when system performance improves, suggesting recalibration rather than persistent aversion. Users also learn about the system and task, and task-based expectations may bias responses to correct advice. Second, trust remains lower than perceived accuracy and converges only under stable, error-free conditions. This indicates a gap between cognitive performance evaluation and willingness to rely on a system. Third, confidence, perceived accuracy, and trust act as distinct mediators linking system experience to utilisation, while baseline beliefs and stable user characteristics play limited roles. Our findings suggest a rather forgiving and adaptive nature of human-AI interaction and highlight the importance of designing systems that support calibrated use over time.

title: Algorithmic Social Systems as Imbalanced Feedback Networks: An Information-Theoretic Formulation of the Universal Balance Feedback Framework (UBFF)

detail.title: Algorithmic Social Systems as Imbalanced Feedback Networks: An Information-Theoretic Formulation of the Universal Balance Feedback Framework (UBFF)
detail.abstract: We present a rigorous formal analysis of algorithmic social media platforms modeled as feedback-driven dynamical systems that systematically violate informational balance. Grounded in the Universal Balance-Feedback Framework (UBFF), which posits that stable systems require structural integrity, distributional balance, and regulatory (negative) feedback dominance, we develop a state-space formulation of platform dynamics and prove analytically that engagement-maximization induces three pathological regimes: (i) Shannon entropy collapse in content distributions, (ii) monotonically increasing Kullback-Leibler divergence from a ground-truth distribution, and (iii) positive feedback instability characterized by exponential amplification of emotionally salient content. We further provide Lyapunov stability analysis demonstrating that the uncorrected system lacks a stable equilibrium aligned with truth, while a proposed multi-objective corrected objective restores Lyapunov stability. Python simulations corroborate all analytical results. This work provides a unified theoretical bridge between information theory, cybernetic systems theory, cognitive science, and algorithmic governance.

detail.title: Experimental Study on Suspicious Activity Detection based on Network Data Flows

declarations.declarationOfInterest: yes
declarations.ethicsApproval: yes
declarations.funderStatement: yes

detail.abstract:
Today, information technology is developing rapidly, and the daily activities of organizations and individuals are increasingly dependent on the Internet and intranet. With this comes the real problem of cyberattacks, unauthorized access attempts, and an increase in the number of suspicious activities. In this situation, monitoring the flow of data passing through the network and distinguishing between normal and suspicious behavior is an important factor in ensuring information security. 
     This research paper explores the concept of network data flow, the definition of suspicious activity, and the theoretical basis of the main methods for its detection. Suspicious behavior is behavior that deviates from normal user behavior in terms of size, frequency, structure, and timing, and is considered likely to evolve into an attack. The study compares rule-based, statistical and anomaly detection, and machine learning-based methods. 
     The results of the study show that while rule-based methods are easy to implement, they are limited in their ability to detect new types of attacks, while machine learning methods have the advantage of increasing detection accuracy. Therefore, it is concluded that it is necessary to use a flexible and learning-based method in order to perform more effective detection in the future.

title:
Solutions for Frontier AI Safety: The Case for Science-Driven International Cooperation 
Limits of Intergovernmental Initiatives and Conventional Standardization at a Time of Geopolitical and Technological Radical Transformations
affiliations: , University of Tokyo - The University of Tokyo,  and Tsinghua University

detail.title:
Solutions for Frontier AI Safety: The Case for Science-Driven International Cooperation 
Limits of Intergovernmental Initiatives and Conventional Standardization at a Time of Geopolitical and Technological Radical Transformations
detail.abstract: As AI systems and their underlying technologies continue to advance at extraordinary speed, eminent scientists are warning of risks, including extreme risks. While high-profile governmental and intergovernmental initiatives such as AI summits, OECD and UN initiatives have raised hopes, substantial gaps remain between the severity of potential harms and the capacity of these initiatives to address them. Owing to limited research, private sector dominance, minimal investment in AI safety, the voluntary nature of most measures recommended, and the current geopolitical context, it is unlikely that multilateral actions will deliver the effective and timely measures required. Other approaches are needed and are possible. They should not be regarded as alternatives to multilateral efforts, but more as complementary actions to provide concrete and timely solutions that, at some point, can be integrated into the multilateral framework. We take inspiration from historical examples of scientific, technical and organizational collaboration in which a plurality of committed entities has achieved outstanding results. These historical examples show that, even with limited resources, collaboration can enormously increase the collective ability to attain far reaching goals. We propose the creation of an international network led by top scientists and composed of AI labs and research groups, think tanks and other organizations keen to share ideas, materials and data, while pursuing three common goals: 1) advance AI safety science; 2) develop practical techniques, tools, best practices, and technologies for building safe AI systems; 3) create standards for operationalizing the use of these tools and technologies, including conformity assessment mechanisms, to support their widespread adoption.

title: Occupations Hardest for AI to Fully Replace in Developing and Lower-Income Countries

detail.title: Occupations Hardest for AI to Fully Replace in Developing and Lower-Income Countries
detail.abstract: Public discussion often asks which jobs artificial intelligence (AI) will replace and which it cannot replace. For developing and lower-income countries, that binary framing is too crude. This article argues that the more useful question is which occupations are hardest for AI to fully replace in the short-to-medium term. Building on task-based labour economics, recent evidence on generative AI exposure, and research on technology adoption in developing economies, the paper proposes a task-systems perspective that is intentionally closer to a computer science and systems view of deployment than to a purely occupational taxonomy. The central claim is that full substitution requires not only model capability, but also robust perception, embodied or organizational actuation, workflow integration, governance, and a favourable total cost of ownership. In developing and lower-income countries, these conditions frequently fail to hold simultaneously because work is often informal, weakly digitized, infrastructure-constrained, multilingual, trust-intensive, and embedded in unstructured physical environments. As a result, occupations in frontline care, teaching, skilled repair and maintenance, site supervision, smallholder agriculture, last-mile field services, and local intermediation are better understood as AI-augmented than fully replaceable. The paper also argues that low wages can slow labourreplacing deployment, but only in interaction with capital constraints, weak digitization, and high integration costs. By contrast, routine clerical, standardized back-office, and other screenbound rule-based occupations remain more exposed. The contribution of the article is therefore conceptual but practical: it offers a deployment-oriented framework for analyzing where AI substitution is most plausible in lower-resource labour markets and where human work is likely to remain central.

title: From AI Governance to AI Decision Defensibility: A Structural Framework for Accountability in High-Stakes AI Systems

detail.title: From AI Governance to AI Decision Defensibility: A Structural Framework for Accountability in High-Stakes AI Systems

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have rapidly transitioned from experimental tools to embedded decision engines across finance, healthcare, public administration, and enterprise operations. While governance frameworks have evolved to address transparency, fairness, and explainability, a critical gap remains: the ability of institutions to defend AI-enabled decisions under scrutiny. This paper introduces AI Decision Defensibility as a structural capability that extends beyond governance compliance. Defensibility is defined as the institutional capacity to reconstruct, justify, and defend AI-enabled decisions across legal, regulatory, operational, and reputational contexts. The paper advances a structural framework linking defensibility to robustness across governance, data, model, and operational domains, and highlights the role of human capability in realizing accountability. It argues that defensibility represents the next phase of AI governance; shifting the focus from principles to provable institutional accountability.

title: Temporal Dynamics of Structural Value in Tension-Based Systems: Trajectories V(t) in the ZTH Model

detail.title: Temporal Dynamics of Structural Value in Tension-Based Systems: Trajectories V(t) in the ZTH Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or personal data and therefore does not require ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
In tension-based systems, static assessments of structural value may hide important temporal patterns. Building on the ZTH model introduced in previous articles, this paper examines the temporal evolution of structural value V(t) generated by time-varying tension vectors τ(t). Structural value trajectories are defined by applying the same multiplicative formulation as in the static case at each time step, using intrinsic value Vi = 1 as a neutral reference. We characterize typical temporal regimes, including transient excursions around the intrinsic state, progressive drift towards degraded or amplified configurations, and oscillatory behaviors. Simple dynamic indicators such as time spent below Vi, excursion depth and recovery time are introduced to summarize these regimes. Stylized scenarios illustrate how different patterns of tension change produce distinct trajectories V(t) despite similar initial and final values. This dynamic perspective extends the ZTH framework beyond static snapshots and prepares the ground for analyzing perceived value trajectories Vp(t).

This paper is also available on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18700813

title: The SEO Floor: Measuring Google Rank Distribution of AI-Cited Pages

detail.title: The SEO Floor: Measuring Google Rank Distribution of AI-Cited Pages
detail.abstract: Whether Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) is a discipline distinct from Search Engine Optimization (SEO), or merely SEO repackaged, has been debated since the rise of consumer-facing AI chat platforms. Empirical resolution requires measuring two things: where on Google's search results AI-cited pages actually rank, and whether content features pre-registered as "GEO levers" predict citation independently of Google rank. We collected 100,411 AI citation events from four production AI platforms (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Google AI Mode) across 2,000 user queries, and assembled a comparison pool of 165,661 unique URLs from Google top-100 SERPs for the same queries. Combining the citation corpus with the comparison pool yields 114,729 (URL, query) observations for a mixedeffects logistic regression of citation probability on Google rank tier and GEO composite score, with query random intercepts. Headline finding 1: While 75.4% of citation events are aggregated to pages outside Google's top 30, per-page citation odds span a 34× range across rank tiers-a top-3 page is 7.82× more likely to be cited (OR vs Tier 3, 95% CI 7.28-8.39) while a rank 31-100 page is 4× less likely (OR=0.23, 95% CI 0.22-0.24). The aggregate "75% deep-tier" figure is a denominator artifact: the internet beyond rank 30 has vastly more pages than the top 30, so even at low per-page citation probability the absolute count of deep-tier citations dominates. The two figures must be reported together. Headline finding 2: A pre-registered GEO composite of seven content features adds small but real predictive power above Google rank (Z-sum OR=1.06; PCA-1 OR=1.15 per 1 SD), driven primarily by schema markup (OR=1.31). Statistics density and list structure show small positive effects after methodological correction; heading density shows a small negative effect. Headline finding 3: The 75% Tier-4+ aggregate is overwhelmingly composed of URLs Google ranks beyond #100 (90% of "Tier 4" events)-not the 31-100 band that the H2 regression speaks to-and these deep-tier citations are 77% one-hit-wonders cited by a single AI platform, with sharp platform divergence on user-generated-content tolerance (Claude 0.6% UGC in deep tier; Perplexity 24%). The Lily-Ray-aligned framing ("AI citation is gated by Google ranking") is empirically supported, with schema markup emerging as the strongest single content-feature predictor inside the gate; whether AI parsers consume schema directly or schema is a proxy for site quality is unresolved by observational data and is the target of a planned follow-up interventional study.

title: EU AI Act Readiness: A Structured Screening of 50 European AI Companies

detail.title: EU AI Act Readiness: A Structured Screening of 50 European AI Companies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Sprinkling Act, an independent pre-conformity advisory firm operating in the EU AI Act compliance market. No commercial relationship existed between Sprinkling Act and any of the 50 European AI companies analyzed in this study at the time of the research.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding. The research was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Independent structured analysis of EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) regulatory positioning across 50 European AI companies in HealthTech/MedTech, FinTech/InsurTech, HRTech/EdTech, and B2B SaaS/Industrial sectors, covering 15+ countries (FR, DE, BE, NL, PL, DK, CH, IE, UK, and others). Screening conducted between 10 and 12 April 2026.

Each company was screened against a 6-gate regulatory framework mapping to Articles 5, 6(1), 6(2) + Annex III, 50, 51/53, and 6(3) of the Regulation. The screening relied exclusively on publicly available information (company websites, CE mark disclosures, ACPR/ECB/MDR/IVDR filings, LinkedIn, press releases). No company was contacted and no confidential data was accessed. The 6-gate framework used in this screening is publicly documented at sprinklingact.com/methodology.

Key findings:

  • 74% of screened companies trigger high-risk classification under Art. 6(1) or Art. 6(2) + Annex III
  • 96% have no public AI Act regulatory position
  • 44% have unaddressed Art. 50 transparency obligations
  • 34% integrate GPAI models (Art. 3(63)) without documented Art. 50, Art. 26, or Art. 53 obligations
  • 0 of 14 companies holding existing sectoral certifications (CE MDR, CE-IVD, ACPR banking licence) have mapped the additional AI Act layer
  • 1 company raises an open question under Art. 5(1)(g) (biometric categorization in publicly accessible spaces)

The report includes aggregate results, sector breakdowns, five anonymized critical cases, a deployer cascade analysis under Art. 26, an enforcement timeline (with Art. 6(2) + Annex III obligations becoming applicable on 2 August 2026), and the full methodology. Sprinkling Act operates as a pre-conformity advisory firm in this market; no commercial relationship with any company listed existed at the time of this analysis.

This report is freely available to download, share, and reference with attribution.

title: Beyond the Degree: A Decentralized Framework for Nano-Credential-Based Human Capital Development

detail.title: Beyond the Degree: A Decentralized Framework for Nano-Credential-Based Human Capital Development
detail.abstract: University degrees have historically served as the preeminent conduit for cultivating workforce capabilities and communicating employability signals to hiring entities. Yet, the precipitous escalation of educational expenditures, the contraction of wage premiums associated with academic credentials, and the hastening depreciation of occupational proficiencies have collectively precipitated skepticism regarding the enduring efficacy of this established paradigm. This inquiry formulates a theoretical schema for Decentralized Peer-to-Peer Certification (DPPC): a cryptographically secured framework that deploys composable micro-attestations to enable instantaneous, fraud-resistant validation of professional competencies. By interlacing scholarly contributions from educational economics, digital badge ecosystems, and distributed computing architectures, the investigation undertakes a systematic juxtaposition of hierarchical versus decentralized credentialing modalities. The analysis posits that DPPC holds substantial capacity to attenuate structural inefficiencies pervading current attestation practices, refine the precision of labor market allocation mechanisms, and extend economic participation opportunities across geographically dispersed populations. While cognizant of governance ambiguities and infrastructural impediments, the manuscript advances the argument that decentralized attestation ecosystems may function synergistically with and under select conditions, partially supplant orthodox degree-centric arrangements.

title: Justice Decision Observability™ (JDO™): Field Definition for Execution-Layer Governance in AI-Supported Justice Systems (Public Edition, Version 2.0)

detail.title: Justice Decision Observability™ (JDO™): Field Definition for Execution-Layer Governance in AI-Supported Justice Systems (Public Edition, Version 2.0)
detail.abstract:
Justice Decision Observability™ (JDO™) defines and advances an emerging governance discipline focused on improving visibility into how human decisions are interpreted, formed, and executed within AI-supported and operational justice environments.

While existing approaches emphasize system outputs, compliance structures, and post-incident review, they may provide limited visibility into how decisions are formed at the point where authority is exercised. This publication introduces the concept of the Decision Visibility Gap the space between signal and outcome where human interpretation, discretion, and institutional context influence results.

This Field Definition establishes the conceptual scope of JDO™, introduces its core capabilities, and outlines the operational methodologies used to observe, reconstruct, and analyze decision environments over time. These include Deployment Context Risk Review (DCRR™), Critical Event Governance Review (CEGR™), and the Decision Risk Pattern Index (DRPI™).

Justice Decision Observability™ operates as a complementary governance approach. It does not evaluate system performance, assign liability, or determine compliance. Instead, it provides a structured method for documenting how decisions are formed, supporting improved visibility, reconstruction, and understanding of decision pathways.

Version Control Notice (Version 2.0 — Public Edition)
This publication (Version 2.0, Public Edition) supersedes all prior versions of the Justice Decision Observability™ (JDO™) Field Definition. Earlier versions may not reflect current language, scope, or boundary conditions and should not be relied upon for interpretation, reference, or citation. Only the most current version should be used. Prior versions are retained for record and version history purposes only.

title: The Informational Worldview of Chinese and Western Astronomy: From Ancient Calendrical Models to Cosmic Information Networks

detail.title: The Informational Worldview of Chinese and Western Astronomy: From Ancient Calendrical Models to Cosmic Information Networks

keywords: Comparative history of Chinese and Western astronomy

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a core thesis: the essence of ancient Chinese and Greco-Arabic astronomical systems lies not merely in "science" or "superstition," but in their roles as early "large models" or "specialized computers" for processing "cosmic information." Through a systematic comparison of their fundamental divergences in origin, core canons, conceptual frameworks, algorithms, and geometric models, this paper reveals that the traditional Chinese periodic-numerical model (zhouqi-shuzi moxing, 周期性-数字模型) and the Western geometric-physical model (jihe-wuli moxing, 几何-物理模型) correspond respectively to two paradigms of information processing: the "algebraic-semantic network" and the "geometric-physical simulator." The article delves further into their "encoding-decoding" mechanisms, interpreting spatiotemporal coordinates, calendrical constants, and tabular algorithms (China) versus cosmic structures, geometric models, and trigonometric deduction (West) as distinct information encoding systems. Finally, it explores the potential for cross-temporal dialogue between these ancient "information ontologies" and contemporary theories of informational cosmology, complexity science, and digital humanities, arguing that the "Eastward Transmission of Western Learning" during the late Ming and early Qing periods was essentially a collision and translation of two informational paradigms. This paper aims to transcend the "internalist" limitations of historiography of astronomy, offering a new interdisciplinary analytical framework for understanding the relationships between science and culture, history and information.

title: Interpreting Environmental Protection: How Canadian Public Servants View the Mitigation Hierarchy

detail.title: Interpreting Environmental Protection: How Canadian Public Servants View the Mitigation Hierarchy

declarations.ethicsApproval: The interview process was authorized by the University of Queensland Human Research Ethics approval process (Project Number 2021/HE002837).
declarations.funderStatement: Financial support for this study was provided by the Policy Dialogue program of the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada.

detail.abstract: The mitigation hierarchy (avoid-minimize-remediate onsite-offset) is a well-accepted, risk-based framework for mitigating the biodiversity impacts of development. There are concerns, however, that the hierarchy is not properly applied in practice, that offsetting may be employed too readily, detracting from substantive on-site conservation measures. To examine how the hierarchy is operationalized in Canada's federal resource regulatory regime, we undertook a policy review and conducted 36 interviews with officials in eight federal entities and stakeholders who interact with federal processes. Transcripts of interviews were coded for themes. Findings revealed a lack of a unified approach to the hierarchy, reflected both in inconsistent expression in policy statements and in the perspectives voiced by interview participants. While many participants shared the concern that offsetting may be used inappropriately, few reported having directly observed that in their work. More commonly, participants opined that offset requirements were an incentive to redouble efforts to avoid and minimize impacts within their sphere of influence. Interviews also showed a wide disparity of opinions as to who is responsible for assuring compliance with the mitigation hierarchy, as well as concern about the late stage-often postpermitting-at which mitigation requirements are determined. The clarity and consistency of policies, terminology, timing of application, and responsibilities were identified as important elements encouraging adherence to the mitigation hierarchy. These findings reinforce the importance of a unified federal policy framework that supports greater clarity, consistency and accountability in decision-making.

title: Beyond a Bimodal Southern Democratic Constitutionalism

detail.title: Beyond a Bimodal Southern Democratic Constitutionalism

publicationDetails.detailsText: Univ. of Wisconsin Legal Studies Research Paper No. 1914
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Wisconsin Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Theunis Roux has made an important contribution in stimulating a debate over the nature of “Southern Democratic Constitutionalism” (SDC). Roux describes two  approaches to SDC which he places in dialogue with one another but argues that they together reflect and contribute towards a single dynamic version of SDC. While the interlocutors in this debate engage in a sophisticated theoretical discussion at a high level of abstraction, I intend in my response to dwell on a few contextual issues that I feel might enrich the discussion, including questions of legal continuity, urban-rural divisions and the role of both the legal profession and legal education more generally. Before turning to these contextual issues, I do however want to question the decision to frame the debate over “southern democratic constitutionalism” as a bimodal discussion rather than as a spectrum of ideological and legal alternatives.

Much of the present debate, which Roux is responding to, focuses on distinguishing between a “liberal” versus a potentially more “de-colonial” notion of constitutionalism.
This dichotomy ignores a variety of constitutional forms that exist in the global South. Variation exists even within the constitutional orders Roux uses as examples in his debate. Apart from different notions of democracy—including the less than democratic forms that exist—there are numerous experiences of democratic constitutionalism today, including in Africa. These include Ghana since 1992, Kenya and Zambia as well as cases across South-East Asia, such as the Philippines and Indonesia that might provide additional dimensions to a debate over SDC. Roux’s dichotomy also tends to preclude an adequate engagement with the rich, critical, and ongoing debate over constitutionalism in Africa, beyond South Africa.

title: Toward Issuer-Based Certification Of Qualified Small Business Stock

detail.title: Toward Issuer-Based Certification Of Qualified Small Business Stock
detail.abstract: Section 1202 of the Internal Revenue Code allows shareholders of qualified small businesses to exclude millions in capital gains from taxation. Despite the provision's enormous cost, the reporting regime remains remarkably thin: shareholders self-certify eligibility on their tax returns with no required documentation from the issuing corporation. This article proposes shifting the burden of establishing QSBS eligibility from individual shareholders to issuing corporations through a mandatory Form 1099-QSBS filed at issuance as a condition of QSBS status, supplemented by annual status reports. The proposal is justified on both practical and normative grounds. Practically, it aligns compliance with the party possessing the relevant information. Normatively, it operates as a screening mechanism:  if neither the corporation nor the investor was aware of Section 1202 at the time of investment, the exclusion conferred a windfall rather than catalyzing investment. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act's 2025 expansion of Section 1202 — which added no new reporting requirements — makes these reforms more urgent. This article also addresses potential objections concerning compliance burden, investment deterrence, and implementation authority.

title: THE GEODESIC ENTROPY COLLAPSE ENGINE™

detail.title: THE GEODESIC ENTROPY COLLAPSE ENGINE™
detail.abstract: This working paper presents the Geodesic Entropy Collapse Engine™ (GECE™), the mathematical architecture of identity resolution under constraint in Human Locomotor Dynamics™ (HLD™) and Combat Engineering™. Filed as Matrix Concepts Claim III, the GECE™ is the computational framework that implements the governing equation of HLD™: Outcome = argmin(Objective | Identity + Constraints + Environment). The GECE™ computes the geodesic path along which a fighter's identity collapses under constraint toward its confirmed elemental rank. The paper presents the formal definition, the structural isomorphism with AlphaFold, the geodesic path properties, and five deployment domains.

title: THE HEISENBERG IDENTITY PRINCIPLE™

detail.title: THE HEISENBERG IDENTITY PRINCIPLE™
detail.abstract: This working paper presents the Heisenberg Identity Principle™, a formally documented epistemological principle of Human Locomotor Dynamics™. The principle draws a structural parallel between Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle in quantum mechanics and the measurement problem of combat identity assessment: the act of applying constraint to reveal identity is the combat itself. The paper presents the formal statement, the precise limits of the parallel, and the asymmetric intelligence property that distinguishes the UMAC™ assessment from classical measurement problems.

detail.abstract: Eastern Afghanistan is characterized by diverse agro-climatic conditions, ranging from lowland semiarid plains to high-altitude zones with higher precipitation. This review examines the potential of dryland fruit cultivation, focusing on pomegranate (Punica granatum L.) and date palm (Phoenix dactylifera L.), in semiarid and arid provinces including Nangarhar, Kunar, Laghman, and Nuristan. Both species are naturally adapted to water-limited, high-temperature, and saline conditions through physiological and biochemical mechanisms such as osmotic adjustment, drought and heat tolerance, and salinity resilience. Pomegranate thrives on marginal, well-drained soils, whereas date palm tolerates lowland irrigated and moderately saline soils, allowing for efficient use of scarce water and land resources. Irrigation infrastructure from rivers supports orchard expansion, enabling multiple cropping cycles and improved agricultural productivity. Despite challenges related to water scarcity, soil salinity, and climatic variability, the cultivation of these crops contributes to food security, income generation, livelihood diversification, and ecological sustainability. The review highlights the strategic role of pomegranate and date palm as cornerstone species for developing resilient dryland horticulture systems in eastern Afghanistan, providing insights for sustainable agricultural practices and policy interventions.

title: Global Governance of Peruvian Mineral Value Chains *

detail.title: Global Governance of Peruvian Mineral Value Chains *
detail.abstract: Peru is one of the world's most important mining economies and a strategic supplier of minerals essential for the global energy transition. However, the governance conditions under which Peruvian minerals enter international markets are shifting rapidly from voluntary corporate social responsibility to mandatory, audit-driven ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) assurance. This paper examines the resulting "legislative disconnect" between Peru's domestic framework-focused on site-based environmental licensing-and the emerging extraterritorial paradigm led by the European Union (CSRD, CSDDD, CBAM). We analyze the role of Switzerland as a primary commercial gatekeeper and develop a conceptual ESG risk-mapping framework. Crucially, the study provides a quantitative proof of concept through a Monte Carlo simulation, demonstrating how integrated ESG data capacity acts as the primary mitigator against market-access risks. The findings suggest that domestic compliance is no longer sufficient; maintaining commercial legitimacy now requires the institutionalization of "ESG Controllers" and interoperable data architectures capable of providing reasonable assurance to global value chain actors.

The essay contrasts the ANC's transformative vision—which sought justiciable social and economic rights and mechanisms to redress apartheid-era inequalities—with the apartheid government's preservationist Law Commission proposals that emphasized robust property protections and rejected enforceable socio-economic guarantees.

Before describing a proposed transformational tax, this chapter first presents a brief historical survey of different forms of wealth taxes in several countries. This comparative analysis demonstrates that capital levies have been a more effective means of ensuring redistribution compared to annual wealth taxes. The conclusion to be drawn from this is that any plans for a transformational tax to address the legacies of apartheid and gross inequality must consider the imposition of a capital
levy. The final section of this chapter applies the analysis of former experiences with capital levies to imagine the outlines of a transformational tax for South Africa.

title: Phoenix Capital Compounding: Why Rebalancing May Be the Wrong Default

detail.title: Phoenix Capital Compounding: Why Rebalancing May Be the Wrong Default

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available financial market data and does not involve human participants or personal data. Ethical approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Periodic rebalancing — resetting position sizes to equal weights at fixed intervals — is the standard capital management convention in most systematic equity frameworks. For selective deployment strategies,
periodic rebalancing can create a compounding drag by repeatedly redistributing capital away from the positions that generated it.

We examine the compounding logic of a per-symbol capital architecture, in which realized gains remain allocated to the symbol that generated them and are redeployed into that symbol’s next qualifying entry.
This approach, which we term Phoenix Capital Compounding, allows winning positions to compound their gains forward while naturally reducing capital allocated to underperforming symbols — without requiring
any active intervention.

Using the Phoenix Equity Timing Strategy (PETS) as an empirical reference, we demonstrate that the per-symbol compounding architecture produces three structural properties: it reinforces signal-based
capital weighting, it eliminates the rebalancing tax on compounding winners, and it creates a self-correcting mechanism that reduces exposure to underperforming symbols over time. We conclude
that for selective deployment strategies, periodic rebalancing is not a neutral convention — it is a compounding cost that is rarely quantified but consistently present.

title: Synchronized Stress Relative Value: Public-Neutral Option Books under Latent Stress Compression

detail.title: Synchronized Stress Relative Value: Public-Neutral Option Books under Latent Stress Compression
detail.abstract: This paper translates latent-stress compression into a listed-option relative-value construction. The trading coordinate is the wedge between index-implied synchronization and an adapted realized synchronization benchmark generated from the latent Volterra-Perron stress state. When index options embed more synchronized stress than admissible single-name variance carriers justify, the book is short index convexity and long carrier-basket convexity. The construction has four components: an implied synchronization coordinate from the index-versus-single-name variance decomposition; a carrier map based on stress co-movement, network pressure, relative variance cheapness, and tradability; a finite listed-option book chosen under public-neutrality constraints and a stress-convexity hedge ratio; and a lower-bound sellability rule with book-risk denominator, mandate caps, cost reserves, danger-state reserves, and capital-at-risk controls. The implementation uses listed OptionMetrics contracts, validated underlying prices, and rolling Oxford-Man Perron stress states. In the 2001--2018 execution ledger, the balanced lower-bound specification forms 1,496 sign-positive candidate books and allocates capital to 906 rows over 805 active dates. At 1x bid-ask costs it reports total execution P&L of 24.567 million, annualized Sharpe of 3.958, expected-shortfall loss of 23,683, and max drawdown of 364,148. The result is reported as an audited sample-developed implementation, not an unused-sample trading record; its main discipline is the adapted lower-bound gate, leakage audit, cost-stress grid, mandate frontier, dormancy audit, and capital-realism report.

detail.abstract: The voluntary carbon market has failed structurally. Over two decades of operation, the market's core instruments-carbon offset credits-have been shown to systematically over-credit emissions reductions, reward non-additional projects, and price themselves as speculative assets rather than as representations of physical atmospheric reality. Reform efforts, from strengthened verification standards to integrity frameworks, have addressed implementation weaknesses without resolving the underlying design problem: a traded credit is the wrong instrument for accounting a physical atmospheric stock. This paper diagnoses the four mechanisms through which the voluntary carbon market fails, examines why standards-based reform cannot resolve them, and proposes the design requirements for an alternative-a non-speculative offset protocol in which supply is determined by the cumulative physical stock of atmospheric CO₂, price is set by a custodial trust, and permanence is secured through direct physical asset acquisition. The paper concludes with a research agenda for the architecture, governance, and verification methodology such a protocol requires.

title: FROM DIGITAL STATE TO PREVENTIVE GOVERNANCE: A THEORY OF REAL-TIME ANTI-CORRUPTION ARCHITECTURE

detail.title: FROM DIGITAL STATE TO PREVENTIVE GOVERNANCE: A THEORY OF REAL-TIME ANTI-CORRUPTION ARCHITECTURE
detail.abstract:
FROM DIGITAL STATE TO PREVENTIVE GOVERNANCE: A THEORY OF REAL-TIME ANTI-CORRUPTION ARCHITECTURE
Traditional anti-corruption strategies, rooted in principal-agent models, focus on post-hoc detection and punishment, yet consistently fail against adaptive, systemic corruption networks in modern digital economies. This paper introduces the Theory of Real-Time Anti-Corruption Architecture (RTACA), arguing that corruption has evolved from discrete transactional events to continuous, networked processes that demand preventive rather than reactive governance through integrated digital state infrastructure.
RTACA proposes a comprehensive three-layer framework: (1) Data Layer enabling real-time anomaly detection across financial, procurement, and social datasets; (2) Institutional Layer deploying automated early warning systems and independent algorithmic responses; (3) Social Layer facilitating citizen participation, quadratic voting, and vulnerable group protections.
The theory models corruption as a dynamic network disrupted by blockchain auditing, predictive analytics, and smart contracts. Formal hypotheses predict 40-60% corruption risk reduction in emerging markets within five years, testable via cross-national panel data. Policy implications balance technological prevention with democratic safeguards, offering scalable blueprints for CBDC-era governance beyond traditional reforms.

title: Truth-Telling Near Ruin: The Revelation Principle Under Absorbing Exit
affiliations: Southern Illinois University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Truth-Telling Near Ruin: The Revelation Principle Under Absorbing Exit
detail.abstract: Standard mechanism design assumes agents survive every outcome. When the mechanism's action can destroy the agent, this assumption fails and four results follow. Incentive compatibility is violated whenever truth-telling triggers destruction, because no transfer compensates for death and the agent lies to survive. An indirect mechanism that screens by survival, acting without soliciting reports and conditioning future allocations on who is alive, achieves outcomes that no incentive-compatible direct mechanism can replicate. The principal's payoff under survival screening strictly exceeds the payoff under any report-contingent direct mechanism when the information rent saved plus the ruin surplus exceeds the forgone contribution of destroyed types. The positive framework replaces individual type paths with the surviving type distribution as the principal's state variable. The survival-filtered impulse response, the Fréchet derivative of this distribution with respect to the action, characterizes the principal's optimal trade-off through an envelope theorem over surviving distributions. An application to bank stress testing shows that regulators who test can strictly dominate regulators who ask.

title: Stubborn by design: When past rewards keep agents betting on known losses
affiliations: University of New South Wales, UNSW Australia Business School, School of Banking and Finance, London School of Economics and University of New South Wales (UNSW) - Decision Neuroscience Laboratory

detail.title: Stubborn by design: When past rewards keep agents betting on known losses
detail.abstract: Why would rational agents cling to reward sources they know have turned harmful? In a preregistered experiment, participants knew whether betting had positive or negative expected value. After profitable streaks, they kept betting in known-loss sessions, relative to a Control Treatment without that reward streak. The anomaly intensifies under uncertainty. Combining panel logits and structural choice modeling, the staged identification strategy points beyond standard accounts—including faulty beliefs, inertia, house-money effects, fatigue, and model-free or hybrid reinforcement learning—and toward Pavlovian theory: past rewards trigger reflex approach toward gambling cues, perturbing rational agency, particularly when the cue-reward link is uncertain.

title: Policy Uncertainty, Rent Seeking and Tax Responsiveness of Firms: Implications for Efficiency and Optimal Taxation
affiliations: School of Economic, Political and Policy Sciences and Joint Committee on Taxation, US Congress

detail.title: Policy Uncertainty, Rent Seeking and Tax Responsiveness of Firms: Implications for Efficiency and Optimal Taxation
detail.abstract: We posit that rent seeking is a largely neglected cost of policy uncertainty. We build on the insights of William Baumol (1990), who contends that entrepreneurship can be not only productive, but also unproductive or even destructive. We argue that policy uncertainty increases the expected returns from rent seeking and thus yields more of this unproductive or destructive entrepreneurship. We develop a model and empirically test the hypothesis that firms respond to tax policy uncertainty by increasing their political contributions and lobbying expenditures. Policy uncertainty is a signal that politicians are receptive to policy changes. With little policy uncertainty, higher returns may be sought from investing in productive activities. However, when government is receptive to policy changes, rent seeking (through lobbying, Political Action Committees, etc.) may offer higher rates of return. Our work also has implications for tax policy. Piketty, Saez and Stantcheva (2014) show that optimal tax rates depend heavily on both the responsiveness of top incomes to taxes and to the avenues by which they respond. We look at the implications of uncertainty and rent seeking for optimal tax rates. We argue that, to the extent that rent seeking targets tax preferences, higher marginal tax rates will raise incentives for rent seeking, increasing the excess burden from taxation. However, to the extent that rent seeking targets government policies not tied to taxes, our results are in line with the Piketty, Saez and Stantcheva bargaining model, which shows that a higher optimal top tax rate discourages rent seeking. Thus, the responsiveness of rent seeking to policy uncertainty, as well as the relative responsiveness of rent seeking targeting tax versus non-tax policies, independent of uncertainty, both have important implications for optimal taxation.

title: Medical Research Funding, Legislative Transparency, and Representation of "Invisible" Disabilities Among U.S. Veterans

Using publicly available data provided by the government along with private sector statistics, we evaluate three main areas in need of attention; the allocation of medical research funds, representation bias among disabled veteran narratives, and the transparency of government allocated funds within veteran disability research and development.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces two new disciplines to the quality management and investment communities: Quality of Operational Continuity (QoOC) and Quality of Valuation (QoV). Despite a century of advancement in quality management theory and practice, no standardized methodology exists to link quality management system maturity to enterprise valuation in the context of mergers, acquisitions, and private equity investment. This gap contributes directly to the 70% to 90% failure rate of M&A transactions. Both concepts derive from a universal definition of quality, Quality = Mindset in Action, first published by the author. QoOC provides a structured framework for assessing an organization's ability to sustain, scale, and defend its operations through periods of stress, transition, and regulatory scrutiny. QoV translates that assessment into a mathematically defensible adjustment to enterprise value. Together, these disciplines establish a new category in the intersection of quality management, operational due diligence, and corporate valuation.

title: MÜHENDİSLİK EKONOMİSİ - Engineering Economy

detail.title: MÜHENDİSLİK EKONOMİSİ - Engineering Economy
detail.abstract:
Bu çalışma, orta gelir tuzağından çıkmak isteyen ülkeler için Mühendislik Ekonomisi kavramını yeni bir paradigma olarak tanıtmaktadır. Türkiye'nin 2001 sonrası ekonomik yörüngesi ile Güney Kore'nin düşük gelirli ekonomiden yüksek gelirli ekonomiye başarılı geçişine dayanan çalışma, geleneksel çerçevelerin —ister Washington Konsensüsü'nün piyasa liberalleşmesi reçeteleri olsun, ister kurumsalcı eleştiri tek başına— yetersiz kaldığını savunur. Bunun yerine ekonomiyi statik bir denge problemi değil, sürekli kalibrasyon gerektiren dinamik bir kontrol sistemi olarak ele almayı önerir. Çalışma, küresel ekonomik rejimleri karakterize etmek için bir yol-zemini metaforu (otoban, tali yol, off-road) geliştirir ve risk sermayesi oluşumu, regülasyon kum havuzları, teknoloji odaklı sanayi politikası ve beşeri sermaye gelişimini kapsayan on bir birbirine bağlı politika sütunu sunar. İçsel büyüme teorisi (Romer), kurumsal iktisat (Acemoğlu), yakalama yazını (Lee), sibernetik sistemler kuramı (Wiener) ve Schumpeter'in yaratıcı yıkım kavramının sentezinden hareketle çerçeve, makroekonomik araçları kontrol-mühendisliği analojileriyle yeniden kavramsallaştırır: faiz oranları enerji gradyanı, maliye politikası enerji akışı, döviz kuru denge motoru ve regülasyon adaptif süspansiyon olarak ele alınır.

Analiz, Türkiye'nin yapısal zorluğunun yalnızca kurumsal zayıflık değil, baskın işletme yapılarından kaynaklanan sistemik bir AR-GE talebi yokluğu olduğunu ve bunun geleneksel reformların kıramayacağı bir kısır döngü yarattığını ortaya koymaktadır. Holdingler teknolojiyi yabancı ortaklarından alarak içsel AR-GE iştahını köreltmiş, KOBİ'ler düşük katma değerli üretimde sıkışıp kalmıştır. ABD-Çin teknolojik rekabetinden doğan yedi fırsat penceresi belirlenmekte ve aşamalı bir uygulama yol haritası önerilmektedir.

Mühendislik Ekonomisi, klasik ekonominin "tek araç–tek hedef" anlayışını terk eder: faiz çekiş kontrolü, döviz kuru pusula, enflasyon arızadan çok sinyaldir. Bu paradigma, off-road küresel ortamda Türkiye'nin orta gelir tuzağından çıkışı için makro ölçekte Kore'nin sanayi disiplinini, mikro ölçekte Silikon Vadisi'nin girişimci ekosistemini hedefleyen operasyonel bir çerçeve sunar.

This paper introduces the concept of Engineering Economy as a new paradigm for understanding and managing macroeconomic policy in middle-income countries seeking to escape the middle-income trap.  The paper develops a road-surface metaphor (highway, side-road, off-road) to characterize different global economic regimes and presents eleven interconnected policy pillars spanning venture capital formation, regulatory sandboxes, technology-focused industrial policy, and human capital development. By synthesizing insights from endogenous growth theory (Romer), institutional economics (Acemoğlu), the catching-up literature (Lee), cybernetic systems theory (Wiener), and Schumpeterian creative destruction, the framework reconceptualizes macroeconomic instruments through control-engineering analogies: interest rates as energy gradients, fiscal policy as energy flow, exchange rates as balance motors, and regulation as adaptive suspension.

The Engineering Economy abandons the "one-instrument, one-target" logic of classical economics: interest rates function as traction control, exchange rates as a compass rather than target, inflation as a diagnostic signal rather than malfunction. This paradigm offers an operational framework for Türkiye's escape from the middle-income trap—targeting Korea's industrial discipline at the macro level and Silicon Valley's entrepreneurial dynamism at the micro level—in today's off-road environment that rewards adaptive design over static equilibrium.

title: When Credit Stops Clearing Markets: Affordability Ceilings and Volume Driven Systemic Stress

detail.title: When Credit Stops Clearing Markets: Affordability Ceilings and Volume Driven Systemic Stress
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of affordability ceilings in credit stabilized markets. It argues that rising prices can be sustained for extended periods when credit expansion, longer maturities, and relaxed payment assumptions convert strained purchasing capacity into completed transactions. These mechanisms, however, do not eliminate affordability constraints; they defer them. Once borrowing limits, payment tolerances, or lender risk thresholds bind, adjustment shifts from prices to quantities. The resulting contraction is not primarily reputational or sentiment driven, but arithmetic: transactions fail to clear at prevailing terms. In high fixed cost systems such as durable goods manufacturing, supplier networks, and distribution channels, declining volume propagates through margins, inventories, employment, balance sheets, and credit conditions. The paper distinguishes affordability driven contractions from ordinary cyclical downturns: cyclical slowdowns defer demand, whereas affordability ceilings exclude demand until prices, costs, incomes, or financing structures realign. The analysis contributes a quantity channel account of systemic stress in markets previously stabilized by credit expansion.

title: Governance, Recognition, and Valuation in Tokenized Finance: A Canonical Framework for Financial Infrastructure and Conditions of Economic Admissibility

detail.title: Governance, Recognition, and Valuation in Tokenized Finance: A Canonical Framework for Financial Infrastructure and Conditions of Economic Admissibility

keywords: Time Value of Money JEL Classification Codes: G21

detail.abstract:
Tokenized financial systems do not become economically admissible at the point of technological deployment, but at the point at which they are governed, recognized, and valued within the structure of financial markets. This paper introduces a canonical, constraint-based framework for evaluating how tokenized financial systems become economically admissible. The framework integrates the Evidence Coverage Framework (ECF), Governance through R Gate™, Recognition, and the Tokenized Valuation Pathway (TVP™) into a unified, non-invertible sequence: E(S) → G(S) → R(S) → V(S).

The Tokenized Valuation Pathway (TVP™) reflects the operationalization of the Time Value Principle within tokenized financial systems. Within this structure, evidence establishes evaluability, governance determines admissibility, recognition governs institutional participation, and valuation reflects economic consequence. The analysis demonstrates that technological capability alone does not produce financial relevance; instead, systems must pass through institutional constraints and coordinated acceptance before influencing economic outcomes. 

The framework is developed in the context of evolving regulatory regimes, including recent U.S. rulemaking and global policy efforts addressing stablecoins and digital financial infrastructure. Observed patterns across financial institutions—including staged adoption, governance-first sequencing, and valuation discipline-are consistent with the structure formalized in the Canon. 

This paper contributes a generalizable model for analyzing tokenized financial systems, clarifying the relationship between innovation, regulation, and market integration. It provides a foundation for understanding why adoption is often incremental, why valuation remains anchored in established financial principles, and how institutional coordination determines whether technological systems become economically operative.

detail.abstract: Micro and small enterprises in the Meta department of Colombia face structural gaps in formalization, administrative management, and export capabilities that limit their integration into higher value-added markets. Addressing this challenge, the Meta Go Global program —held on October 29, 2025, at the Cámara de Comercio de Villavicencio— was designed as a strategic articulation platform between Universidad Santo Tomás, the regional business sector, and governmental and institutional entities. The study adopted a mixed methodological approach, combining quantitative instruments —online QR forms with Likert scales, sales tabulation, and attendance records— with qualitative techniques such as on-site interviews, direct observation, and follow-up matrices, applied to a sample of 48 advised companies and approximately 500 attendees. Results show satisfaction levels above 85%, the formulation of personalized roadmaps for 16 SMEs, the consolidation of over 300 interinstitutional interactions, and the identification of sectors with high export potential, particularly agro-industry, specialty foods, and tourism. This technical report contributes an integrated analysis of the event as a replicable model of academia–business–government articulation, grounded in the Triple Helix framework and dynamic capabilities theory, with concrete implications for the design of territorial business development policies in intermediate regions of Colombia and Latin America.

title: Reassessing Anonymization as a Privacy Control Under Modern Adversarial Conditions and Regulatory Logging Requirements

detail.title: Reassessing Anonymization as a Privacy Control Under Modern Adversarial Conditions and Regulatory Logging Requirements

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any people or organizations that could be perceived to have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research did not involve human subjects, patient data, or primary data collection requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Classical anonymization techniques are widely used to enable data sharing by removing direct identifiers while preserving analytical utility. These methods generally assume that once explicit identifiers are removed, the risk of re-identification becomes acceptably low under reasonable attacker capability assumptions embedded in many cybersecurity and privacy frameworks. This assumption is increasingly strained in modern environments characterized by widespread availability of auxiliary datasets (e.g., open-source intelligence and commercial data brokers), as well as the routine use of machine learning systems and generative AI for correlation, pattern extraction, and record linkage. In parallel, regulatory logging requirements across cybersecurity and compliance frameworks generate increasingly granular behavioral traces, including system events, timestamps, and access logs. Although not collected for identification purposes, these logs are frequently exposed through breaches and may serve as additional auxiliary data in re-identification scenarios. This paper situates record-level anonymization within a broader examination of cybersecurity and privacy control validity under modern adversarial conditions. It argues that anonymization, as commonly deployed in operational systems as either a mandatory or discretionary control, does not provide robust protection against re-identification when adversaries can leverage external datasets and automated linkage techniques. Prior empirical work repeatedly demonstrates that sparse or non-obvious attributes can still uniquely identify individuals in real-world datasets. A structured threat model is presented, along with supporting evidence, suggesting that classical anonymization should not be treated as a standalone privacy control. Instead, it should be understood as a limited preprocessing step within a broader security, compliance, and governance framework whose 1 of 13 effectiveness depends on explicit assumptions about attacker capability and data availability that are no longer stable in modern environments.

title: A Measurement Protocol for National Expansion Force: A Resource-to-Cooperation Conversion Index

detail.title: A Measurement Protocol for National Expansion Force: A Resource-to-Cooperation Conversion Index

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing personal, financial, or institutional interests that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper does not involve human participants, patient data, animal subjects, clinical intervention, or personally identifiable data. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was independently conducted and self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
Building on the first paper’s conceptual boundaries, this paper proposes a calibratable, replicable, and testable measurement protocol for National Expansion Force (NEF). The central question is not whether GDP, capital stock, institutions, or governance quality matter. The stricter question is whether the NEF index provides information that cannot be reduced to existing indicators.
This paper argues that NEF measures neither output scale nor general governance quality. It measures the latent extent to which material capacity, constrained and amplified by cooperative structure, can be converted into scalable, durable, and reproducible social coordination. GDP primarily reports realized output. Governance-quality indices primarily report aggregate assessments of institutional environments. The NEF index instead identifies the conversion structure between the two: whether resources are amplified by cooperative structure, whether cooperative structure is supported by material capacity, and how expansion capacity is compressed when the two become mismatched.
To prevent the index from becoming a reweighted version of GDP, capital stock, governance quality, or state-capacity indicators, the paper defines the model as a pre-specified measurement protocol rather than a causal identification model or a full structural model. Material capacity, denoted by Pt, is restricted to materialized, deployable, and mobilizable carrying capacity, and its underlying indicators are divided into scale, quality, and composition components. Cooperative structure, denoted by Ct, is restricted to four cross-temporal conditions of cooperation: commitment enforcement, information and records, organizational replication, and coordination expectations. Composite governance indicators such as the Worldwide Governance Indicators are downgraded to supplementary or external-validation sources rather than treated as the backbone of Ct.
The core expansion force is written as Et^core = Pt Ct^γ, and the mismatch-adjusted expansion force is written as Et^full = Et^core exp(−λ Dt). The parameters γ, λ, and the positive-shift term ε are treated as calibration constants dependent on normalization rules, not as natural constants or already identified structural elasticities.
The protocol specifies data-source tiers, a locked calibration window, normalization procedures, aggregation rules, parameter grids, directional mismatch, redundancy tests, uncertainty reporting, and pre-specified failure conditions. This second paper does not report country-case results; country cases and historical trajectories are reserved for the third paper. Its task is to fix variable boundaries, data sources, parameter ranges, reporting requirements, and failure conditions before case studies begin, thereby preventing subsequent empirical applications from becoming ad hoc parameter fitting or narrative explanation.
Keywords: National Expansion Force; resource-to-cooperation conversion capacity; latent capacity index; measurement protocol; cooperative structure; redundancy tests; pre-specified failure conditions

title: "An Empirical Study on the Influence of Enterprise Type in the Decision to Secure MUDRA Loans"

detail.title: "An Empirical Study on the Influence of Enterprise Type in the Decision to Secure MUDRA Loans"

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper.

detail.abstract: Loans from the Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency (MUDRA) have become a vital financial instrument for encouraging small enterprises and entrepreneurship in India. However, a number of variables, such as the nature of the business, may have an impact on the decision-making process involved in obtaining MUDRA loans. The purpose of this study is to determine the obstacles involved in obtaining MUDRA loans and to look at how enterprise type affects this decision. Data from a sample of businesses in various industries are analysed in this study using One-Way Single Factor Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) as the statistical method. The study divides businesses into several groups according to their ownership structure, size, and industry. The study uses ANOVA to determine if there are statistically significant differences between the various types of firms' chances of obtaining MUDRA loans. The results point to a number of difficulties in the MUDRA loan decision-making process. First, the analysis shows that the type of firm has a major influence on the possibility of receiving MUDRA finance. When applying for MUDRA loans, small and medium-sized businesses (SMEs) could encounter different obstacles than microenterprises or larger organisations. Second, based on the type of firm, the analysis finds differences in the application and approval procedures, suggesting possible biases or restrictions in the MUDRA lending system. Thirdly, the necessity for specialised financial products and support systems is highlighted by differences in loan usage and payback habits among various business kinds. Overall, this study adds to our understanding of the nuances surrounding the use of MUDRA loans and emphasises how crucial it is to take enterprise type into account when developing and implementing policies. By addressing the issues raised by this study, MUDRA loans will be more successful in encouraging economic growth and entrepreneurship, which will ultimately lead to inclusive growth in a variety of industries and business models.

title: Systemic Financial Risks of Climate Shocks: Empirical Evidence from Major Free-Floating Currencies
affiliations: and Mohammed V University of Rabat

detail.title: Systemic Financial Risks of Climate Shocks: Empirical Evidence from Major Free-Floating Currencies
detail.abstract: Using the Cumulative Average Abnormal Returns (CAAR) approach, we evaluate market reactions of major free-floating currencies (USD, JPY, EUR, GBP, CAD, CHF) to climate disasters. We further apply a Vector Autoregressive (VAR) model with impulse response functions and stress-testing to examine dynamic and persistent weather shocks. VAR-IRF and stress-tests results show temperature shocks affect EUR/USD and GBP/USD, causing sharp depreciations, while USD/JPY, USD/CAD, and USD/CHF are impacted via financial contagion. CAAR results suggest that emotionally charged disasters significantly weaken exchange rates, despite not being the most physically damaging. These findings distinguish immediate market volatility from dynamic responses to climate shocks.

title: The Agentic 3 C's Framework A Reasoning-Layer Risk Governance Model for Agentic AI in Financial Services

detail.title: The Agentic 3 C's Framework A Reasoning-Layer Risk Governance Model for Agentic AI in Financial Services

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships that have influenced or could be perceived to have influenced this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable; this paper is a conceptual and theoretical contribution that does not involve human subjects, patient data, or experimental research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted by the author in an independent capacity.

detail.abstract:
A new failure mode is emerging in agentic AI deployments: systems executing correctly against meaning that no human explicitly approved or authorized. The failure does not originate in data quality, model accuracy, or workflow design. It originates at the reasoning-layer, where agentic systems resolve context across enterprise platforms before execution. Existing governance frameworks do not yet explicitly govern how meaning is resolved at this layer prior to execution.

This paper introduces the Agentic 3 C’s Framework as the operating principles required at the reasoning-layer to enable safe, trusted agentic AI at scale in financial services. The framework establishes Context, Control, and Coordination as the three conditions under which an agentic system’s reasoning can be considered governable. Context establishes the authoritative meaning the system is permitted to resolve against. Control constrains how the system is permitted to act on that meaning. Coordination governs how meaning, authority, and execution propagate across multiple agents and enterprise systems.

The 3 C’s are positioned as the foundational operating principles that the author’s prior work implicitly relied upon. SSRN Working Paper No. 6459612 introduced Agentic Workflow Drift and Agentic Workflow Subversion as failures that occur when these principles are not enforced. SSRN Working Paper No. 6531238 introduced the Semantic Deviation Index as the runtime measurement standard that operates within Control. This paper formalizes the 3 C’s as the framework those constructs sit within, and positions a forthcoming companion paper on the Semantic Control Plane as the runtime enforcement architecture that operationalizes the framework at scale.

The paper demonstrates that reasoning-layer risk does not replace existing risk categories. It conditions them. Each existing category becomes dependent on whether reasoning occurred against authorized meaning before execution. The framework can be mapped against the principal regulatory and supervisory frameworks under which agentic AI in financial services is governed, including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, and the Cyber Risk Institute Financial Services AI Risk Management Framework, while making explicit where those frameworks do not yet specify how the reasoning layer itself should be governed.

Drawing on practitioner expertise in banking controls, model risk governance, and enterprise architecture, this paper is submitted as original practitioner-led research that defines the conditions under which agentic execution becomes governable in regulated financial services environments.

title: AI-Driven Personalization in Marketing

detail.title: AI-Driven Personalization in Marketing

detail.abstract:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an important tool in modern marketing by helping businesses create personalized experiences for customers. AI-driven personalization refers to the use of machine learning, data analytics, and intelligent algorithms to understand customer behavior, preferences, and purchasing patterns. Based on this information, companies can deliver customized product recommendations, targeted advertisements, personalized emails, and relevant content to individual consumers.

This approach improves customer satisfaction by making interactions more convenient, engaging, and meaningful. It also helps businesses increase sales, strengthen customer loyalty, and improve decision-making through accurate consumer insights. Popular companies such as Amazon, Netflix, YouTube, and Spotify successfully use AI personalization to enhance user experiences and maintain competitive advantage.

However, the use of AI in marketing also raises certain challenges, including data privacy concerns, security risks, and the possibility of over-dependence on automated systems. Therefore, businesses must balance innovation with ethical responsibility. Overall, AI-driven personalization is transforming traditional marketing into a smarter and more customer-focused strategy, making it an essential element of future business success.

title: Citizens' Equity: Capital Democratization as a Policy Response to AI-Driven Labor Displacement
