declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted as part of the author’s PhD studies at Middle Tennessee State University and received no external funding.

detail.abstract: In overturning Roe v. Wade, the Supreme Court's 2022 Dobbs decision triggered sweeping abortion restrictions across many U.S. states, dramatically reshaping access to reproductive care. While prior research has examined effects on fertility, births, and abortion access, little is known about how these policies influence child support obligations. This study evaluates the impact of the Dobbs decision on formal child support compliance using a two-way fixed effects difference-indifferences framework. I find that total abortion bans significantly reduce compliance by approximately 0.13 percentage points, with declines concentrated among young, low-income, unmarried, Black, and Hispanic custodial mothers, and particularly among mothers of infants. Event-study estimates show that these reductions emerge sharply at the time of policy implementation and are not driven by pre-existing trends. Robustness checks across alternative specifications and identification strategies consistently validate the baseline findings. These results suggest that abortion bans may exacerbate poverty, increase reliance on unstable financial arrangements, and undermine the economic security of children, underscoring the need for targeted policy interventions to mitigate the financial fallout of restrictive reproductive laws in the post-Dobbs era.

title: Regulating Profitability
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: Regulating Profitability
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether firms strategically raise costs through transactions with vertically integrated entities to avoid exceeding regulatory profitability thresholds, and the consequences for consumers. Using the Affordable Care Act (ACA)’s minimum medical loss ratio (MLR) rule as a plausibly exogenous shock to insurers’ allowable profit margins, we find that among insurers that were vertically integrated prior to the ACA, average costs and transactions to affiliated entities increased, and a one-standard-deviation increase in distance from the profitability threshold is associated with an annual cost increase of 5.7% ($159.6 per consumer), which is 6.2 times of the standalone insurers. Noncompliant standalone insurers are also more likely to vertically integrate following the regulation. Further, we find that profit shifting is associated with increased cost sharing and reflects higher prices. As a result, patients reduce utilization of care, including fewer outpatient visits and shorter inpatient stays. Together, our findings suggest the need for closer regulatory scrutiny of affiliated transactions facilitated by vertical integration and their implications for patient welfare. We also shed light on regulatory circumvention as an important factor contributing to rising healthcare consolidation and expenditures in the US.

title: Frameworks that Cannot See: How AI Governance is Repeating the Recognition Failures of Humanitarian Response

detail.title: Frameworks that Cannot See: How AI Governance is Repeating the Recognition Failures of Humanitarian Response
detail.abstract: AI governance frameworks are reproducing a documented structural pattern: institutions build categories of harm around populations they already recognise, rendering others invisible. Drawing on original empirical research on humanitarian response to conflict-related sexual violence in Africa, this brief argues that the UN Secretary-General's Advisory Body on AI (2024) is replicating the same recognition failures that allowed humanitarian frameworks to systematically exclude male victims for decades. It identifies four structural parallels and advances four recommendations directed at AI governance bodies, researchers, and funders.

title: D'Zilva’s Anti-Capture Economy: Institutional Integrity Under Conditions of Concentrated Power

detail.title: D'Zilva’s Anti-Capture Economy: Institutional Integrity Under Conditions of Concentrated Power

keywords: Private Competition 6. Second Application: Transparent Democratic Funding 7. Third Application: Domestic Market Integrity 8. Fourth Application: Public Banking for Productive Investment 9. System Interactions and Structural Balance 10. What the Anti-Capture Economy Is Not 11. Limitations

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a philosophical and structural framework for understanding institutional degradation under conditions of concentrated political, financial, and regulatory power.
The framework argues that modern institutional systems frequently preserve the procedural appearance of competition, accountability, and democratic legitimacy while progressively reducing meaningful pathways for challenge, correction, renewal, and external accountability. This process is described as structural capture.
The paper introduces two foundational anti-capture principles: Rotational Contestability and Independent External Observation. Rotational Contestability refers to the requirement that participation within political, economic, and institutional systems remain periodically and substantively contestable rather than permanently entrenched through accumulated incumbency advantage. Independent External Observation refers to the requirement that systems retain mechanisms of evaluation and correction that are not fully embedded within the same incentive structures as the systems being observed.
Together, these principles are proposed as conditions necessary for preserving systemic permeability — the continued capacity for corrective information, external critique, competitive renewal, and institutional challenge to penetrate concentrated structures of power.
The paper further introduces several supporting concepts including Managed Contestability, Perceptual Convergence, Nominal Contestability, and Genuine Contestability in order to explain how institutional systems may retain procedural legitimacy while progressively losing substantive correction capacity.
The framework is applied philosophically across four institutional domains: public resource ownership with private operational competition, democratic funding systems, domestic market integrity through standards equivalence, and public banking for productive investment.
This paper is theoretical and structural in nature. Its purpose is not to provide a comprehensive implementation blueprint, but to establish a conceptual framework for analyzing institutional integrity, systemic capture, and long-term correction capacity within complex political-economic systems.

title: Multimarket Contact and the Cost of Trading Corporate Bonds
affiliations: London Business School, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, University of Warwick - Warwick Business School and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Multimarket Contact and the Cost of Trading Corporate Bonds
detail.abstract: We show that multimarket contact (MMC)—the extent to which the same dealers interact across many securities—disciplines pricing in corporate bond markets. In a repeated-game model, dealers alternate between supplying and demanding liquidity. A dealer tempted to widen spreads for a short-run gain is deterred because she would face wider spreads herself when next demanding liquidity. MMC pools this discipline across securities: a deviation in one triggers retaliation in the others. The model predicts that higher MMC for one dealer lowers spreads for all dealers active in that bond, with the largest effects when adverse selection is high or trading is infrequent. Using TRACE data, we exploit within-bond-month variation across dealers and within-dealer-month variation across bonds. Higher MMC compresses interdealer spreads, with reductions passed through to customers. A shift-share instrument based on the sharp increase in investment-grade bond issuance during COVID confirms the result.

title: Governing Critical Minerals in Pakistan: From Investment Treaty Liability to a Sovereign Regulatory Framework

detail.title: Governing Critical Minerals in Pakistan: From Investment Treaty Liability to a Sovereign Regulatory Framework
detail.abstract:
This thesis examines the tension between the strategic importance of critical minerals and the legal constraints imposed by international investment law on state regulatory power. As demand for minerals is essential to the energy transition and advanced technologies increases, governments require regulatory flexibility to manage price volatility, ensure domestic value addition, and respond to national security concerns. However, Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs), through standards such as fair and equitable treatment, indirect expropriation, and umbrella clauses, subject these regulatory measures to investor-state arbitration, creating the risk of regulatory chill.
This thesis argues that this tension is particularly acute in the context of Pakistan, a mineral-rich developing state bound by a set of existing first-generation BITs and exposed to significant arbitral liability, as illustrated by the Reko Diq dispute. It proposes a two-stage legal strategy: first, the exclusion of critical minerals from the scope of protected investments in future BITs to restore regulatory autonomy; and second, the development of a credible domestic legal framework to maintain investor confidence in the absence of treaty protection.
By combining doctrinal analysis with a Pakistan-specific case study, this thesis contributes to ongoing debates on the recalibration of investment law to accommodate the governance needs of strategically critical resources.

detail.abstract: The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 represents a paradigm shift in India's educational landscape, promising equity, inclusivity, and quality for all. Falling into the paradigm of developmental economics, this paper critically examines the policy's potential to address the needs of historically marginalised communities-including socioeconomically disadvantaged groups (SEDGs), Scheduled Tribes, children with disabilities, and gender minorities-through a focused analysis of key provisions such as Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE), Special Education Zones, the Gender-Inclusion Fund, and Open and Distance Learning (ODL). Drawing upon official policy documents, existing educational statistics, and the broader socio-political context, this study evaluates whether NEP 2020 offers not just symbolic inclusion but substantive structural change. The paper argues that while the NEP makes commendable strides in intent and policy design, its success depends critically on effective implementation, inter-sectoral coordination, and sustained financial commitment. By highlighting both the strengths and gaps within NEP 2020, this analysis aims to contribute to ongoing discourse on educational equity and inform future policy refinements to better serve India's most vulnerable learners.

title: Intimate Authority in Romantic Relationships: How Partner Language Heals, Wounds, and Shapes Identity

detail.title: Intimate Authority in Romantic Relationships: How Partner Language Heals, Wounds, and Shapes Identity

detail.abstract:
This paper advances a conceptual framework describing how language within romantic relationships functions as a form of Romantic Lateral Authority-a non-hierarchical yet highly influential mode of interpersonal power grounded in intimacy, attachment, and emotional exposure. While authority has traditionally been examined within institutional contexts such as medicine, education, and religion, this paper argues that romantic partnerships constitute one of the most powerful regulatory systems in adult life.
     Drawing on attachment theory, affective neuroscience, and clinical observation, the analysis conceptualises partner language as a mechanism that shapes affect regulation, identity formation, and behavioural patterns. It highlights the dual potential of intimate language to both heal-through validation, co-regulation, and mutual recognition-and harm-through the repetition of early attachment wounds, subtle forms of control, and the internalisation of critical relational messages.             Integrating the concepts of social amplification and buffering, the paper demonstrates how partner communication can either escalate distress or stabilise emotional states through recursive feedback processes. It further proposes the Romantic Lateral Authority Model (RLAM) as a process framework through which these dynamics can be systematically understood. 
     The findings underscore the ethical and clinical significance of language within intimate bonds and call for a reconceptualisation of relational communication as a central mechanism in psychological regulation and identity development.

title: From transitory scare to persistence risk: Oil shocks and U.S. inflation compensation during the 2026 Iran war

detail.title: From transitory scare to persistence risk: Oil shocks and U.S. inflation compensation during the 2026 Iran war

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A

detail.abstract: This paper studies how the 2026 Iran war altered oil prices, U.S. inflation compensation, and monetary-policy pricing. The analysis combines a hand-coded chronology of conflict news with daily market data from FRED/H.15, Reuters oil-market reports, and monthly Cleveland Fed inflation expectations. Two results stand out. First, the initial March escalation behaved like a short-horizon energy shock. From 27 February to 5 March, the 5-year breakeven inflation rate rose 11 basis points and the 10-year breakeven rose 6 basis points, while the 5-year, 5-year forward inflation compensation rate rose only 1 basis point. Second, as disruption in the Strait of Hormuz persisted into late April and early May, longer-horizon measures also drifted upward. By 4 May, repricing reached 32 basis points for the 5-year breakeven, 25 basis points for the 10year breakeven, and 18 basis points for the 5-year, 5-year forward rate. Event-day regressions, maturity-differential estimates with date fixed effects, local projections, and randomizationbased placebo checks all point to the same qualitative pattern: escalation dates widen shortminus-long inflation gaps, the April ceasefire narrows them, and later persistence-risk dates are associated with broader repricing across horizons. Cleveland Fed estimates suggest that later drift reflected higher model-based expected inflation and a higher inflation risk premium. Given the small number of treated dates, the coefficients are best read as disciplined event-study evidence rather than causal estimates. The overall evidence points to a transition from an initial energy scare to later persistence risk.

detail.abstract:
Background. Clinical psychology occupies an unusually complex position among psychological disciplines. It is simultaneously a scientific specialty, a regulated health profession, an educational pathway, and a clinical practice that operates at the boundary of psychiatry, psychotherapy, медична психологія, психодіагностика, neuropsychology, rehabilitation, and public mental health. Its semantic field is therefore prone to terminological interference and conceptual reduction. 
Aim. The present article offers a pilot analysis of how the concept clinical psychology / клінічна психологія is represented in publicly available institutional and professional sources in English-language and Ukrainian-language contexts. The aim is to identify candidate components of a semantic core and visible zones of terminological interference, and to discuss the methodological consequences for the professional identity of clinical psychologists. The study does not claim to reconstruct the full psychosemantic field of the concept. 
Methods. A pilot corpus-assisted indexing was conducted on 52 publicly available sources (28 English, 24 Ukrainian). The two subsets are not symmetric in source type: the Englishlanguage subset is dominated by professional, regulatory, and training texts (APA, BPS, HCPC, PSI, CORU, DClinPsy programmes), while the Ukrainian-language subset is dominated by university educational programme descriptions. Each source was coded for 21 conceptual markers grouped into semantic zones. The design was descriptive and exploratory rather than a full corpus-linguistic frequency study. Coding was conducted by a single coder; inter-rater reliability was not yet assessed. An auxiliary AI-assisted search via Consensus was used only to identify candidate English-language literature, which was then preliminarily checked for accessibility and thematic relevance. 
Results. The English-language subset appears to be more strongly organised around the professional clinical cycle-assessment, formulation, intervention, supervision, research/evaluation-and around regulation. The Ukrainian subset shows stronger proximity to educational programmes, психотерапія, психодіагностика, психологічна реабілітація, and медична психологія, and includes a war/trauma-sensitive component that was not represented in the sampled English-language sources. These contrasts should be interpreted with caution given the source-type asymmetry between the two subsets. 
Conclusion. Clinical psychology should not be reduced to psychotherapy, to psychiatric diagnosis, or to medical psychology. Its identity rests on a specific type of psychological clinical reasoning: assessment-formulation-intervention-evaluation-supervisionethics-research-professional responsibility.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines major U.S. healthcare policy changes effective in 2026, including updates to Medicare payment structures, Medicaid access requirements, behavioral health integration mandates, and federal interoperability requirements. Drawing on federal rulemaking, agency guidance, publicly available federal datasets, and existing peer-reviewed literature, this analysis presents a policy-informed framework for aligning healthcare delivery systems with value-based care objectives.

The paper evaluates the operational and financial implications of the 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (CMS-1832-F), the CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F), the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2026, and the Inflation Reduction Act's prescription drug cost provisions. It also assesses emerging federal initiatives including MAHA
ELEVATE, Advanced Primary Care Management (APCM), and the BALANCE Model. A conceptual 21-site representative implementation framework is introduced to illustrate how diverse healthcare organizations may operationalize these policy changes across different care settings and populations.

Evidence suggests that successful alignment with 2026 federal policy requires coordinated action across federal, state, and payer systems, as well as strategic organizational adaptation. The paper identifies key compliance windows, financial implications of both action and inaction, and specific implementation priorities for federally qualified health centers, rural hospitals, behavioral health providers, maternal health programs, and tribal health organizations. Policy recommendations are directed at Congress, the CMS Innovation Center, state Medicaid agencies, and private payers.

title: LLM Zero-Shot Replication of SEC Comment Letter Returns: An Out-of-Sample Reproducibility Test

detail.title: LLM Zero-Shot Replication of SEC Comment Letter Returns: An Out-of-Sample Reproducibility Test

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses only publicly available secondary data (SEC EDGAR filings, Yahoo Finance market data, Kenneth French Data Library factors, and the Loughran-McDonald dictionary). detail.abstract: This study tests whether the post-disclosure return channel documented for U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) comment letters by Ryans (2021, Review of Accounting Studies 26(1)) is reproducible out-of-sample under a fundamentally different extraction technology. Where Ryans trains a supervised Naïve Bayesian text classifier on cumulative-abnormal-return labels, this study extracts topic, severity, and registrant-response intent from 1,014 matched UPLOAD-CORRESP letter pairs (Russell 3000 universe, 2015-2024) using zero-shot prompting of three large language models (LLMs): Gemma 3 27B, Llama 3.3 70B, and Claude Opus 4.7 as a label oracle. A pre-registered severity-weighted long-short portfolio constructed against sector-and-size-matched non-recipient controls delivers, in the held-out 2022-2024 window, a Fama-French five-factor plus momentum residual alpha of 11.92 percent annualized (Newey-West t=2.86, p=0.007, deflated Sharpe ratio 1.00, Sharpe 1.43). Two additional Benjamini-Hochberg-FDR-survivor strata emerge from a 43-cell post-hoc grid: the non-GAAP metrics topic and the 0.5-0.8 severity band. Together with the pre-registered headline, three claims survive multiplecomparison correction. The contribution is methodological rather than channel-discovery: this study (i) demonstrates that zero-shot LLM extraction reproduces the Ryans (2021) sign direction without supervised label leakage, (ii) extends the channel with topic-and severity-stratified Benjamini-Hochberg-survivor sorts that Ryans does not perform, and (iii) supplies one-command end-to-end reproducibility from raw filings to alpha. The full pipeline, including extraction prompts, replication scripts, and a locally runnable visualization dashboard, is publicly released on GitHub.

title: An Adaptive Control Analytic Framework for Epidemic Dynamics and Strategy Evolution in Healthcare Systems
affiliations: University of Dhaka, University of Dhaka and University of Dhaka

detail.title: An Adaptive Control Analytic Framework for Epidemic Dynamics and Strategy Evolution in Healthcare Systems
detail.abstract: This study investigates an adaptive optimal control framework for managing infectious disease dynamics using an extended Susceptible–Infected–Recovered–Vaccinated (SIR/V) epidemic model that incorporates human behavioral responses. The model integrates nonpharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) with a non-cooperative game theoretic mechanism to capture the interaction between individual vaccination decisions and population-level transmission dynamics. An adaptive optimal control policy is formulated under resource constraints and heterogeneous susceptibility, and analytical expressions for the optimal control trajectory are derived. The framework is evaluated through numerical simulations calibrated with real-world epidemiological parameters. The results show that adaptive policies, informed by the evolving epidemic state and behavioral dynamics, achieve significant reductions in intervention costs compared to static policies. In addition, the proposed approach leads to lower peak infection levels and faster epidemic suppression. The incorporation of evolutionary game dynamics reveals critical behavioral thresholds that influence vaccination uptake and policy effectiveness, providing actionable insights for designing responsive and cost-efficient public health strategies.

title: Are Fiscal Transfers Inflationary?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, Emory University and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia

detail.title: Are Fiscal Transfers Inflationary?

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Philadelphia Working Paper No. 26-23
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We assess the inflationary effects of fiscal transfers by leveraging advances in the identification of fiscal policy shocks within the recently proposed rotation-invariant time-varying structural vector autoregression. Our analysis suggests that fiscal transfer shocks account for a sizable share of the early post-pandemic increase in the price level through mid-2021. Thereafter, the rise in the price level is dominated by adverse supply shocks (especially supply-chain disruptions), while demand shocks mainly matter later for the lift-off in short-term interest rates. In addition, we find that fiscal transfers were essential for preventing a decline in real output per capita similar to the one experienced during the Great Depression.

detail.abstract: International student mobility has expanded rapidly over the past two decades, with over 6 million students studying outside their home countries. While this growth has contributed significantly to global economies, knowledge exchange, and cultural integration, it has also exposed systemic gaps in how international education is governed. Existing frameworks treat education, migration, and mental health as separate domains, resulting in fragmented policies that fail to address the lived realities of internationally mobile students. This paper argues that the current international education system is structurally misaligned with student wellbeing and equity outcomes. Drawing on qualitative analysis, secondary data, and policy review, it identifies key challenges including psychological distress, cultural displacement, financial pressures, and misinformation in recruitment processes. The paper highlights how students from the Global South are disproportionately affected by these structural gaps. To address these issues, the study proposes an Integrated Global Student Mobility Framework (IGSMF); a policy-driven model that embeds mental health, ethical recruitment, and migration realities into international education systems. The paper concludes with actionable recommendations for governments, universities, and international stakeholders to create a more sustainable and equitable global education ecosystem.

title: Organized Crime, Hidden Pollution, and Long-run Health Costs
affiliations: Catholic University of the Sacred Heart of Milan, University of Bologna - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Organized Crime, Hidden Pollution, and Long-run Health Costs

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study the long-run health effects of illegal toxic waste disposal conducted by organized crime in Italy. We exploit quasi-random variation in historical wind direction around contaminated sites combined with a difference-in-differences design. Using administrative data on cancer deaths spanning four decades, we find that wind exposure to pollutants increases the number of cancer deaths substantially. The effects emerge after long latencies and grow over time. In later years, wind exposure implies roughly two additional cancer deaths per municipality-year relative to unexposed municipalities equally proximate to contaminated sites. Our findings reveal a previously unmeasured health externality of organized crime.

title: Revealed Preference for Redistribution and the Role of Government
affiliations: Bocconi University and University of Chicago

detail.title: Revealed Preference for Redistribution and the Role of Government

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study how Americans trade off the welfare of the poor versus the rich using incentivized transfer experiments. Combining this with estimates of the Elasticity of Taxable Income, we quantify optimal income tax rates in the US. Revealed preferences show strong concern for the poor across the political spectrum, implying tax rates far more progressive than existing political agendas. This creates a puzzle: individuals vote for policies that are less progressive than their distributive preferences imply. We trace this puzzle to aversion toward government-mediated redistribution. Liberals’ support for very progressive tax rates is dampened by misuse of public funds, while conservatives object to taxation on principled grounds tied to coercion and property rights. Our paper illustrates that disagreement over redistribution mostly reflects disagreement over institutions rather than over helping the poor.

title: Regulating Physicians’ Prices in the Presence of Health Platforms
affiliations: Toulouse Business School, University of Padua - Department of Economics and Management, University of Toulouse - Toulouse Business School and The University of Manchester

detail.title: Regulating Physicians’ Prices in the Presence of Health Platforms

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Online platforms connecting physicians and patients are increasingly common and often operate in heavily regulated contexts. We consider a platform that provides cost-reducing services for physicians and quality-enhancing services for patients. The platform also improves the matching between patients and physicians, thereby increasing competition among the latter. When prices are unregulated, physicians charge different prices online and offline, yet not all join the platform, which is suboptimal in terms of social welfare. The platform may also under- or over-invest in the quality level offered to patients, making their participation suboptimal as well. We then analyze price regulation. Under a single regulated price for medical visits, regardless of the booking channel, all physicians join the platform. However, the first-best allocation cannot be implemented: patient participation remains inefficiently low because patients do not internalize the platform’s cost-reducing effect. In contrast, allowing two regulated prices, one for offline visits and one for platform bookings, restores the first best. Overall, our findings suggest that an optimal pricing or reimbursement mechanism should differentiate across booking channels.

title: Triggering the Green Transition; Policies for Transitional Dynamics
affiliations: University of Oxford and University of Oxford

detail.title: Triggering the Green Transition; Policies for Transitional Dynamics

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Using a dynamic model in which heterogenous consumers make forward-looking choices between brown and green durable goods, we establish conditions under which peer effects lead to multiple steady states. There is a critical threshold that policy needs to exceed to create a feasible transition path between states. We analyse the feasibility, speed, and cost of transition. Pigouvian policies internalising the externalities with climate damage and peer effects may be insufficient to lead to a green transition; even if they are, they may not yield net benefits.

title: The Stock Market Effects of the 2022 Russia Sanctions: Evidence from the US and the EU
affiliations: , University of Groningen, University of Groningen and University of Groningen - Faculty of Economics and Business

detail.title: The Stock Market Effects of the 2022 Russia Sanctions: Evidence from the US and the EU

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine how Western sanctions imposed in response to Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine shaped firm-level stock market performance in the EU and the US. To measure sanction exposure, we link firms to the specific products targeted by US and EU sanctions at the HS6 level, producing a detailed, firm-level indicator. We use a classical finance event study to analyze investor reactions around three salient moments in the pre-invasion period: Biden’s initial sanction threat, the collapse of US-Russia diplomatic talks, and the first sanctions announcement. We complement this with a staggered difference-indifferences design that exploits cross-firm variation in the timing of product level listings to trace the effects of sanctions as they accumulated over time. Stock market losses in the EU are substantially larger than in the US, and the gap between sanctioned and non-sanctioned firms is modest and shortlived. Investors price in sanction risk ahead of formal implementation, and subsequent expansions of existing sanction regimes generate little additional market response.

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We characterize the time-consistent solution to the cartel-fringe model of exhaustible resource extraction when the cartel acts as a von Stackelberg leader and renewable substitutes exist. For this feedback von Stackelberg equilibrium (FBSE), we show for each combination of stocks which equilibrium sequence will prevail. The equilibrium outcomes for the FBSE differ significantly: it features either an initial phase of simultaneous supply by the cartel and fringe or an initial phase where the cartel is the sole supplier on the market. We furthermore compare the FBSE with the Nash Cournot and the open-loop von Stackelberg equilibria.

title: Ball Possession Heterogeneity: An ML-Sim-Meta-analysis

detail.title: Ball Possession Heterogeneity: An ML-Sim-Meta-analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Countdown to the 2026 FIFA World Cup, this study provides a picture of ball possession analytics for FIFA World Cup 2022’s football matches (n = 64). The purpose was to predict best ball possession values for a team to display a performance, which shows highest probability for winning. The study included a combined design of machine learning, simulation, and meta-analysis in three main contexts: Team 1, Team 2, and their Game. After data augmentation, a total of 194 features entered into correlation analysis that identified the top six correlates of Team 1’s ball possession (poss1) among features pertinent to Team 1, Team 2, and Game (Graphical Abstract). The predictive analysis kept these features for poss1, and evaluated them alone and in all possible combinations using four models (GBR, RFR, LR, and SVR), resulting in a total of 252 models over features pertinent to each of Team 1, Team 2, and Game. LR outperformed other models, achieving a MSE between 0.0002 and 0.006 on the combination of four to five features. Simulation provided us with new data (n = 10,000) to monitor model performance. Fixed thresholds (0.4, 0.6) obtained high proportions of unexpected poss1 values on simulated data across features and models. At the optimal threshold values, unexpectedness was reduced to zero, demonstrating ideal model performance. SVR was the fittest model on simulated data that yielded the smallest optimal threshold width for all 18 features. Applying optimal threshold bounds to actual data broke down heterogenous poss1 values into three assemblies: below-expectation (low), according-to-expectation (medium), and beyond-expectation (high). Meta-correlation quantified the strength of poss1’s association with success and failure features by defined assemblies. There was an increasing trend in correlation magnitude over low to medium to high assemblies across success features (0.76, 0.86, and 0.99). It was so for low and medium assemblies across failure features (-0.78 and -0.83), but the correlation turned into direct in the high assembly. Prolonged ball possession or frequent ball possessions in this assembly – where top failure features peak – is not inversely associated with failure – as it is in low and medium assemblies, but is directly associated with failure. Times – when failure features highly dominate, the team must adopt another style. The proposed model enables analysts and managers estimate an ideal status for poss1 values and ensure their own authentic styles dynamically re-configure during the game, centering around the history and live data available for success/failure features.

detail.abstract: This policy brief reframes disinformation as a problem of state-dependent cognitive control rather than content distortion. It explains why current interventions systematically underperform and outlines high-level counter-architectures for policy and platform governance. Key Points • Current counter-disinformation strategies underperform because they assume stable cognitive conditions. • Disinformation operates by shaping cognitive and affective states, not primarily by changing beliefs. • Under pressure, cognition shifts from evaluation to coherence and social alignment. • Effective responses must stabilize cognitive conditions, not only correct content.

title: Capital and Labor Income Mobility
affiliations: University College London,  and Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU)

detail.title: Capital and Labor Income Mobility

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This article investigates whether capital or labor income drives overall relative income mobility. To this aim, we use Norwegian income registers covering 293,875 individuals over 26 years. A new framework decomposes total income mobility into capital and labor components across the life cycle. Results show: (1) traditional capital and labor mobility measures yield no clear factor ordering; (2) upward mobility is driven by labor income and joint upward movements; and (3) downward mobility is driven by capital income and joint declines. Findings are robust to large jumps, income definition and cohort selection.

title: The Signal Credibility Index for Prediction Markets: A Microstructure-Grounded Diagnostic with Weighted and Time-Varying Extensions

detail.title: The Signal Credibility Index for Prediction Markets: A Microstructure-Grounded Diagnostic with Weighted and Time-Varying Extensions
detail.abstract: Prediction-market price moves are widely treated as informationally equivalent: a price jump is read the same way regardless of whether it reflects durable Bayesian updating, transient liquidity pressure, strategic position adjustment, or genuine disagreement. This paper formalizes the Signal Credibility Index (SCI) introduced in Nechepurenko (2026) as a stand-alone diagnostic. We make four contributions: (i) a revised persistence component using the persistence ratio PR(t,w) on logit prices, well-defined on short rolling windows; (ii) a weighted Cobb-Douglas form SCI(α\alpha α) with flow-based concentration HHI_flow; (iii) a time-varying specification SCI(t; w) for real-time monitoring; and (iv) Monte Carlo validation including an out-of-distribution stress test, coordinated multi-wallet manipulation, and a logistic-regression benchmark. The validation establishes discrimination among designed microstructure regimes, not external evidence of downstream coordination effects. We document two failure modes consistent with the index targeting coordination credibility rather than pure information content: a Type II error on informed-but-concentrated whale repricing, and a Type I error on coordinated multi-wallet manipulation.

title: Physical climate risk, credit risk and lending activity
affiliations: ECB -DG Monetary Policy,  and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Physical climate risk, credit risk and lending activity

publicationDetails.journalName: ECB: Working Paper Series (Topic)

detail.abstract: We study how physical climate risk shapes bank lending activity and credit quality by combining high-resolution Copernicus flood geospatial maps with loan-level AnaCredit data. We exploit four major European floods (2021–2024) in a spatial regression discontinuity design comparing firms located just inside versus just outside flood boundaries (within 300–500 meters). We find that immediately after floods there is an increase by about 3.5 to 5% in lending, driven by liquidity demand, followed by a contraction of similar magnitude in the subsequent quarter. Interest rates follow a similar pattern, while default rates rise persistently by around 0.7 percentage points. Exploiting multiple lending relationships and firm–time fixed effects, we show that demand factors dominate: banks with greater exposure to affected firms do not systematically tighten credit supply. Nonetheless, relationship banks extend roughly 10 percentage points more credit to affected firms while imposing tighter collateral requirements, consistent with risk-sharing rather than unconditional support. Sectoral composition and pre-existing firm risk are the primary axes of heterogeneity in the immediate response. The findings shed light on how physical climate shocks propagate through credit markets and inform financial stability analysis.

title: Collaborative Experience, Team-Specific Human Capital, and Team Performance: The Case of Co-Heads in Audit Teams

detail.title: Collaborative Experience, Team-Specific Human Capital, and Team Performance: The Case of Co-Heads in Audit Teams
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether team-specific human capital between co-heads improves team performance in knowledge-intensive business services. Using the unique setting of Japanese financial audit services, where audit teams are typically led by two or three audit partners functioning as co-heads, I investigate how collaborative experience among partners affects audit quality. I construct a measure of team-specific human capital based on audit partners' past co-signature histories from publicly available audit reports, covering over 4,000 audit partners from 2000 to 2015. I find that greater collaborative experience among audit partners is significantly associated with higher audit quality. The effect is more pronounced when audit partners have less experience auditing the focal client firm, suggesting that team-specific human capital complements client-specific experience at the individual level. Additionally, the effect is stronger for larger and more complex client firms, indicating that team-specific human capital becomes more valuable as coordination challenges increase.

title: The Human Factor in Project Management: Decision-Making, Coordination, and Performance in Complex Technical Projects

detail.title: The Human Factor in Project Management: Decision-Making, Coordination, and Performance in Complex Technical Projects
detail.abstract: Project management frameworks in technical and engineering domains traditionally emphasize planning, scheduling, cost control, and risk management methodologies. While these elements are necessary for project execution, empirical evidence consistently shows that project outcomes are often determined less by technical adequacy than by human and organizational factors. This paper examines the role of the human factor in project management, focusing on decision-making, coordination, and performance under uncertainty. The analysis argues that project success and failure are strongly shaped by how individuals and teams perceive risk, process information, and interact within constrained decision environments. Rather than treating human behavior as a source of deviation from optimal plans, the paper frames it as a structural component of project dynamics. By adopting a system-level perspective, the paper positions human factors as a primary design variable in project governance, particularly in complex technical projects characterized by high uncertainty, time pressure, and interdependency. The framework contributes to a more realistic understanding of project performance by integrating technical execution with cognitive, organizational, and behavioral dimensions.

title: Human Factors and System Performance in Critical Infrastructure Projects: A Socio-Technical Framework for Stability, Resilience, and Decision-Making

detail.title: Human Factors and System Performance in Critical Infrastructure Projects: A Socio-Technical Framework for Stability, Resilience, and Decision-Making
detail.abstract: Critical infrastructure projects operate at the intersection of technical complexity, organizational coordination, and sustained external pressure. While engineering and project management methodologies provide sophisticated tools for planning and control, many large-scale infrastructure projects continue to exhibit fragility in execution and operation. This paper argues that the human factor constitutes a primary structural variable shaping system-level performance in critical infrastructure projects, particularly under conditions of uncertainty, high demand, and persistent stress. Building on socio-technical systems theory, the paper develops an integrated framework linking human decision-making, organizational dynamics, and technical constraints across the project lifecycle. Rather than treating human behavior as a source of deviation from optimal plans, the analysis positions it as an endogenous component of system stability and resilience. By synthesizing insights from engineering systems, project management, and human factors research, the paper provides a conceptual architecture for understanding how infrastructure projects transition from design intent to real-world performance. The framework is especially relevant for energy and other capital-intensive infrastructures operating in constrained environments, where human and organizational choices strongly influence long-term system robustness.

keywords: Climate and Disaster Risk Finance and Insurance (CDRFI)

detail.abstract: As climate shocks intensify, the financial protection gap in disaster risk finance is widening, particularly in vulnerable economies. This paper develops an economic rationale for global interventions in Climate and Disaster Risk Finance and Insurance (CDRFI). We identify three binding frictions that prevent endogenous financial protection: financial constraints, missing or underdeveloped risk markets, and institutional capacity mismatches. To measure these frictions, we construct a novel Global CDRFI Need Indicator for over 190 countries for the period 2000 to 2024, measuring the structural inability to absorb tail climate risk given the three frictions. The findings indicate significant CDRFI needs in Sub-Saharan Africa and, to a lesser extent, in middle-income countries driven by market deficiencies. Thus, global intervention on CDRFI is needed. We derive a risk-layered policy instrument taxonomy, arguing that allocative efficiency requires moving beyond uniform subsidies toward targeted interventions.

title: The Finance Value Pyramid: A Conceptual Framework for Repositioning Value Creation in Finance in the Era of Generative AI

detail.title: The Finance Value Pyramid: A Conceptual Framework for Repositioning Value Creation in Finance in the Era of Generative AI

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Finance Value Pyramid a three-level conceptual framework that classifies finance function activities according to their strategic value contribution: Data Work (Level 1), Analytical Work (Level 2), and Narrative Work (Level 3). Unlike prior finance-transformation research that focuses primarily on technical efficiency, this article argues that the emergence of generative AI and large language models (LLMs) accentuates a pre-existing value asymmetry: LLMs substantially automate Data Work (Eloundou et al., 2024), augment Analytical Work while preserving human interpretive judgment (Yigitbasioglu et al., 2023), and leave Narrative Work—the highest-value domain—as the most resilient human advantage. Through critical synthesis of three literature domains—decision usefulness theory (Beaver, 1968; IASB, 2018), the evolution of management accounting toward business partnering (Lambert & Sponem, 2012; Goretzki & Messner, 2019), and AI impact on cognitive work (Frey & Osborne, 2017; Eloundou et al., 2024)—the framework derives each pyramid level analytically from decision-usefulness criteria and proposes an extension of that theory to incorporate narrative translation as an explicit dimension of actual usefulness. Three conceptual propositions are advanced together with a falsifiable empirical research agenda.

detail.abstract: This paper experimentally dissects preferences for honesty into two components: lying aversion and deception aversion. To achieve separate identification, we examine two reputation-building environments with a two-dimensional belief domain, where lying without deception occurs in one environment and deception without lying in the other. The choice data, combined with belief data collected in the lab, allows us to differentiate between individuals' aversion to making literally untrue statements (lying aversion) and their aversion to statements intended to manipulate others' beliefs (deception aversion), while excluding other plausible explanations such as erroneous inferences and misunderstanding.

detail.title: The Macroeconomic Effects of Tax Policy Shocks
detail.abstract: I exploit new digitalized data on Federal Reserve expectations of tax receipts to construct an instrumental variable for the identification of tax policy shocks. The instrument recovers that contractionary tax policy shocks have permanent negative effects on real GDP, personal consumption, investments and inflation. I also find that this shock has positive temporary effects on Federal spending which dampens the negative effects on real GDP but also vanishes the fiscal adjustment and keeps the federal debt unchanged. Unlike Romer and Romer (2010) approach, the new instrument avoids the subjective judgment inherent in the narrative approach and satisfies the relevance condition also over the post-1950s sample.

title: Retail Leverage, Margin-Financing Overheating, and Market Reversal Predictability

detail.title: Retail Leverage, Margin-Financing Overheating, and Market Reversal Predictability
detail.abstract:
Can retail-investor leverage predict aggregate market reversals? This paper examines this question using daily margin-financing and market-index data from Taiwan, a retail-investor-dominated equity market. Using TEJ data from January 1991 to May 2026, I construct market-wide overheating indicators from the TAIEX, aggregate margin balances, trading value, the short-selling-to-margin-financing ratio, and the account maintenance ratio. The baseline measure scales aggregate margin balances by the TAIEX level, capturing the extent to which leveraged retail participation is elevated relative to the market level. I then develop additional indicators that capture margin-chasing behavior, margin crowding relative to market liquidity, speculative exhaustion, and high-maintenance complacency. These components are combined into a composite overheating index designed to summarize broad-based retail-leverage overheating.

The empirical design identifies overheating episodes using rolling three-year percentile thresholds that rely only on information available up to the previous trading day. This approach avoids fixed nominal thresholds and mitigates look-ahead bias. Preliminary visual evidence shows that extreme readings of the composite overheating index often arise near major market peaks and periods of subsequent market weakness. The findings suggest that aggregate margin-financing conditions contain useful information about market fragility and reversal risk. More broadly, the paper highlights the role of retail-investor leverage in shaping aggregate return dynamics in equity markets with active individual-investor participation.

title: Institutional Trust, Criminal Justice, and Social Stability: A Governance Perspective on Public Confidence and Legal Accountability Author

detail.title: Institutional Trust, Criminal Justice, and Social Stability: A Governance Perspective on Public Confidence and Legal Accountability Author
detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between institutional trust, criminal justice systems, governance accountability, and long-term social stability. The paper argues that when legal systems are perceived as excessively delayed, procedurally weak, or disproportionately lenient in severe crimes, public confidence in institutions may gradually decline. Such erosion of trust may contribute to frustration, social instability, and the emergence of extra-legal reactions among sections of society. The study does not endorse violence, retaliation, or vigilante justice. Rather, it argues that peaceful societies depend upon justice systems capable of delivering timely, transparent, proportionate, and victim-sensitive justice while simultaneously preserving constitutional safeguards and procedural fairness. Using a normative governance framework combined with criminological and institutional analysis, the paper evaluates themes such as deterrence theory, victim-centered justice, institutional accountability, public administration, remission policies, procedural delay, and governance legitimacy. The study further examines the role of strong yet accountable legal institutions in preventing violence and strengthening democratic stability. The paper concludes that sustainable peace cannot be achieved solely through moral instruction or philosophical ideals. Instead, stable societies require credible institutions, transparent investigations, proportionate punishments, accountable governance structures, and consistent public confidence in the rule of law.

title: Hierarchical Modeling for Detecting Hidden Variability in Multi-Site Manufacturing Systems
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Bundeswehr University Munich, Volkswagen AG and Ostfalia Hochschule für angewandte Wissenschaften

detail.title: Hierarchical Modeling for Detecting Hidden Variability in Multi-Site Manufacturing Systems
detail.abstract:
!This paper is a pre‑print and has not yet undergone peer review!
Industrial experiments in multi-site manufacturing systems are often affected by unobserved sources of variability that are not captured by documented tolerance bands or standard experimental factors. Identifying such latent variance components is statistically challenging in hierarchical and partially unbalanced designs, where classical fixed-effect analyses may obscure systematic effects. This paper demonstrates how a combined framework of nested factorial ANOVA and linear mixed-effects modeling enables the detection and quantification of hidden variability in complex industrial datasets. The approach accounts for nested sampling structures and interaction effects, while mixed-effects modeling is used to decompose variance components and avoid pseudo-replication. The methodology is illustrated using fatigue lifetime data from a multi-site manufacturing process involving multiple test types and load cases. The nested ANOVA reveals a statistically significant site effect (p = 0.017) and a substantially stronger site-by-test interaction (p = 1.2 × 10-5), indicating that site-related variability manifests primarily through interaction effects. In contrast, the mixed-effects model shows negligible variance attributable to production batches within sites. Although the effects are small at the level of factor means, their accumulation corresponds to a practically relevant lifetime deviation of approximately ±16%.

title: Market Power Is Power
affiliations: UNSW Australia Business School, School of Economics and ETH Zürich

detail.title: Market Power Is Power
detail.abstract: We argue that in market democracies firms can wield political power through a mechanism that does not rely on lobbying, campaign contributions, or persuasion. When voters cannot commit to future regulation, firms can use irreversible technological investments to reshape ex-post political incentives. We call this mechanism the political holdup problem. We show that, in equilibrium, a firm's de facto power to avoid regulation coincides with standard measures of market power. This form of power is robust to a wide range of regulatory instruments, including bans, taxes, self-regulation, and delegation to technocrats, and limits the effectiveness of reforms targeting political influence. The political holdup problem distorts the direction of technological progress and may increase political demand for populism and nationalization. Institutional remedies instead require commitment: supermajoritarian institutions and independent oversight of industry standards.

detail.abstract: We present fast-vollib, an open-source Python library that provides high-performance European option pricing, implied volatility (IV) computation, and Greeks under the Black-76, Black-Scholes, and Black-Scholes-Merton models. The library is designed as a drop-in alternative to the de-facto-standard py_vollib and py_vollib_vectorized packages, with pluggable PyTorch and JAX execution backends, a CUDA fused-kernel Triton contribution for batched IV workloads, and a compatibility-first public API. detail.abstract: This manuscript reconstructs the making of the Copyright Act of 1976 through a close comparative study of the major drafts, reports, hearings, and compromise provisions that emerged over a twenty-year legislative process beginning in 1955. By charting the evolution of the principal draft provisions and their transformation into enacted law, the manuscript provides a detailed roadmap for understanding both the structure of the 1976 Act and the legislative choices that continue to shape modern copyright interpretation.

title: Climate Political Leadership and Financial Market Perception of Regulatory Exposure
affiliations: Edinburgh Napier University, University of Strathclyde, University of Strathclyde - Department of Accounting and Finance and University of Birmingham - Birmingham Business School

detail.title: Climate Political Leadership and Financial Market Perception of Regulatory Exposure
detail.abstract: We examine how an exogenous shift in climate political leadership affects financial markets’ perception of firm-level climate regulatory exposure. Using the unexpected outcome of the 2016 U.S. presidential election as a quasi-natural experiment and a propensity score-matched difference-in-differences design comparing U.S. and European firms, we find that the transition to climate-skeptic leadership is associated with a reduction in the perceived climate-regulatory exposure of U.S. firms by approximately fourfold relative to their European counterparts. We identify evidence consistent with a regulatory cost channel as the mechanism underlying this effect. Our findings reveal that political leadership is a first-order determinant of climate-related information environments.

title: The Metaverse Is Not a Place Apart: Law, Code, and the Recursive Governance of Digital Space: A Review Essay on Mark Findlay, Governing the Metaverse: Law, Order and Freedom in Digital Space (2025)

detail.title: The Metaverse Is Not a Place Apart: Law, Code, and the Recursive Governance of Digital Space: A Review Essay on Mark Findlay, Governing the Metaverse: Law, Order and Freedom in Digital Space (2025)
detail.abstract: This review essay examines Mark Findlay's Governing the Metaverse: Law, Order and Freedom in Digital Space. Findlay offers an ambitious and timely account of the metaverse as a social and imaginative space that should be governed for freedom, personhood, community, and resistance to enclosure. The essay argues, however, that the book's two central categories-"the metaverse" and "new law"-remain insufficiently theorised. The book relies on a realspace/virtual distinction that its own analysis repeatedly destabilises. Once digital environments are understood as dependent on physical infrastructures, platform architectures, AI systems, data pipelines, and external legal institutions-and as capable of generating real-world harms for individuals and society-the governance problem is no longer how to devise a separate law for a separate virtual realm. It is how to govern a hybrid socio-technical order in which law, code, platforms, and public oversight recursively interact. The essay further argues that Findlay's account of "new law" does not adequately theorise how normative authority operates across a recursively layered governance architecture in which code, platform rules, and legal oversight interact without any single level exercising decisive control. Drawing on algorithmic constitutionalism, speech-act pluralism, and fuzzy legality, the essay suggests that addressing this architecture requires a jurisprudence capable of reasoning about normative force that is layered, defeasible, and recursively unstable.

title: Superstition belief and insider selling: Evidence from Chinese Zodiac year
affiliations: Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Superstition belief and insider selling: Evidence from Chinese Zodiac year
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether cultural beliefs constrain insider selling by corporate insiders. To address the identification challenges in cultural research, we exploit Chinese zodiac-year superstition as an individual-specific, time-varying source of variation in perceived risk. Using transaction-level data on insider sales of Chinese A-share listed firms, we find that insiders significantly reduce the magnitude of their stock sales during their zodiac year, even after controlling for insider fixed effects. The effect is stronger where traditional beliefs are more salient and where insider sales are more likely to trigger adverse market reactions and personal costs. It is also concentrated in opportunistic rather than routine sales, stronger among less-educated insiders, core executives, and non-SOEs, and reflected in less salient execution patterns. Our findings are robust after addressing endogeneity concerns and alternative explanations. Overall, the results highlight the role of beliefs and perceived risk in shaping financially consequential decisions in capital markets.

title: The Vulnerability Amplifiers: How Foreign-Currency Debt Turns Exchange-Rate Shocks into Corporate Defaults
affiliations: Government of the Republic of Turkey - Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, CBRT and Gebze Technical University

detail.title: The Vulnerability Amplifiers: How Foreign-Currency Debt Turns Exchange-Rate Shocks into Corporate Defaults
detail.abstract: The relationship between foreign-currency borrowing and corporate default risk remains theoretically ambiguous, balancing the vulnerability of the balance-sheet channel against the benefits of natural hedging. We investigate this relationship by evaluating the causal effect of foreign-currency exposure on corporate default risk during the 2018 Turkish currency crisis. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset of non-financial firms and applying Double Machine Learning (DML) alongside Causal Forests, we uncover a highly non-linear, dose-dependent relationship. We find that moderate levels of foreign-currency debt provide a protective effect against default, whereas high levels of exposure strictly amplify default risk. Furthermore, we identify significant heterogeneity in treatment effects, documenting a "participation-sensitivity paradox." Firms with strong natural hedging capabilities—such as exporters, large enterprises, and those with multiple banking relationships—benefit the most from participating in foreign-currency credit markets. However, these same high-quality firms exhibit the greatest sensitivity to marginal increases in their exposure during a severe macroeconomic shock.

title: Environmental Impact on Agriculture and Forestry Loss due to Hurricane Helene's Surge

detail.title: Environmental Impact on Agriculture and Forestry Loss due to Hurricane Helene's Surge
detail.abstract: Hurricanes are destructive enough, but with changes, some are becoming more destructive, like Hurricane Helene which was a Category 4 storm that caused major damage with high winds and heavy rains that caused a surge throughout the different states in the Southeast (Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, and parts of Virginia). Want to show how the change in losses to crop damage, livestock feed loss, destruction of infrastructure, and other losses caused by the surge from the hurricane. Using GDP and SRAS, I hope to show what losses there were in agriculture and forestry due to Hurricane Helene.

title: Plagiarism Ex Machina: Structural Appropriation in Large Language Models

detail.title: Plagiarism Ex Machina: Structural Appropriation in Large Language Models
detail.abstract:
The transformation of human-authored textual corpora into predictive generative capacity without transparent source attribution or recoverable provenance. The paper shifts the AI plagiarism debate from copying and memorization toward structural appropriation, recombinative authorship, and generative provenance.

Large language models introduce a form of plagiarism that cannot be reduced to verbatim copying or copyright infringement. Their central operation is structural appropriation: the absorption, recombination, and redeployment of human intellectual labor under conditions of referential opacity and attribution collapse.

Structural appropriation; Recombinative plagiarism; Referential opacity; Attribution collapse; Synthetic originality; Predictive authorship; Latent intellectual debt; Corpus parasitism; Invisible intellectual labor; Generative provenance.

title: Prior Art in AI Paradox Ontology: How the Process-Paradox Framework Anticipates and Surpasses the Abstraction Fallacy

detail.title: Prior Art in AI Paradox Ontology: How the Process-Paradox Framework Anticipates and Surpasses the Abstraction Fallacy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research was conducted independently, with no financial or personal relationships with any organization that could have influenced the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a theoretical and philosophical study involving no human participants, patient data, clinical trials, or empirical data collection. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was self-funded by the author as part of independent scholarly work conducted under the WorldValue research platform.

detail.abstract: This paper establishes the independent priority of the Process-Paradox Framework in the current debate on AI consciousness, and advances it as a more complete and foundationally deeper account than Alexander Lerchner's Abstraction Fallacy (DeepMind, March 2026). The author's core arguments-that AI is ontologically barred from consciousness by three structural absences: (1) irreversibility, (2) the death threshold, and (3) paradoxical self-transcendencewere published in full between January and February 2026, two months prior to Lerchner's paper, across six works spanning philosophy, mathematics, and political economy. In particular, two foundational philosophical determinations were independently established prior to Lerchner: that consciousness is ontologically constituted by human mortality and irreversibility, and that AI is structurally one ontological dimension below the threshold at which consciousness becomes possible.Unlike Lerchner's purely epistemological critique of computational functionalism, the Process-Paradox Framework provides both a negative argument (why computation cannot generate consciousness) and a positive ontological account (what consciousness actually requires). The mathematical dimension, grounded in Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems and Chaitin's Omega Constant, demonstrates that human intelligence constitutes an (N+1)dimensional system that no N-bit AI can internally derive or replicate. The philosophical dimension, drawing on Whitehead's event ontology, Zhuangzi's process metaphysics, and Popper's falsifiability principle, identifies the specific ontological structures-mortality, irreversibility, paradox-that computation cannot instantiate. Lerchner's mapmaker hypothesis, while correct in its negative claim, remains circular and constructively empty. This paper proposes that the Process-Paradox Framework, developed independently and prior, constitutes the more complete resolution to the AI consciousness debate.

title: Market prices or made-up prices? -Evidence from the iron ore market
affiliations: The University of Western Australia, University of Western Australia - Business School, The University of Western Australia and The University of Western Australia

detail.title: Market prices or made-up prices? -Evidence from the iron ore market
detail.abstract: This paper examines how price reporting agencies (PRAs) collect and use information to create index prices in one of the most mature mineral markets, the iron ore market. We document shortcomings in the price reporting process and show with two different approaches that the index price deviates substantially from the market clearing price. Inelastic demand and supply result in modest welfare losses but large wealth transfers between buyers and sellers. Our findings extend to a large portion of the $3.7 trillion mining industry which relies on PRA prices to settle trades.

title: From Aggregate Hedger Positioning to Firm-Level Tradable Alpha: A Pre-Registered Cross-Sectional COT Shock Strategy on Commodity Producer Equity

detail.title: From Aggregate Hedger Positioning to Firm-Level Tradable Alpha: A Pre-Registered Cross-Sectional COT Shock Strategy on Commodity Producer Equity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that may be perceived to have influenced this study. The research was conducted independently. All data sources used (CFTC public filings, the Kenneth French Data Library, and a public price feed for sector ETF returns) are publicly available, and the computational pipeline was implemented and run on the author's own resources. This study uses only publicly available secondary data on financial market positions (CFTC Disaggregated Commitments-of-Traders weekly reports), publicly listed firm equity prices, publicly distributed factor returns from the Kenneth French Data Library, and a publicly traded sector exchange-traded fund. No human or animal subjects, no patient data, and no personally identifying information are involved at any stage of the analysis. The work was self-funded by the author, used exclusively publicly available data sources, and was conducted on personally funded computational resources.

detail.abstract: We document a tradable cross-sectional alpha on US-listed commodity producer firm equity, conditioned on Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Disaggregated Commitmentsof-Traders producer/merchant/processor/user weekly net-position |𝑧| > 1.5𝜎 first-week shocks. Using 700 events across 12 commodities (June 2006-April 2026), 36 producer firms, and a sign convention frozen prior to estimation, we apply a strict Bonferroni-𝐾 = 36 critical |𝑡| ≈ 3.10 cell-level test, a five-component factor absorption (FF5 + Mom + IVOL + aggregate hedgingpressure + relative-basis), and a four-gate robustness battery (shift-placebo decay, sub-period stability, walk-forward five-fold, post-cost). Ten of 36 cells are significant under naive Welch one-sample 𝑡 (4 of 36 under event-date cluster-bootstrap, reported as a rigor caveat), all concentrated in the energy front-end (BZ, CL, HO, NG); zero cells in metals (GC, SI, HG, PL) or agriculture (C, S, W). Portfolio information ratios are 0.64, 1.19, and 1.01 at the one-, four-, and twelve-week horizons respectively, all clearing the 0.40 floor. Among the four robustness gates, only the twelve-week portfolio passes all four. A sector-ETF-hedged twelve-week longshort construction (energy producer firms long, XLE short, equal-dollar) delivers post-cost net Sharpe +0.704 with cluster-bootstrap 95 percent confidence interval [0.236, 1.233], preserved as the conservative baseline. Producer-type stratification by NAICS and GICS sub-industry then resolves two competing structural interpretations of the underlying mechanism: a refiningmargin-compression hypothesis (H1) predicting negative refiner forward CAR is rejected, because the refiner standalone hedged long-short delivers a positive (not negative) net Sharpe of +0.040 with cluster-bootstrap upper bound +0.776; a commodity-price-beta differential hypothesis (H2) predicting an information-ratio ranking of upstream pure-play exploration-andproduction firms above integrated majors above refiners is confirmed, because the realized ranking is exactly 1.24 > 1.03 > 0.92 and the deployable upstream-only × four-week × post-2014 × XLE-short cell delivers net Sharpe +1.146 with cluster-bootstrap 95 percent confidence interval lower bound +0.500, a 63 percent uplift over the aggregate baseline. The contribution is a strictpre-registered conversion of the aggregate hedger-positioning predictability literature (Bessembinder and Chan 1992; Hong and Yogo 2012; Roon et al. 2000; Acharya et al. 2013) into a firm-level cross-sectional tradable alpha that goes beyond the aggregate cross-section of Centaur (2016), with a falsifiable structural mechanism test that resolves the practitioner refining-margin narrative against the price-beta channel under pre-registration. The full pipeline, including the pre-registered specification, replication scripts, and a locally runnable visualization dashboard, is preserved in a public Git repository.

title: Quan Hệ Kinh Tế Hoa Kỳ - Việt Nam Sau Khi Ký Hiệp Định Khung Về Thương Mại Đầu Tư (TIFA) 2007-2019 / United States-Vietnam Economic relation after signing the Trade and Investment Framework Agreement (TIFA) 2007-2019
