detail.title: Quan Hệ Kinh Tế Hoa Kỳ - Việt Nam Sau Khi Ký Hiệp Định Khung Về Thương Mại Đầu Tư (TIFA) 2007-2019 / United States-Vietnam Economic relation after signing the Trade and Investment Framework Agreement (TIFA) 2007-2019
detail.abstract: Quan hệ kinh tế giữa Việt Nam và Hoa Kỳ luôn là một trong những nội dung quan trọng, được đề cập trong chiến lược phát triển kinh tế - xã hội của Đảng và nhà nước. Bên cạnh đó đây cũng là một trong những nội dung được các nhà khoa học quan tâm nghiên cứu. Trong những năm qua, quan hệ Việt Mỹ đã đạt được nhiều thành tựu đáng kể trên mọi lĩnh vực, trong đó có quan hệ hợp tác kinh tế. Trong khuôn khổ bài báo này, sẽ nghiên cứu vai trò của đối tác Hoa Kỳ đối với hoạt động kinh tế của Việt Nam. Dựa trên nguồn số liệu từ các báo cáo phân tích của Tổng cục Hải quan, từ các tổ chức kinh tế trong bài viết này chúng tôi sẽ tổng hợp và phân tích các nội dung liên quan đến quan hệ kinh tế giữa Việt Nam và Hoa Kỳ. Thông qua đó chúng tôi sẽ đánh giá sự tác động của đối tác Hoa Kỳ đối với hoạt động thương mại của Việt Nam từ sau khi Hiệp định khung về Thương mại đầu tư (TIFA) được ký (2007-2019).

title: Endogenous financial architecture under regulatory pressure
affiliations: University of Trento - Department of Economics and Management and

detail.title: Endogenous financial architecture under regulatory pressure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: We develop an agent-based model in which the architecture of credit intermediation-the split between regulated and shadow banking-emerges endogenously from regime-switching decisions by heterogeneous banks. Intermediaries are periodically allowed to adjust their business model by choosing between a regulated mode subject to capital requirements and Cournot oligopoly pricing, and a shadow mode funded via asset-backed securities with higher lending intensity. Three channels drive the dynamics: i) a Cournot markup channel that makes regulated banking more profitable as competitors migrate to shadow; ii) a balance-sheet contagion channel through which shadow stress spills over to regulated funding costs; iii) a procyclical lending channel enabling co-expansion of both credit volumes during booms. Simulations show that tighter capital requirements induce persistent migration toward shadow intermediation, with wavelet analysis revealing an endogenous financial cycle at lower frequencies. We document co-expansion of regulated and shadow credit during booms, and a markup effect whereby reduced competition raises the profitability of remaining regulated banks, partially offsetting the regulatory burden that triggered the migration. Monte Carlo experiments confirm robustness across regulatory parameterizations. These results suggest that microprudential capital requirements alone cannot control systemic leverage when the regulatory perimeter is permeable.

title: Positional Preferences, Uninternalized System Costs, and the Divergence Between Growth and Well-Being

detail.title: Positional Preferences, Uninternalized System Costs, and the Divergence Between Growth and Well-Being
detail.abstract: Modern economies can expand material throughput without corresponding gains in societal well-being. This paper develops a model in which decentralized activity exceeds the welfareconsistent scale through two mechanisms. First, positional preferences induce excessive labor supply in pursuit of status, even though relative gains cancel in aggregate. Second, individuals experience disutility from social stress and ecological degradation but treat these system-level conditions as exogenous, failing to internalize their contribution. Firms exhibit a parallel distortion by overusing labor and resources when social and ecological harms are unpriced. Extending the model to heterogeneous agents shows that unequal vulnerability to system-level harms generates distribution-dependent welfare losses. The model therefore provides a microfoundation for why economic throughput can diverge from societal well-being and, under convex system costs, for an inverted-U relationship between throughput and welfare.

title: The Architecture of Property Rights

detail.title: The Architecture of Property Rights
detail.abstract:
Property law theory is divided between two competing models of the architecture of property rights. One holds that property rights have a limited scope but an unlimited strength; the other reverses these commitments, positing an unlimited scope but a limited strength. I argue that instrumentalist approaches to the justification of property law generate this impasse and lack the conceptual resources to resolve it.

Christopher Essert’s remarkable book, Property Law in the Society of Equals, does not directly address this stalemate, yet it nonetheless offers a powerful means of escaping it. Essert develops a non‑instrumental justification of property law in which the idea of yours and mine uniquely enables persons to interact as equals with respect to objects and spaces. At the same time, his account provides critical resources for explaining and justifying limits on both the scope and the strength of property rights.

title:
The impact of liquidity regulation on financial performance of
banking industry

detail.title:
The impact of liquidity regulation on financial performance of
banking industry
detail.abstract: liquidity and profitability are contemporary issues in the banking sector of emerging countries. We examine how Basel iii liquidity regulation, as reflected in the liquidity coverage ratio (lcR) and non-performing assets (nPas), affects banks' financial performance using balanced panel data from 25 banks' annual reports from 2018 to 2024. By applying the collapse instrument technique in a two-step system generalized method of moments (gMM) estimator, the study found a significant and strong positive relationship between lcR and return on assets (ROa). this finding is in line with the liquidity-profitability trade-off theory (Modern Risk-adjusted Version) and financial intermediation theory. a novel finding is that lcR exerts a negative effect on net interest income (nii). another result reveals that higher liquidity (lcR) has a statistically significant inverse relation with nPas, indicating that higher liquidity reduces bad loans (nPas). the result suggests that Basel iii has successfully set liquidity requirements to mitigate the industry-wide liquidity crisis. Our results remain robust when using alternative methods. the results provide guidance for financial institutions to maintain liquidity and profitability better. the study's contribution is meaningful for banks, national and international regulators, and policymakers in making strategic decisions to support financial stability and long-term growth in the banking industry.

title: How vital are Relationship Bankers in the rural credit decision making and loan approval process?

detail.title: How vital are Relationship Bankers in the rural credit decision making and loan approval process?
detail.abstract:
This study examines the role of relationship banking and information asymmetry in the agricultural credit decision-making and loan approval process in New Zealand. Despite accounting for over 60 percent of New Zealand's export earnings, the agricultural sector continues to face significant inefficiencies in accessing formal credit, with loan approval timelines for large capital transactions averaging 15 to 20 days — a timeframe driven largely by information asymmetries between farmers and their financiers rather than by genuine credit risk complexity.

Drawing on a qualitative research design, the study combines semi-structured interviews with six experienced agricultural consultants and a survey of twelve farming operations to investigate how credit decisions are made, what information is required, and where the process can be improved. The Five Cs of Credit — Character, Capacity, Capital, Collateral, and Conditions — are confirmed as the foundational framework for agricultural lending assessment. Findings demonstrate that relationship banking remains indispensable to the credit approval process, providing the subjective, contextual intelligence that structured financial data alone cannot capture.

The study further finds that a significant mismatch of expectations exists between farmers and financial institutions, with farmers largely unaware of lending criteria and financiers slow to adopt digital tools that could reduce this information gap. The majority of survey respondents expressed support for a third-party, self-service credit readiness tool that would provide indicative loan outcomes based on a farmer's existing financial data, suggesting viable market demand for such an innovation.

The research concludes that while digital transformation and data analytics offer meaningful efficiency gains for agricultural lenders, the relational dimension of rural banking cannot be replaced by automated systems alone. The study contributes the first empirical examination of credit decision-making and information asymmetry in New Zealand's agricultural lending sector and offers practical recommendations for banks, fintech developers, and agricultural consultants seeking to reduce approval times, improve customer experience, and unlock untapped demand in the rural credit market.

Keywords: agricultural finance; credit decision-making; information asymmetry; relationship banking; New Zealand; Five Cs of Credit; loan approval; agribusiness; fintech; rural banking

title: Discounting as a Distributional Weapon: When Time Structure Asymmetry Reverses Welfare Signs

detail.title: Discounting as a Distributional Weapon: When Time Structure Asymmetry Reverses Welfare Signs
detail.abstract: Under exponential discounting, when gains and losses have asymmetric time structures — a lump-sum gain versus a perpetual loss — the discount factor β determines the sign of the welfare comparison, not merely its magnitude. This paper characterizes the β-Reversal Effect, proposes a β-Invariance Test to diagnose when welfare conclusions are artifacts of discounting, and shows that quasi-hyperbolic discounting, often invoked as behavioral realism, sharpens rather than resolves the problem. The choice of discount function and parameter value is a distributional stance disguised as a technical calibration.

title: Hub-Contestability: A New Antitrust Paradigm for Platform Competition

detail.title: Hub-Contestability: A New Antitrust Paradigm for Platform Competition

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Competition Law and Economics (Forthcoming)

detail.abstract: This Article champions a new paradigm-hub-contestability-to counter the threat posed by network effects entrenching dominant platforms. While prior work has shown that competition over highly connected hubs operating on platforms ("hub-plucking") can breach the seemingly insurmountable competitive moat arising from network effects, this Article confronts the risk that dominant platforms will act to eliminate this potent mode of competition. The Article identifies three primary types of tactics that dominant platforms may deploy to neutralize their exposure to hub-plucking. First, platforms may engage in "hub-locking" through acquisitions of hubs and longterm exclusivity arrangements, thereby precluding hubs from operating across rival platforms. Second, platforms may engage in "hub-crushing," either by restricting API accessthereby suffocating the lifeline of hubsor by replicating their functionalities while simultaneously disadvantaging them within the platform. Third, platform design choices may suppress the emergence of hubs, preventing the scaling necessary to transform ordinary platform participants into entities of meaningful competitive significance. Fusing network science and contestability theory, the hub-contestability paradigm aims to hone antitrust law to thwart such tactics, thereby ensuring that hubs remain sufficiently "contestable" to sustain a dynamic competitive landscape. Embracing this paradigm will streamline antitrust's hitherto cumbersome decisionmaking in complex platform cases. It will recalibrate antitrust's various doctrines, from merger-control through the prohibitions on abusive conduct to the employment of remedies, to foster vibrant inter-platform competition. * Raz Agranat (LL.B., LL.M., JSD), Assistant Professor, Harry Radzyner Law School, Reichman University, Member of the International Association of Competition Law Scholars (ASCOLA) and Affiliated Scholar at the Dynamic Competition Initiative (DCI). I am grateful for invaluable comments and discussions to Baruch Barzel, Omri Ben-Shahar, Ariel Ezrachi, Michal Gal, William Hubbard, and Eric Posner. Thanks as well to the participants of the 17 th ASCOLA Conference 2022 and the Junior Scholars Colloquium at the University of Chicago Law School for discussing the issues explored here. All errors are my own. There are no conflicts of interest in relation to this article.

title: Potential Failure Modes of the Coordinated Framework for the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: Potential Failure Modes of the Coordinated Framework for the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

detail.abstract: The two preceding papers in this series argued, first, that risk assessment under Symmetric Risk Obligation (SRO) and not the precautionary principle should govern artificial intelligence (AI), and second, that the institutional vehicle for that argument is a three-tier coordinated framework operating under existing federal statutory authority, modeled on the 1986 Coordinated Framework for the Regulation of Biotechnology. This third paper addresses the question that any honest proponent of a governance framework owes to their own proposal: where does it fail? This paper identifies nine plausible failure modes of the proposed architecture. For each, it specifies whether the failure mode is mitigated by the framework's design, must be accepted as residual risk, or could falsify the approach in whole. The framework holds against the majority of the failure modes examined, with the remaining as residual risk. The framework faces three genuine structural vulnerabilities: post-Chevron judicial review of agency reach into AI applications, the persistent information asymmetry between regulators and frontier labs, and the operationalization of SRO under conditions of deep uncertainty. Each potential failure mode requires explicit design responses, which this paper supplies.

title: The Role of Optimal Disaster Resilience and Recovery in Estimating Benefits of Adaptation
affiliations: University of Southern California - Sol Price School of Public Policy, Ohio State University (OSU) and Ohio State University (OSU), John Glenn College of Public Affairs

detail.title: The Role of Optimal Disaster Resilience and Recovery in Estimating Benefits of Adaptation

keywords: Optimal Control Theory JEL Classification: Q54

detail.abstract: Many studies have evaluated climate adaptation as a major strategy to reduce the potential negative economic impacts of climate change induced disasters, focusing primarily on property damage. However, averting stock losses is not the only measure of benefits of adaptation; it is also important to consider reducing the loss of the flow of goods and services stemming from property damage, typically measured in terms of loss of net revenues or GDP. These losses begin when the disaster strikes and continue until damaged property is restored. This paper presents a formal model of optimal economic recovery from disasters for the individual firm as a lower bound estimate of flow losses, blending aspects of climate change economics and the economics of disasters. The paper combines important objectives, background considerations and functional relationships in an optimal control theory approach to analyze how investment in repair and reconstruction (R&R) reduces disaster flow losses in the assessment of the benefits of adaptation measures such as the construction of seawalls, installation of storm shutters, or enhanced vegetation management practices. R&R can be facilitated and enhanced by tactics referred to as dynamic economic resilience, which promotes the efficient allocation of resources over time. We distinguish two classes of tactics: those that hasten the implementation of the investment and those that lower its cost and thereby accelerate recovery. Tactics to accomplish the former include speeding up the removal of debris, insurance payments, and applying for public assistance. Tactics to accomplish the latter include shortening the gestation period for reconstruction activity and improving the efficiency of the repair/reconstruction effort. The results yield insights into optimizing behavior, trade-offs, and recovery time-paths with and without dynamic economic resilience.

title: Anti-Oligarchy, Anti-Authoritarianism, The Constitution, and the Court

detail.title: Anti-Oligarchy, Anti-Authoritarianism, The Constitution, and the Court
detail.abstract: In the 1930s, like today, our nation faced a crisis of oligarchy: too much wealth and political power concentrated in too few hands. Like today's liberals and progressives, the New Dealers aimed to enact social and economic reforms that would ensure a much broader distribution of wealth and power, but they faced a hostile, right-wing Supreme Court that would certainly thwart such reforms. Thus, like liberals and progressives today, New Dealers proposed various measures aimed at curbing judicial review to safeguard the legislative reforms they saw as essential to making democracy work. Yet at the same time they hoped to preserve the Court's power-which they hoped the Court would exercise-to defend civil liberties, protect vulnerable minorities against state violence, and safeguard the rule of law in a moment of rising authoritarianism.

title: A Hybrid Origami-Quantum Graph Neural Network Framework for Adaptive Structural Design and Optimisation
affiliations: Delhi College of Engineering - Delhi Technological University

detail.title: A Hybrid Origami-Quantum Graph Neural Network Framework for Adaptive Structural Design and Optimisation
detail.abstract: Adaptive and deployable structures are increasingly important in modern engineering systems including aerospace mechanisms, soft robotics, deployable space structures, and responsive architectural components where lightweight and reconfigurable designs must operate reliably under varying loads and environmental conditions. Origami-inspired engineering structures provide a promising solution by enabling foldable geometries capable of large and controllable shape transformations while using minimal material and maintaining structural efficiency. However, optimising origami crease patterns is a computationally challenging task because the configuration space defined by fold angles, geometric constraints, and material properties is highly nonlinear, high-dimensional, and often non-convex. Traditional optimisation approaches such as gradient-based methods or evolutionary algorithms frequently struggle to efficiently explore this complex design space and may converge to suboptimal folding configurations. In this work, we propose a hybrid Origami-Quantum Graph Neural Network (OQ-GNN) framework for adaptive structural optimisation of origami-based systems. In the proposed approach, origami crease patterns are represented as graphs in which nodes correspond to fold joints and store structural attributes such as fold angles, crease types, and material stiffness, while edges represent crease connectivity and geometric constraints between folds. A graph neural network performs message passing across the crease network to capture relational structural interactions and learn expressive embeddings that describe the global folding configuration. These learned representations are then processed by a quantum-inspired amplitude exploration module that encodes candidate structural states using complex-valued probability amplitudes, enabling simultaneous exploration of multiple design configurations through a superposition-like sampling mechanism implemented entirely on classical hardware. Experimental evaluation on a dataset of procedurally generated origami crease patterns with finite-element-based structural responses demonstrates that the proposed method achieves improved optimisation accuracy, reduced structural stress, and faster convergence compared with classical optimisation baselines and standard graph neural network approaches. The results suggest that combining graph-based structural learning with quantum-inspired probabilistic exploration provides an effective and scalable strategy for the design and optimisation of adaptive origami engineering structures.

title: Institutional Barriers, Defensive Innovation, and Market Dynamism: Evidence from China’s Strengthened Competition Policy
affiliations: Renmin University of China, Renmin University of China, University of Rijeka and Renmin University of China

detail.title: Institutional Barriers, Defensive Innovation, and Market Dynamism: Evidence from China’s Strengthened Competition Policy
detail.abstract: In transition economies characterized by deep government–business ties, dismantling administrative monopolies is crucial for enhancing market dynamism. Using a city–three-digit-industry panel dataset from China over the period 2003–2023, this paper evaluates the causal impact of the Strengthened Competition Policy (SCP) on firm entry through a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) model. The results show that SCP significantly promotes new firm entry, increasing entry density by approximately 0.69 units. Mechanism analysis indicates that while the policy weakens government–firm connections and triggers “creative destruction,” thereby releasing resources, it also induces defensive expansion by high-quality incumbents. Through innovation and scale expansion, these firms raise effective entry thresholds. Despite this offsetting effect, the institutional dividend dominates overall, particularly in historically entrenched markets where the policy exhibits a strong “ice-breaking” effect.

title: Democracy and Economic Structural Drivers of Green Supply Chain Management: Evidence From European Economies

detail.title: Democracy and Economic Structural Drivers of Green Supply Chain Management: Evidence From European Economies
detail.abstract: Achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals: 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) and 13 (Climate Action) requires transformative changes in global value chain systems, yet progress remains inadequate to meet 2030 targets. While green supply chain management (GSCM) has been a strategic mechanism for advancing sustainability through emissions reduction and circular economy integration, substantial variation in GSCM performance across nations indicates that firm-level capabilities alone cannot explain adoption effectiveness. This study draws on Economic Modernization and Institutional Theory to examine how digital connectivity, services sector development, innovation, financial inflows, and democracy influence GSCM across European Economies. Results show that democracy, digitalization, services development, and remittance inflows are significant GSCM drivers, whereas innovation exerts counterproductive effects reflecting a bias toward competitiveness over ecological efficiency. Policymakers should strengthen democratic accountability, invest in digital infrastructure, and redirect innovation incentives toward environmental innovation to advance GSCM.

title: Why Formalisation Policies Fail in Africa: Informal Trade as a Socially Learned Cognitive System

detail.title: Why Formalisation Policies Fail in Africa: Informal Trade as a Socially Learned Cognitive System
detail.abstract: Informal cross-border trade remains the dominant mode of exchange in many African border corridors despite sustained policy efforts to promote formalisation through regulatory simplification, infrastructure investment, and regional trade agreements. Conventional explanations attribute this persistence to high compliance costs, weak administrative capacity, and limited enforcement offormal rules. While these factors are important, they do not fully explain why traders continue to systematically avoid formal channels even where simplified regimes and trade facilitation measures have been introduced. This paper argues that informality is better understood as a learned responseto structurally unstable border environments in which enforcement variability, procedural unpredictability, discretionary decision-making, and cost uncertainty prevent the formation of reliable expectations about formal trade. In response, traders develop recurrent informal practices that, over time, consolidate into shared avoidance strategies, stabilising informality as the dominant mode of cross-border exchange and producing a self-reinforcing institutional equilibrium that policy reforms so far have failed to disrupt.

title: AI in Logistics: Mitigating War and Pandemic Risks

detail.title: AI in Logistics: Mitigating War and Pandemic Risks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study included a small exploratory pilot survey of logistics professionals using voluntary and anonymized responses. No sensitive personal data were collected. Participants provided informed consent. Given the minimal-risk exploratory nature of the study, formal institutional ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: India's logistics and supply chain sector faces escalating vulnerabilities from successive global shocks since the COVID-19 pandemic. Wi th logistic s costs at appr oxi mately 13-14% of GDP, that fragility carries serious economic consequences (KPMG, 2022). This study, grounded in a unified Resource-Based View and Dy namic C apabilities lens (Barney, 1991; Teece et al., 1997), synthesises peer-revi ewed literature, Ind ian policy documents, docu mented case evidence, and a pilot survey of twelve Indian logistics professionals to examine how AI technologies can build resil ient supply chains in the Indian context. Five AI capabilities are examined: machine learning for demand forecasti ng, reinfor cement learning fo r route optimisation, warehouse automati on, p redictive maintenance, and digital twin s. A mini case study of Delhivery and a pilot survey provide empirical grounding in Indian deployment conditions. The paper finds that AI's most pronounced value occurs during acute disruption events rather than under stable conditions. A central finding is that India's PM Gati Shakti and ULIP infrastructure creates a policy-technology nexus with few parallels among comparable economies, but this advantage risks being captured exclusively by large corporates. Without deliberate equity intervention, India faces a dual-speed logistics system: AI-enabled resilience concentrated among large firms, while the MSME-dominated majority of freight operators remains reactive and fragile. This paper contributes a unified RBV-Dynamic Capabilities analytical framework that explicitly integrates AI capabilities, India's policy infrastructure, and MSME equity constraints into a single conceptual model.

title: Cost and Value Analysis of the Beef Supply Chain in a Nomadic Livestock Economy: Empirical Evidence from Mongolia

detail.title: Cost and Value Analysis of the Beef Supply Chain in a Nomadic Livestock Economy: Empirical Evidence from Mongolia
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes cost formation and value creation in Mongolia's beef supply chain, a nomadic livestock system characterized by dispersed herder production, seasonal supply, informal intermediation, limited traceability, and weak formal processing capacity. Using a mixed-method approach based on document review, interviews, field observation, consumer survey evidence, and participant level cost calculations, the study compares the traditional beef supply chain, the reserve-meat supply chain, and the emerging fresh-meat supply chain. The findings show that the price of bone-in beef increases by approximately 30 percent from herders to final consumers in the traditional supply chain, while the fresh-meat supply chain increases the final price by approximately 40 percent because of additional costs related to animal health control, short-term feeding, hygienic slaughtering, sorting, processing, packaging, and organized retailing. However, these additional costs also create value by improving hygiene, reliability, traceability, freshness, and consumer confidence. The proposed cluster-based fresh-beef supply model can supply hygienic and traceable beef at a lower price than existing premium retail channels, provided that sufficient scale, coordinated procurement, and processing efficiency are achieved. The study contributes to agricultural value-chain literature by showing how participant-level cost analysis can identify bottlenecks, distinguish simple price increases from value-adding activities, and support the design of a more efficient and food-safe meat supply system in a nomadic livestock economy.

title: Inclusive Exclusion: Caste, Religion, and the Surface Empowerment Gap in Urban Microfinance

detail.title: Inclusive Exclusion: Caste, Religion, and the Surface Empowerment Gap in Urban Microfinance

detail.abstract: Microfinance has been widely promoted as an instrument for women's empowerment in urban India, yet aggregate outcome reporting routinely obscures how social identity mediates these benefits. Using data from the fifth round of the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019–21) restricted to urban women who were aware of microfinance programmes (N = 12,918; analytical N = 9,177 currently-in-union women), this study applies an intersectional quantitative framework to examine three hypotheses: (H1) whether microfinance participation is positively associated with household decision-making autonomy; (H2) whether caste and religion moderate this relationship; and (H3) whether a measurable surface empowerment gap—high behavioural autonomy combined with conservative gender attitudes—is predicted by caste, religion, and microfinance participation. Binary logistic regression, Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis, Spearman correlation, and interaction-term models were employed alongside original reliability and multicollinearity diagnostics. H1 is rejected: after controlling for age, education, employment, wealth, bank account ownership, and asset ownership, microfinance participation is associated with 21% lower odds of high decision autonomy (OR = 0.790, 95% CI: 0.681–0.917, p = .002), consistent with selection into patriarchal household contexts rather than a causal effect of loans. H2 is partially supported: caste moderates the microfinance–autonomy relationship through both main effects (OBC: OR = 0.817, p = .003; ST: OR = 1.333, p = .036) and a significant interaction term (MF×OBC: OR = 0.651, p = .009), while religion operates through robust baseline differences (Muslim: OR = 0.707, p < .001; Christian: OR = 1.675, p = .016) without significant MF-specific interactions. H3 is fully supported: a three-item autonomy index (Cronbach's α = .781) reveals that 27.9% of apparently autonomous urban women simultaneously accept at least one form of domestic violence, and this surface empowerment gap is most strongly predicted by microfinance participation (OR = 1.483, p < .001), OBC caste (OR = 2.276, p < .001), and SC caste (OR = 1.844, p < .001). Variance inflation factors (maximum VIF = 1.59) confirm multicollinearity is absent. The study contributes an operationalised construct of surface empowerment, demonstrates that credit access produces behavioural agency without normative transformation, and identifies OBC women as a structurally disadvantaged group underserved by both policy frameworks and empirical research.

title: Data Science for Retail Demand Prediction

detail.title: Data Science for Retail Demand Prediction
detail.abstract: Retail businesses face significant challenges in accurately predicting product demand due to rapidly changing consumer behavior, seasonal variations, promotional activities, and external economic factors. Accurate demand forecasting is essential for efficient inventory management, supply chain optimization, and improved customer satisfaction. This study explores the application of data science techniques for retail demand prediction using historical sales data, customer purchasing patterns, and external influencing variables. The research employs Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA), statistical modeling, and machine learning techniques to identify patterns in retail sales data and uncover key factors affecting product demand. Variables such as historical sales trends, seasonal fluctuations, promotional events, pricing strategies, and regional purchasing behavior are analyzed to understand their impact on demand variability. Data preprocessing techniques including data cleaning, feature engineering, and normalization are applied to ensure data quality and improve predictive accuracy. Predictive models such as linear regression, decision trees, and random forest algorithms are implemented to forecast future product demand. The results demonstrate that historical sales patterns and promotional activities are among the strongest predictors of retail demand, while seasonal trends significantly influence product consumption in specific time periods. Machine learning-based forecasting models provide more accurate and scalable predictions compared to traditional statistical methods. The findings highlight the importance of data-driven decision-making in retail operations, enabling businesses to optimize inventory levels, reduce stockouts and overstock situations, and enhance supply chain efficiency. This study contributes to the growing field of retail analytics by demonstrating how advanced data science techniques can improve demand forecasting accuracy and support strategic planning in modern retail environments.

detail.abstract:
The contemporary economy is undergoing a profound transformation, in which technological, organizational, and social innovations permeate digitalization processes. These changes are systemic and multidimensional, encompassing enterprises, labor markets, government structures, consumption patterns, and interpersonal relationships. Digital transformation has ceased to be merely a source of competitive advantage—it has become a prerequisite for long-term development and resilience to global shocks.

Innovation, understood more broadly than just technological progress, is defining new paths for economic growth. In the knowledge and data economy, the ability to generate, absorb, and diffuse these processes is crucial, determining the position of countries, regions, and organizations in global value chains. We are witnessing a redefinition of innovation: from classic product and process innovations to business, social, ecological, and systemic models based on networked collaboration.

This monograph analyzes the processes of innovation and the digital transformation of the economy – from theoretical foundations to practical implications for public policy, businesses, and society. It integrates the contributions of innovation economics, innovation systems theory, digitalization studies, and the concept of sustainable development. Emphasis is placed on the evolution of innovation models and the changing role of the state, technology, and human capital.

Digital technologies are transforming innovation organizationally and cognitively. Data, algorithms, and AI systems enable the identification of problems, the testing of hypotheses, and the scaling of solutions. They foster open innovations that engage users, communities, and external actors. At the same time, they generate regulatory, ethical, and social challenges that require holistic management.

The monograph's structure moves from theoretical concepts to practical dimensions. The chapters form a coherent narrative, presenting innovation as a dynamic process embedded in technological, institutional, and social conditions—with a perspective on future scenarios.

This work is intended for researchers, business practitioners, policymakers, and students seeking a comprehensive understanding of the connections between innovation and the digital transformation of the economy.

detail.abstract: El Estado Islámico (ISIS) articuló un ecosistema de financiamiento que integró coerción fiscal, control territorial, captura de activos y convergencia con redes criminales preexistentes. A partir de un enfoque de inteligencia estratégica (ciclo de inteligencia, OSINT, HUMINT y FININT), este trabajo mapea sus principales economías ilícitas, su arquitectura de transferencias y lavado, y las adaptaciones que le permitieron sostener la actividad insurgente tras la pérdida del territorio. Se propone un cuadro de mando con indicadores operativos y se desarrollan tipologías accionables para cumplimiento y fuerzas de seguridad. El análisis concluye con lecciones y líneas de disrupción que combinan sanciones específicas, vigilancia de TBML1, presión selectiva sobre corredores de hawala y medidas económicas que erosionen las rentas locales que apuntalan la extorsión.

title: When the Margin Becomes the Constraint Marginal Adaptive Capacity and the Hidden Limits of Transformation

detail.title: When the Margin Becomes the Constraint Marginal Adaptive Capacity and the Hidden Limits of Transformation

detail.abstract: Organisations and public systems often remain functional under ordinary load but degrade sharply when exposed to additional demand, variation, risk, scrutiny, or change. Existing literatures on constraints, queues, slack, resilience, high reliability, absorptive capacity, attention, legitimacy, and dynamic capabilities help explain aspects of this pattern. Yet they do not always isolate the specific adaptive margin that becomes binding at the point of incremental pressure. This paper develops the concept of Marginal Adaptive Capacity Constraints: conditions in which a system's ability to absorb one more unit of pressure is limited by depleted capacity, coordination, decision, assurance, or legitimacy margin. The paper defines the construct, proposes identification and falsification criteria, distinguishes it from rival explanations, and applies it to transformation-intensive settings including healthcare reform, AI governance, risk management, and energy-system resilience. The central argument is not that all failures are margin failures. Some are better explained by simple under-capacity, flawed strategy, technical defect, or misconduct. Rather, the claim is narrower: many systems that appear efficient, governed, or strategically aligned in steady state become fragile because the margins required for adaptation have already been consumed. In such cases, the practical question is not only what visible problem should be solved, but which margin is no longer able to absorb the next increment of pressure.

title: Under Pressure? Forced Migration and Public Health
affiliations: Universitat de València, University of Tübingen and Duke University

detail.title: Under Pressure? Forced Migration and Public Health
detail.abstract: We study how Venezuelan refugee inflows affect healthcare outcomes and municipal public finances in Brazil's universal, decentralized public healthcare system. For identification, we exploit cross-municipality variation in refugee exposure and use distance to Brazil's only official border crossing with Venezuela as an instrument. A one-percentage-point increase in the local refugee share raises overall mortality by 4.2 percent and infant mortality by up to 9 percent. We show these effects operate through both the poorer baseline health of arriving refugees and congestion in local health facilities. Municipalities increase the share of spending on healthcare, but absent compensating federal transfers, they do so at the expense of education's budget share. These results highlight the limits of decentralized service provision in absorbing the health and fiscal costs of concentrated migration shocks.

detail.title: From Nakba to Genocide: A Systematic Analysis of Israel's War Crimes, Illegal Land Seizures, and the Destruction of Palestine Under International Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research was conducted independently with no financial or personal relationships that could influence the findings.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a systematic analytical examination of Israel's military campaign in Gaza and its parallel settlement expansion in the West Bank, assessed through the frameworks of international humanitarian law, the UN Genocide Convention, the Rome Statute, the Fourth Geneva Convention, and the advisory opinions of the International Court of Justice. Based on verified data from the UN, ICC, ICJ, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, B'Tselem, and Israel's own military intelligence, this paper documents: the historical trajectory from the 1948 Nakba to the present; the specific war crimes and crimes against humanity for which ICC arrest warrants have been issued; the systematic destruction of civilian infrastructure, the use of starvation as a method of warfare, the killing of journalists, the torture and abuse of detainees, and the use of prohibited weapons; the illegal settlement enterprise and its acceleration in defiance of the July 2024 ICJ ruling; and the systemic international accountability failure that has enabled continued impunity. The paper does not argue from political or ideological premises. It argues from law — from the specific provisions of international humanitarian law that Israel has violated, as determined by the world's highest courts and most credible human rights institutions.

title: Mapping the Individual and Social Impacts of Foundation Models on Transportation Recommendation

detail.title: Mapping the Individual and Social Impacts of Foundation Models on Transportation Recommendation
detail.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly deployed in transportation recommendation systems, yet their impacts beyond raw accuracy remain unmeasured. This paper maps how these models affect travelers individually (satisfaction, autonomy, trust) and socially (equity, discrimination, spatial bias). Using a pre-trained foundation model in a simulated urban mobility environment, we find systematic trade-offs: individual-optimized recommendations consistently exacerbate social inequities, while fairness constraints reduce individual utility. Our computational framework reveals algorithmic assimilation effects, where minority neighborhoods become topological "pass-throughs" rather than destinations. We contribute replicable metrics for multi-impact assessment and argue that transportation AI must be evaluated by its distributional consequences, not efficiency alone.

title: Fatiga estructural: cuando la organización no puede sostener lo que construyó

detail.title: Fatiga estructural: cuando la organización no puede sostener lo que construyó
detail.abstract:
Este trabajo propone el concepto de fatiga estructural como categoría analítica para nombrar un fenómeno organizacional que la literatura existente no ha formulado con suficiente precisión: el proceso mediante el cual una organización pierde progresivamente su capacidad de sostener coordinación distribuida bajo carga sostenida, sin que ese proceso sea visible en los indicadores que habitualmente se usan para evaluarla. A diferencia de la inercia estructural, el declive organizacional o el burnout, la fatiga estructural puede coexistir con resultados estables o crecientes. Se instala a través de tres mecanismos-recentralización por excepción, vaciamiento del ownership y normalización de la dependencia-y no se vuelve visible hasta que una presión externa o un proceso de transformación más ambicioso que los anteriores exige más de lo que el sistema puede compensar. El trabajo describe el concepto, lo distingue de categorías adyacentes, explica sus mecanismos de instalación, analiza por qué permanece invisible y formula tres desplazamientos que implica para el diseño y la intervención organizacional.

This paper proposes the concept of structural fatigue as an analytical category to name an organizational phenomenon that existing literature has not formulated with sufficient precision: the process by which an organization progressively loses its capacity to sustain distributed coordination under sustained load, without that process being visible in the indicators typically used to evaluate it. Unlike structural inertia, organizational decline, or burnout, structural fatigue can coexist with stable or even growing results. It is installed through three mechanisms —recentralization by exception, ownership depletion, and normalization of dependence— and does not become visible until external pressure or a more ambitious transformation process demands more than the system can compensate. The paper describes the concept, distinguishes it from adjacent categories, explains its installation mechanisms, analyzes why it remains invisible, and articulates three diagnostic shifts it enables for organizational design and intervention.

detail.abstract: The global mobile accessories industry is undergoing a significant transformation driven by increasing environmental awareness and the urgent need to reduce plastic waste. Phone cases, traditionally manufactured using non-biodegradable plastics, contribute substantially to landfill accumulation and microplastic pollution. This paper examines the emergence of sustainable phone cases as a response to these environmental challenges, focusing on material innovation, corporate sustainability strategies, and evolving consumer behavior. Through analysis of industry practices such as those adopted by CASEKOO and OtterBox, the study highlights the integration of recycled plastics, plant-based biopolymers, and natural alternatives like cactusbased materials. The research further explores durability advancements, circular economy principles, and packaging innovations that support reduced environmental impact. The findings suggest that sustainable phone cases represent not only a product innovation but also a broader shift toward responsible consumption in the mobile device ecosystem.

title: Policy Impact of Exchange Rate Regimes on Financial Inclusion: Global Empirical Evidence and Causal Effects
affiliations: and Mohammed V University of Rabat

detail.title: Policy Impact of Exchange Rate Regimes on Financial Inclusion: Global Empirical Evidence and Causal Effects
detail.abstract: We assess the policy impact of exchange rate regimes on financial inclusion using rigorous econometric methods. Logit regressions examine associations between regime policies and inclusion, while panel fixed effects identify transmission channels through inflation, capital openness, and financial infrastructure. A Difference-inDifferences design evaluates the causal effect of transitioning to a floating regime. Results show that fixed regimes are negatively associated with financial inclusion, whereas floating regimes show positive effects. Financial infrastructure is the strongest positive channel. The Difference-inDifferences indicates higher inclusion in countries transitioning to floating regimes. Our study offers policymakers innovative insights for designing policies that enhance financial inclusion.

title: Data Mining Approaches to Social Discrimination in Foundation Model-Based Transportation Recommendation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Texas A & M University, Students

detail.title: Data Mining Approaches to Social Discrimination in Foundation Model-Based Transportation Recommendation
detail.abstract: The integration of foundation models (FMs) into transportation recommendation systemsranging from ride-hailing and route planning to multimodal transit-has brought unprecedented personalization and efficiency. However, these large-scale generative models are susceptible to learning and amplifying historical and systemic social biases, leading to discriminatory outcomes based on protected attributes such as race, gender, socioeconomic status, or disability. This paper presents a novel data mining framework to detect, quantify, and mitigate social discrimination in FM-based transportation recommendations. First, we propose bias-aware auditing methodologies that leverage counterfactual fairness testing and association rule mining to uncover hidden disparities in recommended travel times, surge pricing, ride acceptance rates, and accessibility options. Second, we introduce a discrimination pattern mining approach using sequential rule mining and graph neural networks to trace how biased representations propagate from training data through FM embeddings to final recommendations. Finally, we develop an adversarial debiasing mechanism integrated with prompt tuning to reduce disparate impact while preserving recommendation utility. Experiments on real-world ride-hailing and urban mobility datasets demonstrate that our approach successfully identifies discriminatory patterns overlooked by traditional fairness metrics and reduces group-level disparities by up to 40% without substantially degrading accuracy. This research underscores the critical need for fairness-aware data mining in the lifecycle of foundation models, offering practical tools for regulators, platform designers, and auditing bodies to ensure equitable transportation access in the age of generative AI.

title: From Cultural Barrier to Hermeneutic Bridge: Classical Chinese Literature in the Practice of Intercultural Learning

detail.title: From Cultural Barrier to Hermeneutic Bridge: Classical Chinese Literature in the Practice of Intercultural Learning
detail.abstract: This paper examines the potential of classical Chinese literature as a space for modeling and analyzing the深层 mechanisms of intercultural interaction. Drawing on the experience of working with the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms in a classroom of Russian students of international relations, the study demonstrates how a text that constitutes a concentrated expression of a national cultural code becomes a zone of "hermeneutic rupture." The actions of characters, motivated by Confucian, Daoist, and strategic concepts, are often perceived by the unprepared reader through the lens of Western rationality as illogical or irrational. The author proposes a pedagogical method-the "cultural-hermeneutic circle" (identification of rupture → contextual expansion → return and rereading)-aimed at overcoming this rupture. Using the episode of the "Empty City" strategy as a case study, the paper shows how this method transforms the initial perception of the protagonist's act from an "irrational gamble" into an understanding of it as a supreme manifestation of the traditional strategic paradigm. It is concluded that such analytical work with a literary text serves as an effective simulator for developing key intercultural competence-the ability to recognize, investigate, and interpret alternative value-semantic systems.

detail.abstract: China has developed one of the world's most operationally sophisticated AI governance systems. Whilst much Western commentary frames China's approach primarily through censorship or industrial policy, this paper argues that China's regulatory architecture is better understood as a procedural governance infrastructure embedded across the AI lifecycle. Drawing on regulatory instruments, enforcement activity, judicial decisions, technical standards and policy developments through April 2026, this paper analyses China's layered governance model across algorithm regulation, generative AI, synthetic content, ethics review, cybersecurity, content provenance and lifecycle accountability. The paper compares China's approach with the European Union and United States governance models and argues that China has moved further than most jurisdictions in operationalising governance through filing obligations, ethics review structures, technical provenance requirements and procedural enforcement mechanisms. The paper concludes with implications for international companies operating in China and argues that global AI governance is shifting from principle-based oversight towards procedural, technical and operational governance infrastructures.

title: Why is EV Charging So Unreliable? The Effects of Competition on Supplementary Service Quality

detail.title: Why is EV Charging So Unreliable? The Effects of Competition on Supplementary Service Quality

detail.abstract: Supplementary services—such as coffee shops providing free wi-fi and airlines offering airport lounges—are increasingly important to operational performance and customer experience. Yet little is known about what drives variation in their quality. While prior research shows that competition improves core service quality, we theorize that its effects on supplementary service quality depends on the source of competition. Competition from establishments offering the same core service enhances supplementary service quality, whereas competition from those offering different core services diminishes it. We test our hypotheses using data on the reliability of U.S. public EV charging stations, a widely-offered supplementary service across hotels, retailers, parking facilities, and other establishments. Analyzing 49,902 charging stations with 805,639 consumer reviews from 2011 to 2024, we apply machine learning methods to measure charging reliability. We find that competition among establishments offering the same core service is associated with higher reliability, suggesting that the positive effects of core service competition spill over to the quality of supplementary services. In contrast, competition from charging establishments with different core services is associated with lower station reliability. This latter effect is more consequential, as most nearby charging competitors provide different core services. Our results indicate that, within our sample period, a one-standard-deviation increase in such competition is associated with a 10.4% to 32.2% decline in service reliability scores over the subsequent five years. These findings have important implications for firms’ demand management and for public policy aimed at improving EV charging infrastructure performance.

detail.abstract: Places with similar mobility intensity can differ in the access conditions that support stable visitation and VIIRS-proxied local economic intensity. This distinction creates an observability problem: conventional spatial indicators and scalar mobility measures show where movement occurs, but not whether movement forms a durable structure of local access. We addressed this problem by developing a reproducible Spatial AI framework that makes mobility-based market infrastructure empirically observable from tract-level visitation behavior in Brazil. We define mobility-based market infrastructure as the inferred spatial organization of repeated access conditions; it is neither mobility intensity, directly observed market performance, nor physical infrastructure alone. Using 387,779 verified census tracts, we evaluated seven standardized mobility indicators and verified that the stored Market Infrastructure Index (MII) strongly aligned with the dominant mobility covariance dimension: PC1 explained 61.43% of the total variance and correlated 0.9447 with the stored MII. We then identified four localized mobility infrastructure regimes, evaluated their differentiation with VIIRS nighttime light intensity as an external proxy for local economic intensity, and reconstructed sub-tract variation in the São Paulo metropolitan window through mass-preserving downscaling. The results showed that mobility-based market infrastructure was not reducible to mobility intensity. Regimes differed in mobility profiles, nighttime-light distributions, and the fitted association between visit volume and nighttime light intensity, while the downscaled surface revealed within-tract variation concealed by administrative boundaries. The study contributes a spatial concept and a composite-index workflow for observing market-relevant access conditions through human mobility while preserving the distinction among movement, inferred infrastructure, and proxied economic intensity.

title: Quantum Consumer Strategy and the Percent Tool: A Practitioner Diagnostic for Consumer-Brand Relationships

detail.title: Quantum Consumer Strategy and the Percent Tool: A Practitioner Diagnostic for Consumer-Brand Relationships

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: not applicable

detail.abstract: Most strategy models assume that consumers behave in a rational, mostly stable, and predictable fashion. They are assumed to have clear choices, evaluate alternatives carefully, make trade-offs, and move through their journey in a linear manner. The reality is often different from this ideal picture. Consumers hold multiple and sometimes conflicting desires at the same time; they form emotional linkages with brands that go beyond conventional notions of value; and they often remain invested in a brand until a mental, financial, emotional, or practical block is removed-after which they may move suddenly. The central contribution of this paper is to convert an abstract theory of consumer behavior into a practical diagnostic instrument. It suggests that durable consumer positions are not built merely through differentiation, persuasion, convenience, or lock-in, but through the simultaneous alignment of product/ desire fit, emotional bond, and ease of action.

title: AI-Augmented Operations Research for Adaptive and Resilient Carbon Capture, Transport and Storage Networks: A Structured Review and Research Agenda

detail.title: AI-Augmented Operations Research for Adaptive and Resilient Carbon Capture, Transport and Storage Networks: A Structured Review and Research Agenda

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no specific funding for this work.

detail.abstract: Carbon capture, transport and storage (CCTS) networks are expected to support the decarbonization of hard-to-abate industrial sectors, especially where shared infrastructure can connect multiple emitters to reliable geological storage. Planning such networks is a complex Operations Research (OR) problem involving uncertain capture demand, storage capacity and injectivity, multimodal transport options, phased investment, disruption risks, regulatory constraints and capacity-allocation mechanisms. Although the CCTS and CCUS optimization literature has developed increasingly sophisticated models, recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) remain only partially integrated into network-level planning. This paper provides a structured review of CCTS network planning at the interface between OR and AI. It synthesizes optimization models for CO₂ capture, transport and storage systems, including supply chain design, multimodal transport, phase-based deployment, resilience and shared infrastructure. It then examines AI methods relevant to CCTS planning, including scenario generation, geological storage surrogate modelling, physics-informed learning, data assimilation, graph-based learning and learningassisted optimization. The review identifies a central gap: AI and OR advances remain fragmented, with limited translation of AI outputs into OR-compatible scenarios, constraints, parameters, uncertainty sets and decision rules. To address this gap, the paper proposes an AI-augmented OR framework linking data and policy inputs, AI-based uncertainty modelling, storage surrogate layers, multimodal network optimization, resilience analysis and governance mechanisms. The paper concludes with a research agenda for scalable, interpretable and policy-aligned CCTS planning models.

title: The impact of governance structures on the financial performance of Brazilian financial cooperatives
affiliations: Federal University of Santa Catarina (UFSC) and Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina (UFSC)

detail.title: The impact of governance structures on the financial performance of Brazilian financial cooperatives
detail.abstract: Financial cooperatives play an important role in promoting financial inclusion and community development. This study investigates how board characteristics, including size, gender diversity, and tenure, influence the financial performance of 930 Brazilian financial cooperatives between 2008 and 2022. Using panel data and the System Generalized Method of Moments (SYS-GMM), the results reveal that larger boards negatively affect performance due to coordination inefficiencies, while longer tenure on supervisory boards enhances stability and oversight. Female representation on the board of directors shows a significant negative association with financial performance, reflecting potential cultural and institutional challenges in governance. Cooperative size positively affects performance, reflecting economies of scale, while leverage and network affiliations pose financial challenges. The findings highlight the importance of designing governance structures that balance inclusivity, representation, and financial sustainability, providing insights for improving governance in cooperatives operating in emerging markets.

title: Is Crypto the New Oil?
affiliations: Texas A&M University School of Law

detail.title: Is Crypto the New Oil?
detail.abstract:
In spring of 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order No. 14233 to establish the U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, mimicking the nation’s Strategic Petroleum Reserve and elevating cryptocurrencies to the same essential-commodity status as oil. The analogy between crypto and oil came as a surprise to many. After all, oil and other hydrocarbons are increasingly viewed as relics from a bygone era of manufacturing-heavy early industrialization. By contrast, Bitcoin and other crypto assets represent a new tech-driven economy, where even our currencies are no longer held in leather purses but digital wallets. And, yet, there are an astounding number of parallels between the “black gold” of yore and the “digital gold” of tomorrow. 

Economically, both oil and crypto have turned savvy investors into millionaires, if not billionaires. Both assets have also been prone to boom-and-bust cycles as evidenced by the latest crypto crash. Environmentally, the world’s reliance on oil has long been criticized for its contributions to air pollution and global warming, among other environmental harms. Bitcoin’s near-insatiable thirst for energy has brought crypto assets in similar disrepute with the eco-minded crowd. These and other parallels notwithstanding, this Essay makes the case that crypto and its enabling blockchain technology are not path-dependent to follow the same trajectory as oil. Instead, they can generate enormous economic value without the environmental harms left in the oil industry’s wake. Thoughtful deployment of blockchain technology can dramatically improve climate and energy outcomes across a wide range of use cases—from accounting of carbon credits to peer-to-peer trading of electricity among neighbors. As a platform for smart contracts, blockchain technology can further enhance the efficiency and legitimacy of transactions, delivering climate benefits that far outweigh the blockchain’s own carbon footprint. Rather than vilify crypto and the blockchain, it is time to embrace this disruptive technology’s potential to be part of the solution to many of the world’s pressing energy security and sustainability challenges.

title: The Spillover Effect of Negative Narratives on Household Financial Decisions: Evidence from Community Suicides
affiliations: Sichuan University, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE) and Sichuan University

detail.title: The Spillover Effect of Negative Narratives on Household Financial Decisions: Evidence from Community Suicides
detail.abstract: Narrative economics posits that viral narratives drive economic fluctuations, yet causal micro-level evidence remains limited. Exploiting community suicides as exogenous narrative shocks, we investigate their spillover effects on household stock market participation using data from the China Household Finance Survey (2013--2021). Results show that exposure to community suicides reduces the probability of participation by 1.7 percentage points (a 10.6% relative decline), and this effect persists for 2--3 years. Mechanism analysis identifies belief, rather than emotion, as the dominant mechanism. While the impact on emotions increases linearly with community population, the negative impact on stock participation follows a U-shaped pattern synchronized with economic expectations, highlighting the cognitive nature of belief and narrative. Macro-level internet search indices for suicide corroborate these findings by predicting stock market contractions, further validating narrative contagion.

title: Hetero Behaviorus: A Complementary Agent Abstraction for Macroeconomics

detail.title: Hetero Behaviorus: A Complementary Agent Abstraction for Macroeconomics
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a complementary agent abstraction for macroeconomic analysis. While representative-agent and heterogeneous-agent models introduce heterogeneity primarily through variation in state variables such as wealth or liquidity, they typically retain a common decision-theoretic and expectation-formation structure across agents. The Hetero Behaviorus abstraction instead treats heterogeneity in decision architecture-including expectation formation and information processing-as potentially primitive. A minimal formal representation is provided in which aggregate outcomes depend on a distribution over decision mappings rather than solely on a distribution of states. The analysis clarifies conditions under which representative-agent reductions are valid and identifies environments in which aggregation depends on the distribution of behavioral architectures. The contribution is conceptual: by distinguishing heterogeneity in states from heterogeneity in decision rules, the paper refines the scope of representative reasoning in macroeconomic modeling.

title: Bayesian Persuasion and Cryptography
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: Bayesian Persuasion and Cryptography

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of New York Staff Report No. 1194
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Bayesian Persuasion assumes that a sender can commit ex ante to an information structure and then release the realized signal ex post. This paper asks when that commitment technology can itself be implemented. After observing the state, a sender who also observes the realized signal can suppress unfavorable draws even if every disclosed signal is verifiably correct. We define Receiver-Private Certified Bayesian Persuasion, a benchmark in which the receiver obtains the signal and a certificate of correct generation while the sender does not learn the realized branch of the experiment. The main theorem shows that this benchmark is equivalent in cryptographic power to secure two-party computation. Thus cryptography is not merely an implementation device for persuasion; when the sender must be prevented from changing the signal sent to the receiver, hiding the signal from the sender is necessary. In stress-test applications, the primitive removes ex post discretion over which realized disclosure reaches depositors.

title: Do AI Expectations Reduce Unemployment in the United States? Evidence from an AI Attention Index
affiliations: University of Nottingham,  and University of Bradford

detail.title: Do AI Expectations Reduce Unemployment in the United States? Evidence from an AI Attention Index

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper constructs an AI Attention Index from LexisNexis news coverage and embeds it within an augmented Phillips curve framework. It then examines the relationship between AI attention and unemployment in the United States using monthly data from January 2000 to December 2025. We find that greater AI attention is associated with lower unemployment. Nonlinear estimates reveal a U-shaped relationship, indicating diminishing marginal effects within the observed data range. The relationship weakens after the onset of COVID-19, with both linear and nonlinear effects reduced. These findings indicate that labour market effects of AI-related expectations are sensitive to macroeconomic regime shifts.

title: Stress Tests of Euro Area Banks with Skewed Normal Credit Risk Distributions

detail.title: Stress Tests of Euro Area Banks with Skewed Normal Credit Risk Distributions

publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper describes the 2023 euro area consultation top-down stress test that focused on the resilience of 91 systemically important banks’ capital buffers as of end-2022 to macro baseline and adverse scenarios over the period 2023-25. As a result, the paper is an illustration of a top-down stress test framework with an application to euro are banks. The 2023 euro area consultation top-down stress test included unbiased dynamic panel data estimators based on Lancaster (2002) for projecting profitability components and information on Pillar 3 disclosures (exposure-at-default, probability of default, loss-given-default, expected losses). The paper also expands the 2023 euro area consultation top-down stress test by considering risk-weight functions with Skew-Normal and Transmuted-Normal probability distributions for the idiosyncratic and systemic risk factors. The results of the stress test with both distributions indicate that most euro area banks were resilient under the 2023 euro area consultation baseline and adverse scenarios as of July 2023 (publication of the Staff report).

title: Cognitive Distance in Document Submission Systems: Why Users Struggle with Simple Digital Tasks

detail.title: Cognitive Distance in Document Submission Systems: Why Users Struggle with Simple Digital Tasks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental procedures. Ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Document submission workflows are widely used across public services, finance, healthcare, and digital platforms. Despite their apparent simplicity, these interactions frequently result in confusion, repeated failure, and task abandonment. Existing usability frameworks often explain such outcomes in terms of complexity or user effort, but these explanations do not fully account for breakdowns that persist even in low-effort interactions.

This paper analyzes document submission systems through the lens of cognitive distance, defined as the gap between a system’s conceptual structure and the mental model constructed by the user during interaction. Using a qualitative conceptual case analysis of file upload workflows, the paper shows how routine design choices, such as file format restrictions, size constraints, and ambiguous terminology, generate systematic misalignment between system logic and user understanding.

The paper introduces externalized processing as a design-level mechanism through which systems shift reasonably automatable preprocessing tasks, such as format conversion and file compression, to users. This shift increases both procedural effort and interpretive burden, often requiring users to rely on external tools and trial-and-error strategies.

The analysis suggests that many breakdowns in document submission workflows are not incidental usability issues but reflect a broader problem in how systems distribute computational and interpretive responsibilities. The findings have implications for designing more interpretable, accessible, and cognitively aligned information systems.
