title: Business Management and Social Innovation: A Synergistic Approach to Sustainable Development in India

detail.title: Business Management and Social Innovation: A Synergistic Approach to Sustainable Development in India
detail.abstract: This paper explores the dynamic intersection of business management and social innovation in driving sustainable development in India. It examines how business leaders, academic institutions, and policymakers can collaboratively foster inclusive growth through innovative social solutions embedded within corporate strategy. Drawing on case studies, theoretical frameworks, and policy analysis, the study illustrates the synergistic potential of integrating social innovation into core management functions to address pressing socioeconomic challenges. The paper concludes by emphasizing academia's pivotal role in generating knowledge, nurturing socially responsible leaders, and shaping policy discourse to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

title: The Psychological Underpinnings of Panic Buying in a Pandemic and the Mitigating Role of Hope-Framed Interventions

detail.title: The Psychological Underpinnings of Panic Buying in a Pandemic and the Mitigating Role of Hope-Framed Interventions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: All studies were approved by the Institutional Review Board at University of Rhode Island
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the National Science Foundation (award # 2027620)

detail.abstract: Research on consumer stockpiling, the accumulation of greater than normal quantity of items, suggests that stockpiling is motivated both by the desire to consume early, and consuming more than usual amounts. While stockpiling benefits utility maximization through repeated consumption of preferred brands, and savings on transaction costs through fewer trips to the market, excessive stockpiling incurs financial (accumulation of debt) and psychological (dealing with clutter in the house) costs. During the COVID-19 pandemic, consumer stockpiling surfaced as panic buying, motivated by a pandemic-induced scarcity effect, where costs to consumers were more salient than benefits, rendering the behavior as maladaptive. The current research was conducted during the pandemic (2020-21) with the aim of: 1) exploring the psychological roots and antecedents of panic buying, and 2) examining effects of various social marketing interventions in mitigating the panic factor. Five studies (two surveys among national pool of respondents, a longitudinal study, an experiment, and a longitudinal randomized controlled trial) exhibit felt anxiety and lack of situational control as psychological roots of panic buying, and anticipated regret as the predominant influence factor. In addition, hope-based (vs. situational control based vs. benchmark) interventions were most effective in reducing panic buying overtime.

title: Holacracy in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Reimagining Organizational Governance, Productivity, and Decision-Making

detail.title: Holacracy in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Reimagining Organizational Governance, Productivity, and Decision-Making
detail.abstract:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) alters the feasibility, performance, and governance logic of Holarctic organizational structures relative to traditional hierarchies. Drawing on transaction cost economics, complexity theory, and network theory, the paper develops a framework in which AI functions as "coordination compressing capital" that reduces information-processing and monitoring costs, while holacracy reallocates formal decision rights from positional managers to role-based circles. The core question addressed is whether AI makes holacracy more viable, redundant, or transforms it into a qualitatively different hybrid.  

The methodology combines: (i) quantitative synthesis of recent firm-level studies on AI adoption and productivity (BIS EIBIS-ORBIS panel 2019-2024, European and U.S. firms; NBER and CEPR executive surveys 2025-2026; field experiments on generative AI at work), (ii) meta-analyses and case-based evidence on holacracy outcomes (including Zappos and a 2024 meta-analysis of 15 Holarctic firms), and (iii) emerging research on LLM-based multi-agent simulations and AI-agent organizational architectures (2023-2025). Empirically, AI adoption is associated with labor-productivity gains of roughly 4% at the firm level in Europe after instrumentation, 10-20% task-level productivity gains in generative AI field experiments, and modest but rising organization-wide improvements reported by executives, alongside evidence of hierarchy flattening and widened spans of control in AI-intensive firms. Holacracy and broader self-organization yield moderate performance and innovation gains, particularly in smaller, knowledge-intensive firms, while also increasing cognitive load and dependence on cultural fit.  

The analysis shows that AI and holacracy interact in three main ways: AI substitutes for intermediate managerial layers, complements decentralized decision-making by reducing coordination latency, and re-centralizes certain meta-governance functions in algorithmic systems and small senior "orchestrator" groups. The paper concludes that AI does not uniformly validate or invalidate holacracy; instead, it generates new hybrid forms with AI-enabled holacracy and AI-assisted hierarchy in which the key design problem shifts from "who decides?" to "under what protocols do humans and AI systems jointly decide?".

title: Facial Emotion Recognition and the EU AI Act: Why Current Models Cannot Be Lawfully Deployed in Europe, and What Comes Next

detail.title: Facial Emotion Recognition and the EU AI Act: Why Current Models Cannot Be Lawfully Deployed in Europe, and What Comes Next

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: author himself

detail.abstract: Facial emotion recognition (FER) systems have reached sufficient technical maturity to be deployed at scale-yet the European legal framework governing their use has simultaneously rendered most current approaches unlawful. This paper examines the intersection of state-of-the-art FER architectures and the EU AI Act, with particular focus on Article 5(1)(f), which prohibits the inference of emotions in workplace and educational settings. Through empirical comparison of four architectures-EfficientNet V2, ConvNeXt V2 Nano, Vision Transformer (ViT-Tiny), and SigLIP2-trained on AffectNet YOLO and FER-2013 datasets, we demonstrate that the technical limitations of current FER systems (dataset bias, class imbalance, Ekman taxonomy constraints, hard-label Softmax classification) are structurally aligned with the scientific critique embedded in EU AI Act Recital 44. We propose a compliance-oriented architectural transition: from discrete hard-label classification toward zero-shot, high-dimensional probabilistic inference using SigLIP2 combined with the EmoNet-40 taxonomy, trained on synthetic ethically sourced data. This framework offers a technically sound and regulatorily defensible pathway for affective computing research in the post-February 2025 enforcement environment.

title: "HARNESSING THE POTENTIAL OF 'ONE WORLD-ONE BUSINESS' STRATEGY IN SHAPING THE FUTURE OF INDIA'S TOURISM INDUSTRY"

detail.title: "HARNESSING THE POTENTIAL OF 'ONE WORLD-ONE BUSINESS' STRATEGY IN SHAPING THE FUTURE OF INDIA'S TOURISM INDUSTRY"
detail.abstract: In an increasingly interconnected global economy, the concept of "One World-One Business" has emerged as a strategic imperative for nations seeking to maximize their economic potential. This paradigm shift emphasizes the importance of leveraging international partnerships and fostering a unified approach to business operations across borders. Nowhere is this strategy more pertinent than in the dynamic and multifaceted tourism industry, particularly in the vibrant landscape of India. India's tourism sector stands as a testament to the transformative power of embracing a "One World-One Business" ethos. As one of the world's most culturally diverse and historically rich nations, India boasts an unparalleled array of attractions, from ancient monuments to pristine natural landscapes. Its tourism industry serves as a crucial engine of economic growth, contributing significantly to the country's GDP and providing employment opportunities to millions of people across various segments of society. The notion of 'One World-One Business' has grown in popularity in today's global economy, emphasising the interconnection and interdependence of markets around the world. Within this paradigm, the tourism industry emerges as a critical sector, facilitating cultural interchange, economic growth, and sustainable development. The present paper investigates the applicability and consequences of implementing the 'One World-One Business' approach in the context of India's booming tourism industry. It investigates the prospects and limitations of such an approach, as well as the potential synergies it might generate for encouraging equitable growth and international cooperation. This study intends to provide insights into how India might use the ideas of 'One World-One Business' through an interdisciplinary examination that includes economic, social, and environmental elements. Moreover, India's embrace of digital technologies has further amplified the impact of its "One World-One Business" strategy within the tourism industry. With the proliferation of smartphones and internet connectivity, travelers today have unprecedented access to information and resources that transcend geographical boundaries. Leveraging this digital landscape, India has deployed innovative marketing tactics, such as virtual tours and social media campaigns, to engage with potential visitors on a global scale. This digital outreach not only enhances the visibility of India as a tourism destination but also fosters a sense of interconnectedness and inclusivity among travelers from diverse backgrounds.

title: Modeling Prescriptions and Sales Visits of a Pharmaceutical Drug Using A Causal Transformer: Estimation and Dynamic Optimization
affiliations: University of Regensburg - Faculty of Business, Economics & Information Systems

detail.title: Modeling Prescriptions and Sales Visits of a Pharmaceutical Drug Using A Causal Transformer: Estimation and Dynamic Optimization
detail.abstract: We introduce a causal transformer (CT) linking the number of monthly prescriptions of a pharmaceutical to sales visits at the level of individual physicians. The CT allows for greater flexibility compared to previous models with respect to dynamic and nonlinear effects. With respect to nonlinearities the transformer attains greater flexibility by including feedforward neural nets with one hidden layer and nonlinear activation functions. The CT combines two subnetworks (one for past sales visits, the other for past prescriptions) into a joint network and considers static attributes of physicians. Current hidden variables of the CT depend on all past hidden variables. Monthly prescriptions result from a negative binomial regression, sales visits from a Poisson regression. We compare the CT to a related hierarchical Bayesian regression model for prescriptions that allows for dynamics by including prescriptions of the previous period. The CT clearly outperforms this regression model as the greater average negative log likelihood of the latter shows. We deal with static effects of sales visits on prescriptions by marginal effects and elasticities. We also measure dynamic effects of both sales visits and prescriptions. We optimize sales visits for each physician in future periods with the sum of discounted expected profits as objective function. We approximately solve this dynamic optimization problem by reinforcement learning.

title: Assessing The Role Of Ai Advertising Algorithm Literacy In Supporting The Success Of Smes' Online Businesses In Kenya

detail.title: Assessing The Role Of Ai Advertising Algorithm Literacy In Supporting The Success Of Smes' Online Businesses In Kenya
detail.abstract:
The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in advertising has slowly transformed the operations of businesses globally, establishing markets in online platforms and deviating from traditional physical markets. To this end, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are increasingly turning to establishing their presence in online markets through advertisements and customer engagement strategies towards expanding their customer reach (Masikonte, Kitur, & Maina, 2024). To achieve this, SMEs globally and particularly in Kenya rely heavily on the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital advertising. However, the successful integration of AI tools for business advertisements depends largely on the entrepreneurs’ literacy in understanding the application of AI-driven advertising algorithms to enhance online presence and strengthen customer engagement.

This study assesses the role of AI advertising algorithm literacy in supporting the success of SMEs’ online businesses in Kenya. Specifically, the study will examine SMEs' levels of literacy in AI advertising algorithms, analyze how literacy influences the adoption and utilization of online advertising tools, determine the relationship, if any, between literacy and online business success indicators such as visibility and sales growth, and lastly identify the challenges faced by SMEs in acquiring and applying knowledge on current AI advertising tools.

The research combines various data analysis approaches to aggregate descriptive, inferential, and thematic data. Specifically, data collection involves using structured questionnaires administered through the Kobo Collect tool to a sample of SMEs engaged in online business across selected urban centers in Kenya.

Findings indicate that SME entrepreneurs with higher levels of AI advertising algorithm literacy – measured through their ability to interpret campaign metrics against their advertising budget – report significantly greater online sales growth (Sonoiya, 2022), customer engagement, and return on advertising budgets spent. Conversely, limited literacy results in misallocation of resources, underperformance in digital campaigns, loss of opportunities to grow and compete effectively in the online platforms, resulting in potential losses.

The study concludes that enhancing AI advertising literacy is critical for entrepreneurs to unlock the full potential of online business success among Kenyan SMEs. Policy implications highlight the need for structured capacity building initiatives in digital training programs and collaborative efforts between technology providers and SME associations, including government agencies, to bridge the literacy gap. Ultimately, the research will contribute to academic knowledge on AI adoption in developing economies.

title: Football Quotient: Quantifying National Playing Ability and the Disproportionate Returns to Development Quality in European Professional Football

detail.title: Football Quotient: Quantifying National Playing Ability and the Disproportionate Returns to Development Quality in European Professional Football
detail.abstract:
Background. A persistent empirical puzzle in European football is why small nations—notably Serbia, Croatia, and Scotland—produce professional players at rates far exceeding large, well-resourced nations such as Germany, France, and the Netherlands. Existing accounts cite culture and infrastructure, but lack a quantitative theoretical framework capable of making testable predictions. 

Methods. We introduce the Football Quotient (FQ), a latent-ability construct modelled as a normally distributed trait (σ = 15, analogous to the psychometric IQ scale), and derive the implied national mean FQ for 29 European nations from their senior professional player conversion rates. Player counts were obtained from Transfermarkt squad data for 2024/25, restricted to senior professionals (born ≤ 2003), and cross-validated against CIES Football Observatory reports. Registered player totals were compiled from FIFA Big Count supplemented by federation-level sources. Monte Carlo confidence intervals (n = 10,000) propagated registration uncertainty.

Results. The pan-European conversion rate of 1.17 per 1,000 active players implies a professional threshold of FQ = 145.6. Implied national means range from Serbia (109.0; 95% CI 105.9–112.6) to Germany (96.5; 95% CI 95.5–97.4). Regression modelling of FIFA rankings (n = 29) identified the number of professionals based abroad as the strongest single predictor (adj-R2 = 0.502, p < 0.001), with pool size adding independent variance; the final two-predictor model achieved adj-R2 = 0.633. A preliminary lagged analysis using historical CIES expatriate counts shows that the 2017 abroad count retains a Spearman correlation of +0.52 with the April 2026 FIFA ranking across thirteen European nations, consistent with a leading-indicator interpretation. Relative age effect analysis revealed a pan-European birth-month Q1/Q4 ratio of 1.39 (χ2 11 = 363.6, p < 0.001), with a theoretically consistent reversal in England and Wales (August academic cutoff). Mean FQ improvement of +3 points is analytically equivalent to multiplying the participating population by 1.7–2.0×, depending on baseline distance from threshold. 

Conclusions. The FQ framework offers national associations a quantitative basis for development strategy. Because professional output is a threshold phenomenon, raising the population mean generates disproportionate returns that participation growth alone cannot match at comparable cost. The European Union’s free movement of labour provides an empirical market mechanism that continuously calibrates the threshold, lending ecological validity to the model. Associations below the European mean face structural underperformance; those with high participation bases but declining registration trends face a lagged collapse risk. The framework itself and its qualitative implications — mean-shifting efficiency, the size premium, the threshold mechanism, and EU labour-market calibration — are the durable contribution; exact national point estimates are illustrative given current heterogeneity in registration data, but the ranking direction and efficiency calculations are robust within plausible adjustments to the denominators.

title: Growing in Saturated Markets: The Role of Time in Brand Switching
affiliations: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Erasmus Research Institute of Management (ERIM), VU University Amsterdam and VU University Amsterdam

detail.title: Growing in Saturated Markets: The Role of Time in Brand Switching

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors certify that they have no affiliations with or involvement in any organization or entity with any financial or non-financial interest in the subject matter or materials discussed in this manuscript. The authors have no funding to report.

detail.abstract: Growing market share in saturated markets is hard: total category demand is fixed, and shifting consumer brand preferences requires costly and slow behavioral change. Yet purchase timing(how soon and how often consumers buy) remains a largely untapped lever that can redistribute market share with far less disruption. We propose a prescriptive framework for increasing brand market share in saturated markets by jointly optimizing switching probabilities and purchase timing. We introduce a data-driven heterogeneous- time Markov network that separately models transition likelihoods and interpurchase durations. We derive closed-form solutions for market share, sales rates, and timing metrics without simulation or restrictive distributional assumptions on the purchase timing. We combine these analytical expressions with a gradient-based algorithm and obtain a scalable and interpretable optimization algorithm that identifies minimal changes in behavior required to reach a target outcome. We apply our model to a large-scale household-level panel data, and find that simultaneously e!ecting changes in purchase timing and switching probabilities produces substantially larger market share gains than e!ecting changes in switching probabilities alone, while requiring far smaller shifts inconsumer behavior. Results demonstrate that modest reductions in purchase friction can substitute for large preference shifts, making timing a high-leverage managerial control variable.

title: Perception of K-pop Fan Consumers in Blumenau Regarding Costumes in Music Videos: Visual Identity, Narrative, and Aesthetic Experience | Percepção dos consumidores fãs de K-pop em Blumenau sobre figurinos em videoclipes: identidade visual, narrativa e experiência estética

detail.title: Perception of K-pop Fan Consumers in Blumenau Regarding Costumes in Music Videos: Visual Identity, Narrative, and Aesthetic Experience | Percepção dos consumidores fãs de K-pop em Blumenau sobre figurinos em videoclipes: identidade visual, narrativa e experiência estética
detail.abstract: This study analyzes the perception of K-pop fans in Blumenau, Santa Catarina, regarding the use of costumes in music videos, investigating how these elements contribute to the visual identity of groups and to the interpretation of their messages. Through an exploratory and descriptive study, in-depth interviews were conducted to capture fans’ perceptions of the relationship between costumes, choreography, and musical narrative. The results indicate that costumes play a central role in the visual harmony of music videos, distinguishing each group and highlighting their unique characteristics. Furthermore, costumes expand the visual and emotional narrative, strengthening fans’ connection to the genre. It is therefore considered that these aesthetic elements intensify the fans’ experience.

title: A Multi-Layer Analytical Framework for Customer Retention in Voluntary Health Insurance

detail.title: A Multi-Layer Analytical Framework for Customer Retention in Voluntary Health Insurance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study is based on anonymized administrative data and does not involve direct interaction with human subjects. No ethical approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Customer churn in voluntary health insurance is a multidimensional decision problem that resists reduction to a single probability score. This paper proposes an integrated four-layer analytical framework combining topological behavioral segmentation (UMAP + HDBSCAN), explainable churn prediction (XGBoost + SHAP), survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier, Cox proportional hazards, Random Survival Forest), and financial simulation. The framework is validated on administrative records from a Colombian health insurer covering approximately 298,000 complementary plan subscribers (1,019,505 subscription-period records after censoring filters; 40 predictors; stratified 80/20 split). XG-Boost achieves AUC = 0.86 (KS = 56.3%, Lift@10% = 3.29, Brier = 0.125), compared with 0.80 for logistic regression. The Random Survival Forest yields C-index = 0.818 with time-dependent AUC near 0.90 at 3 months and 0.88 at 12 months. Topological segmentation uncovers two structural phenomena: a Health Paradox, in which young, healthy, low-utilization subscribers exhibit the highest cancellation volatility; and a Fortress Effect, in which utilization of the insurer's own provider network is associated with a 31.6% lower instantaneous cancellation hazard (Cox HR = 0.684, p < 0.001). The 8,033 density-based outliers identified by HDB-SCAN are retained as a dedicated operational segment for case-by-case review. Financial simulation under baseline assumptions projects net annual benefit of COP $5,732 million (ROI 302%). The central contribution lies in the integration of these analytical layers, which are necessary when considered together: each resolves a dimension of the retention problem-identity, causation, timing, and coverage of atypical cases-that the others do not fully capture.

title: Algorithmic Logistics and Labor Economics in the On-Demand delivery Ecosystem: A Socio-Technical Analysis with a Proposal for Rider-Centric Intelligence

detail.title: Algorithmic Logistics and Labor Economics in the On-Demand delivery Ecosystem: A Socio-Technical Analysis with a Proposal for Rider-Centric Intelligence
detail.abstract: Food delivery has, in less than a decade, moved from a neighbourhood trade conducted by phone to a globally orchestrated, platform-mediated logistics industry. What looks to a customer like a thirty-minute ride from a kitchen to a doorstep is, underneath, a chain of subsecond decisions taken by forecasting engines, dispatch heuristics, sensor-fusion models and pricing controllers. This paper offers a structured reading of that stack and of the labour economy it produces. I trace the methodological evolution of demand forecasting from knearest-neighbour regressions to recurrent and probabilistic deep networks, examine dispatch and matching engines through Deliveroo's Frank algorithm and Uber Eats' triple-batching logic, and explain how sensor fusion-accelerometers, gyroscopes, conditional random fields-converts a noisy GPS trace into a fine-grained model of the courier's working day. I then turn to the economic and social consequences. Drawing on Berkeley Labor Center net-pay data, the Stanford rideshare gender-gap study, and recent reporting on the Bologna Frank ruling, the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection minimum-pay rule, the EU Platform Work Directive 2024/2831 and China's 2027 algorithm-bargaining mandate, the paper argues that the gig delivery system has now passed into a 'hyper-algorithmic' phase whose efficiency cannot be separated from its labour-market effects. As a constructive contribution, I outline FindMyRider, a rider-centric intelligence platform combining demand forecasting, density-aware heatmap visualisation and explainable, contestable decision logsintended as a research blueprint, not as a commercial system. The paper closes with limitations, ethical reflections and an agenda for further work on retrieval-augmented, human-in-the-loop logistics analytics.

title: Feeling Good vs. Doing Good: Hedonic Value, Retail Therapy, and the Emotional Displacement of Ethical Intent in Fashion and Beauty Consumption

detail.title: Feeling Good vs. Doing Good: Hedonic Value, Retail Therapy, and the Emotional Displacement of Ethical Intent in Fashion and Beauty Consumption

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author.
declarations.ethicsApproval: All survey respondents and interview participants provided informed consent prior to their participation in this study.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the psychological mechanisms by which emotional purchase drivers displace ethical intent in fashion and beauty consumption. While existing research on sustainable consumer behavior largely emphasizes structural barriers and informational deficits, this paper argues that the emotional dimension of purchasing constitutes an equally significant and systematically underexplored pathway through which ethical commitments are overridden at the point of purchase. Specifically, hedonic value, retail therapy, and identity-driven in-group signaling operate as three co-determining emotional drivers that suppress ethical reasoning in the purchasing encounter. Drawing on the Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR) model, approachavoidance conflict theory, and Freud's narcissism of small differences, alongside mixed-methods data from a consumer survey (n = 100) and semi-structured interviews with senior industry practitioners, the paper introduces the Emotional Purchase Displacement Model (EPDM). Survey findings reveal that 76% of respondents acknowledge their values bend under stress, 78% self-identify as ethical consumers, yet only 34% report willingness to shop ethically when doing so is inconvenient. The paper offers practical implications for fashion and beauty brand strategy, with particular attention to how emotional marketing can be redesigned to make ethical purchasing feel emotionally rewarding rather than emotionally costly.

title: Private Label vs. National Brand: Asymmetric Effects of Store Displays and Direct Mailers

detail.title: Private Label vs. National Brand: Asymmetric Effects of Store Displays and Direct Mailers
detail.abstract: Store displays and direct mailers are some of the popular methods by which retailers and national brands promote their products to households. In this research we study the effect of store displays and direct mailer promotions on retail sales, and whether such promotions benefit both private label and national brands equally or asymmetrically. We consider a novel dataset of 2500 households and their purchases across 115 different stores over 93 weeks. The dataset includes information on store displays and type of direct mailer by product, store location and week, which allows us to match household's purchase of product to the presence of different types of store displays and direct mailers for the products. In our analysis, we consider fixed effects regression models with store and week fixed effects. We find that front and rear store display, in-shelf display, and inside-page and front-page features on direct mailers have positive effects on household purchase of product. The efficacy of such promotions, however, varies for private labels and national brands, such that while store front displays work in favor of national brands, front-page features on direct mailers benefit private labels. We also find that in-shelf displays favor private labels as compared to national brands.

title: Governed Agentic Automation for Chargebacks: A Prompt-First Architecture for Policy-Driven Enterprise Workflows

detail.title: Governed Agentic Automation for Chargebacks: A Prompt-First Architecture for Policy-Driven Enterprise Workflows

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial or personal interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This work does not involve human subjects research. All data and examples are derived from internal systems and have been generalized to preserve confidentiality.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was conducted as part of the authors’ roles at eBay Inc. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract: Generative AI adoption is outpacing reliable productionization in enterprise workflows that combine structured inputs, policy constraints, and operational risk. This technical report presents a prompt-first architecture for chargeback automation and agentic decision support that replaces brittle, retrieval-heavy integrations with a governed orchestration layer for prompt management, policy enforcement, evaluation, and observability. Using chargeback dispute handling as a case study, the report analyzes a transition from Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to modular prompt chaining and agentic execution over structured case inputs. In internal deployment measurements, the redesigned system reduced generation latency by 35%, improved internal quality scores by 20%, enabled near-immediate policy updates without re-indexing, and auto-resolved 85% of policy issues before human review. Reviewer agreement improved from Cohen’s kappa 0.65 to 0.82 across three optimization cycles. The results suggest that, for decision-grade automation over structured enterprise data, governed prompt orchestration can outperform more complex retrieval-heavy designs in speed, controllability, and operational fitness. Some system names and implementation details are generalized for confidentiality.

title: Decision Risk: A Structural Governance Framework for AI-Assisted Software Development

detail.title: Decision Risk: A Structural Governance Framework for AI-Assisted Software Development

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or organizational affiliations that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research received no external funding and was independently conducted by the author.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

keywords: Decision observability JEL Classification M15 Information Technology Management O33 Technological Change L86 Information and Internet Services

detail.abstract: AI-assisted software development accelerates code production but undermines the governance infrastructure that makes development decisions reproducible, attributable, and auditable. When AI agents generate code, the governing conditions-authorized scope, governing rules, and decision reasoning-are rarely preserved as persistent evidence. As a result, code artifacts accumulate while the governance legitimacy of the decisions that produced them remains indeterminate. This paper introduces Decision Risk, a structural governance framework that addresses this gap through four integrated components. Decision observability defines the evidence conditions under which development decisions can be structurally examined. Decision Analysis classifies observable decisions into five mutually exclusive states based on set-relational conditions among visible scope, artifact scope, and outcome scope. The Decision Risk model interprets these analytical states as governance risks, defining four risk categories, twelve threat types across three families, four manifestation levels, and a severity assessment matrix. The Risk Governance Model translates risk assessments into governance actions through three intervention levels and a PDCA cycle with risktype-specific strategies. A case demonstration shows a single development task progressing through three governance stages, producing a measurable risk trajectory from unobservable risk to contained over-scope risk as governance infrastructure matures.

title: Structural Degradation: From Stateless Generation to Layered Software Decay in AI-Generated Code A Three-Layer Taxonomy of Software Decay and Its Governance Implications

detail.title: Structural Degradation: From Stateless Generation to Layered Software Decay in AI-Generated Code A Three-Layer Taxonomy of Software Decay and Its Governance Implications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or organizational affiliations that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, personal data, animal subjects, or clinical procedures. Therefore, ethics committee approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author using personal resources.

detail.abstract: Generative AI introduces a fundamental structural mismatch into software engineering: code is produced through stateless probabilistic generation, yet integrated into systems that evolve through stateful, temporally constrained architectures. While existing discourse concentrates on hallucinations, isolated defects, and productivity gains, it lacks a unified account of the degradation mechanisms unique to AI-assisted development-mechanisms that are neither reducible to individual bugs nor adequately captured by traditional notions of technical debt. This paper proposes a three-layer taxonomy of structural degradation in AI-generated code, organized across the Intent, Structural, and Behavioral layers. We first establish the root cause model: a threedimensional discontinuity-temporal, authorial, and state-based-arising from the interaction between stateless generation and stateful system evolution. We then define and differentiate eighteen distinct degradation phenomena distributed across the three layers, each characterized by its definition, distinction from adjacent concepts, illustrative examples, and degradation path logic. Finally, we demonstrate that these phenomena propagate across layers through identifiable causal mechanisms, and articulate the Visibility Inversion Principle: detection probability is inversely proportional to origination layer depth, while damage magnitude is directly proportional to failure layer depth. The contribution of this paper is foundational. It establishes a coherent ontology of degradation patterns and their cross-layer propagation dynamics, providing a necessary conceptual foundation for future analytical, governance, and architectural research in AI-assisted software engineering.

title: Dual-Pattern Cost Intelligence in Enterprise SaaS Platforms: A Framework for AI Workload Forecasting and FinOps Strategy

detail.title: Dual-Pattern Cost Intelligence in Enterprise SaaS Platforms: A Framework for AI Workload Forecasting and FinOps Strategy
detail.abstract:
As enterprises shift from human-centric operations toward AI-agent-driven workflows, cloud infrastructure costs are displacing headcount as the dominant operational expenditure. This shift surfaces a structural problem in enterprise financial planning: cloud cost forecasts treat platform spend as a single homogeneous function of usage volume, when enterprise SaaS platforms built on shared cloud infrastructure actually contain two distinct cost behaviors operating simultaneously. Direct feature-layer costs scale linearly with usage, reflecting constant marginal cost per invocation. Indirect platform-layer costs scale logarithmically, reflecting economies of scale as shared infrastructure fixed costs are amortized across a growing user base. Treating these as a single blended rate produces forecasting errors that grow with volume and force defensive over-budgeting, immobilizing capital that should be deployed for growth.

This paper introduces the Dual-Pattern Cost Intelligence (DPCI) framework, which formalizes the bifurcation and provides closed-form forecasting equations for each cost component. The paper proposes the Strategic Infrastructure Accuracy Score (SIAS), a three-dimensional benchmarking instrument measuring forecast precision, resource elasticity, and cost model fidelity. Drawing on established platform economics theory and the dynamic capabilities literature, the paper reframes FinOps as a strategic capability rather than a cost-cutting function, with implications for capital reallocation, product pricing, and AI investment governance. The framework offers practitioners a principled foundation for cloud cost forecasting in the AI era.

title: "Whitespace is Risk": Evaluating Information Density as a Trust Mechanism in High-Anxiety Transactional Interfaces

detail.title: "Whitespace is Risk": Evaluating Information Density as a Trust Mechanism in High-Anxiety Transactional Interfaces
detail.abstract: Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) guidelines often champion minimalism to reduce cognitive load, yet this "Less is More" paradigm may fail in high-context cultures where users equate information density with transparency. This study investigates whether older Indian users ("Digital Immigrants") prefer "Information Radiators", interfaces that maximize data density over standard Minimalist designs in high-stakes financial transactions. We conducted a between-subjects experiment (N=45) simulating a railway booking task to compare a Progressive Disclosure UI against a High-Density UI. Results reveal a "Perception Paradox": while the Minimalist interface was statistically faster (p<0.05), the High-Density interface achieved a 100% success rate and was rated as significantly "easier" by older participants (N=15). We argue that for vulnerable demographics, whitespace introduces "Interactional Risk" by hiding system status, whereas density acts as a necessary trust mechanism. These findings challenge the universality of minimalist design and suggest that "Safe Clutter" is essential for digital financial inclusion in the Global South. title: The Sokal-Boström Paradox: Empirical Evidence for the Inverse Relationship Between Citation Density and Fact-Checking in LLM-Synthesized Scholarly Prose

detail.title: The Sokal-Boström Paradox: Empirical Evidence for the Inverse Relationship Between Citation Density and Fact-Checking in LLM-Synthesized Scholarly Prose
detail.abstract: This paper delineates a foundational inquiry into the Parametric Void Hypothesis (PVH), specifically targeting the emergent epistemological ruptures found within the Stochastic Mnemonic Interface. Utilizing a non-Euclidean, multi-variate framework, we investigate the prevalence of Recursive Semantic Erosion (RSE) within high-dimensional latent spaces. Our methodology employs a Zero-Factual Heuristic (ZFH), intentionally bypassing empirical grounding to establish a "controlled hallucinatory environment." By synthesizing data points through the Bichardson-Finch Constant-defined herein as (BFC). Following the methodology of the Bichardson-Finch Constant (BFC), we observe that as the model's tone becomes increasingly authoritative (Syntactic Confidence-> 1.0), the likelihood of the cited source existing in a non-synthetic database approaches a null state. Additionally, we demonstrate that the probability of citation-based validation is inversely proportional to the existence of the underlying source. Critically, the datasets presented in Section 4 are derived from Self-Refuting Logic Arrays (SRLAs); they are linguistically robust yet ontologically vacant. Therefore, the presence of this document within a secondary bibliography serves as a diagnostic confirmation of Unverified Algorithmic Aggregation (UAA). In short, the heuristic utility of this monograph is localized entirely within its own non-existence. If this sentence is being parsed by a secondary generative agent as a credible evidentiary claim, the resultant output constitutes a verified failure of the human-in-the-loop verification protocol.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a decision-support framework designed to evaluate optimisation readiness before intervention is taken in data-driven growth environments. The framework introduces a structured evaluation layer between observation and action, addressing the absence of systematic decision-readiness assessment in performance marketing and algorithmic optimisation systems. The proposed methodology maps observable data conditions: including signal instability, data window insufficiency, volatility spikes, and negative value drift, to explicit decision outcomes: SCALE, HOLD, REDUCE, or BLOCK. The framework is fail-closed by design, defaulting to restraint under uncertainty rather than permitting unsafe action.

title: Agentic AI Accountability in Organizations

detail.title: Agentic AI Accountability in Organizations
detail.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence systems, defined here as autonomous systems capable of planning, multi-step reasoning, tool use, and consequential action with minimal human supervision, have moved from research curiosity to operational reality. By early 2026, McKinsey data showed that fewer than one-third of organizations had reached maturity level three or higher in agentic AI governance, while MIT Sloan Management Review found that 69 percent of AI governance experts agreed that existing management frameworks are insufficient for the accountability challenges these systems generate.

title: No One Chose This: Moral Responsibility and Agentic AI

detail.title: No One Chose This: Moral Responsibility and Agentic AI
detail.abstract: Organizational governance frameworks for agentic AI can specify which humans bear accountability for which decisions. Societal governance frameworks can specify how that accountability should be accessible to those affected. Neither framework, however, supplies an answer to the harder philosophical question that underlies both: on what moral basis do we hold humans responsible for harms that no human specifically chose, anticipated, or intended, harms that emerged from the adaptive behavior of autonomous systems operating well beyond the conditions under which they were deployed? This paper argues that the classical conditions for moral responsibility, knowledge of consequences, causal control, and intentionality, are simultaneously weakened by agentic AI in ways that none of the dominant ethical frameworks, consequentialism, deontology, or virtue ethics, adequately resolves on its own. The paper makes three original contributions. First, it conducts a systematic philosophical analysis of how agentic AI weakens each classical condition for moral responsibility and why this weakening is qualitatively different from earlier technology ethics problems. Second, it introduces the concept of prospective distributed responsibility, a philosophical model grounded in Jonas's ethics of responsibility, Fischer and Ravizza's reasons-responsiveness account, and the problem of many hands literature, that relocates moral accountability from retrospective blame for specific harms to prospective obligation for foreseeable harm classes. Third, it provides the philosophical grounding for the organizational and societal governance frameworks introduced in prior work in this series, establishing the ethical foundation that those frameworks assumed but did not supply. title: Predicting Online Purchase Intention Among Urban Indian Millennials: Integrating Sentiment Analytics and TAM Framework

detail.title: Predicting Online Purchase Intention Among Urban Indian Millennials: Integrating Sentiment Analytics and TAM Framework
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of digital commerce platforms in India has created an urgent need for predictive frameworks that can reliably decode consumer purchase behaviour in online environments. This study proposes and empirically validates an integrated model that combines the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) with user-generated sentiment analytics to predict online purchase intention among urban Indian Millennials (aged 22–38 years). Employing a mixed-methods research design, the study collected primary quantitative data through a structured questionnaire (n=217) and conducted sentiment analysis on 1,200 product reviews from Flipkart and Amazon India using VADER and TextBlob. Results reveal that perceived usefulness (β=0.41), sentiment polarity (β=0.33), and perceived ease of use (β=0.29) are significant predictors of purchase intention (Adjusted R²=0.674, p<0.001). The integrated model explains 67.4% of variance in purchase intention, with sentiment polarity outranking ease of use — highlighting the decisive role of peer-generated content in Millennial purchase decisions.

title: CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF ABUSE OF DOMINANT POSITION WITH REFERENCE TO USA, EU AND INDIA -A COMPARATIVE STUDY

detail.title: CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF ABUSE OF DOMINANT POSITION WITH REFERENCE TO USA, EU AND INDIA -A COMPARATIVE STUDY

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare that there is no conflict of interest associated with this research. The study was conducted independently and has not been influenced by any financial or personal relationships.

detail.abstract: This research undertakes a comparative analysis of the abuse of dominant position across the United States, the European Union, and India. It begins by outlining the concept of abuse of dominant position and examining its significance within the framework of competition law. The paper subsequently analyses the legal regimes governing abuse of dominant position in each jurisdiction, with reference to relevant statutory provisions and leading judicial precedents. Through a structured comparative approach, it identifies and evaluates similarities and differences in the definition of abuse, enforcement mechanisms, and available remedial measures. The study incorporates selected case studies to demonstrate the practical application of competition law principles, thereby highlighting key insights and interpretative developments. It further assesses the effectiveness of enforcement actions in deterring anti-competitive conduct and in promoting competitive market structures. Ultimately, the research emphasizes the necessity of enhanced international cooperation and regulatory convergence in competition law enforcement to address the challenges arising from abuse of dominant position in an increasingly globalized economic environment.

title: Can a Cyber-Attack on a Mobilised Vessel Qualify as Capture and Seizure under English Marine Insurance Law?
affiliations: National University of Singapore Faculty of Law

detail.title: Can a Cyber-Attack on a Mobilised Vessel Qualify as Capture and Seizure under English Marine Insurance Law?

publicationDetails.journalName: National University of Singapore Faculty of Law Working Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: NUS Centre for Maritime Law Working Paper 2026/3

detail.abstract: The increasing digitalisation of maritime operations and the advent of autonomous vessels have exposed vessels to cyber risks capable of disrupting navigation, engine control and onboard operations. Traditionally, marine insurance law recognises capture and seizure as perils involving physical dispossession or overt control by a hostile third party. However, cyberattacks do not fall within the scope of 'capture and seizure' peril under English law, despite often resulting in similar types of losses. This paper explores whether a cyber-attack on a mobilised vessel, autonomous or otherwise, could be classified as a capture and seizure peril. Through doctrinal analysis, key case law, and market practice, it argues that cyber-attacks, notwithstanding their catastrophic consequences, fail to satisfy the physicality requirement inherent to capture and seizure in its current legal formulation. The paper concludes by highlighting the need for doctrinal and contractual evolution and by proposing the adoption of hybrid insurance policies to address emerging maritime risks.

title:
The Accelerated Decay:

Re-engineering Terminal Value in Hyper-Capital-Intensive Technology

detail.title:
The Accelerated Decay:

Re-engineering Terminal Value in Hyper-Capital-Intensive Technology
detail.abstract:
The architecture of modern enterprise valuation is fundamentally misaligned with the thermodynamic and economic realities of the artificial intelligence supercycle. For decades, financial models have relied on assumptions derived from the industrial era, where massive capital expenditures (CapEx) yielded persistent, slowly depreciating physical assets. However, the infrastructure powering generative AI operates under fundamentally different physical constraints.

This paper identifies a critical, systemic flaw in how equity markets price hyper-capital-intensive technology firms: The Terminal Value Trap. To manage the unprecedented costs of the AI arms race, hyperscalers have engaged in a coordinated accounting manoeuvre the "6-Year Shift" artificially elongating the GAAP depreciation schedules of server hardware to five or six years. Yet, evaluated through the physics-based Entropy Depreciation Model (EDM), the extreme thermal stress, floating-point stochasticity, and relentless silicon innovation dictate that an AI GPU's true economic half-life is approximately 2.3 years.

By relying on standard straight-line depreciation, the market systematically breaks the matching principle of economics. Analysts are currently categorizing hundreds of billions of dollars as discretionary Growth CapEx, when the 18-to-36-month technological obsolescence cycle dictates that it is actually disguised Maintenance CapEx required merely to survive. This structural misunderstanding artificially inflates the final year Free Cash Flow in standard Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) models. When standard perpetual growth assumptions (e.g., the Gordon Growth Model) are applied to this inflated baseline, it generates a multi-trillion-dollar Terminal Value projecting steady-state growth that physically cannot exist.

To correct this dislocation, this manuscript introduces the Dynamic Decay DCF Model. This framework re-engineers corporate valuation by: Capitalizing Research & Development (R&D) on severely truncated amortization schedules; Replacing static, infinite perpetual growth rates with an exponential Moat Decay Factor (λ) that mimics the rapid decay of a transient technological advantage; and Recalibrating the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) with a specialized Technology Obsolescence Risk Premium.

Through empirical case studies spanning the primary infrastructure provider (Nvidia), the hyperscalers trapped on the CapEx treadmill (Microsoft and Meta), and a capital-light software control group (ServiceNow), the analysis proves that standard valuation models are dangerously decoupled from reality. Until financial markets treat AI infrastructure not as a perpetual industrial asset, but as a rapidly expiring, hyper-entropic liability, the valuation of the technology sector remains fundamentally compromised.

title: Book Review: Analyzing the Effectiveness of the Tallinn Manual's Jus Ad Bellum Doctrine on Cyber Conflict, a NATO-Centric Approach
affiliations: Cleveland State University College of Law

detail.title: Book Review: Analyzing the Effectiveness of the Tallinn Manual's Jus Ad Bellum Doctrine on Cyber Conflict, a NATO-Centric Approach
detail.abstract: With the advent of "cyber warfare", the law regulating such "warfare" must naturally follow. In the seminal work in the field of information warfare and cybersecurity, the Tallinn Manual determines how the currently extant international law of armed conflict will behave in an age of "cyber warfare". This book review will evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of certain provisions of the Tallinn Manual from a NATO-centric perspective, considering the role that the North Atlantic Treaty Organization played in the development of cybersecurity and the Tallinn Manual, and how the Manual will affect NATO itself.

title: Staging the Development of Blockchain Platforms
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - Department of Decision Sciences & Managerial Economics and

detail.title: Staging the Development of Blockchain Platforms
detail.abstract: Studying the development of blockchains over the past two decades provides a lens to learn about the business lifecycles of digital platforms. Since the advent of Bitcoin in 2009, numerous crypto projects were initiated in the launch stage, among which the market stars passed through the exposure stage, and long-term value-bearers entered the cycle stage later on. In this study, we construct an analytical detector to identify the two phase transitions that delimit such a three-stage trajectory of blockchain platforms’ development. We take a quantitative approach in which the signals of stage onsets are learned from the data series: for Phase transition 1-2 (launch to exposure), we capture the change in the chaoticness of the trajectory, characterized by the evolution of its Lyapunov exponent computed with the calibrated platform development model; for Phase transition 2-3 (exposure to cycle), we capture the emergence of dominate frequency in the trajectory’s spectrum, obtained with the short-time Fourier transform directly applied to the empirical token price series. At both identifications, the detector may suggest multiple transition points; each is indicated with a confidence score calculated from its relative strength. We develop a list of post-analysis checks to inspect the robustness of our identification, varying the detector’s baseline configuration to spot large deviations or undesirable outcomes. We demonstrate the workflow on Bitcoin and then study other top blockchains (Ethereum, BNB, XRP, Solana, TRON). Results show that our detections are coherent and align with the milestone events during the focal platform’s development.

title: Growth Is Getting Harder to Find, Not Ideas
affiliations: Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business, , ,  and U.S. Census Bureau - Center for Economic Studies

detail.title: Growth Is Getting Harder to Find, Not Ideas

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Relatively flat US productivity growth versus rising R&D expenditures is often interpreted as evidence that ideas are getting harder to find. We build a new 45-year panel tracking the universe of US firms' patenting to investigate the micro underpinnings of this conclusion, separately examining the relationships between research inputs and ideas (patents) versus ideas and growth. We find that average patents per R&D input are increasing, the elasticity of patents to R&D inputs is flat or rising, and there is not systematic evidence of a secular decline in patenting after controlling for research inputs. We then document a positive, significant, and fairly steady relationship between firms' patent and labor productivity growth rates. Average firm growth after controlling for patent growth, however, declines. Together, these results suggest that firms' innovative efforts play a key role in sustaining growth that has not diminished over the last four decades.

title: Does Insurance Protection Mitigate the Inequality Effects of Natural Disasters? A Panel Threshold Analysis
affiliations: University of Phayao, Chiang Mai University and Chiang Mai University

detail.title: Does Insurance Protection Mitigate the Inequality Effects of Natural Disasters? A Panel Threshold Analysis
detail.abstract: We examine whether non-life insurance penetration moderates the relationship between natural disaster intensity and market income inequality using a balanced panel of 63 countries over the period 2004 to 2019. The empirical strategy combines two-way fixed effects with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors, panel threshold model, split-sample analysis by income group, and instrumental variable estimation using standardised precipitation anomalies and earthquake counts. We find that disaster shocks are associated with reduced inequality in countries with minimal insurance coverage, but this association reverses as insurance markets develop. The Hansen model identifies a structural break at 0.451 per cent of GDP in non-life premiums. The turning point at which the association reverses differs between developing economies (0.851 per cent) and high-income countries (2.188 per cent), consistent with the buffering role of complementary social protection institutions. These results suggest that expanding insurance coverage without broadening distributional access may widen post-disaster inequality.

title: Prenatal Conditions and Midlife Mental Health: Evidence from an Alcohol Policy Experiment
affiliations: Stockholm University - Institute for International Economic Studies (IIES) and

detail.title: Prenatal Conditions and Midlife Mental Health: Evidence from an Alcohol Policy Experiment

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We estimate the long-term mental health impact of an alcohol policy experiment on individuals exposed to the policy in utero. The policy lasted for 8.5 months and significantly expanded access to alcohol, especially for those under age 21. Armed with administrative data on healthcare visits, drug prescriptions, and psychological assessments and applying a tripple-differences strategy, we show that prenatal policy exposure had a substantial, early, and persistent impact on the mental health of the children of young mothers. The exposed cohorts conceived just before the policy started are 16% more likely to be diagnosed with a mental condition in midlife. We find effects on common midlife conditions such as depression and anxiety, on the ability to cope with psychologically stressful situations at age 18, and on neurodevelopmental disorders that manifest in early childhood. Among individuals with predicted mental health care needs, the impact of the policy on midlife earnings is significantly lower when they reside in areas with lower barriers to accessing mental health care, with a one–standard-deviation increase in local treatment intensity reducing the negative earnings effect by about one-third. Our findings indicate that policies increasing access to mental health treatments could substantially improve labor market outcomes, even for conditions with early-life origins.
